paragraphs.text: First Discourse

An exposition that explains the commandments and shows what each commandment refers to in its own context; and why and to whom our Lord Jesus Christ gave the greater and the lesser commandments; and how a person can distinguish perfection from righteousness: through the greater commandments one becomes perfect, and through the lesser ones one becomes righteous.

Brothers and fathers, our brothers and sisters in Christ, we ought to ask one another about the words of our Lord, as the apostle said: “Seek them today and tomorrow and forever and ever.” And again he said: “Inquire among yourselves every day, as long as the day is called ‘Today’”— that is, until your departure—so that you may be built up through them and may build up your brothers and sisters. And again he said: “Discern and see what the acceptable and perfect will of God is.” And again he said: “Discern and recognize the things that are modest, humble, and fitting, and hold fast to them.” And again he said: “When two or three passages of Scripture are read, and so on, let the one who interprets explain them”—that is, someone who has come to share in the Spirit. And again he said that the fruits of the Spirit, taken together, are goodness and humility, endurance and patience, kindness and gentleness, joy and peace with everyone, and love toward everyone.

We must therefore seek the truth, so that the truth itself may set us free, as our Lord said. That is, we must humble ourselves and make our minds contrite, for these are the sacrifices of God, and this is his will; and he reveals his truth to anyone who is like this. For there are people who have humbled themselves a little, but not before everyone, and have not made their minds contrite. For this reason they have not known the truth as it is. And there are those who have made their minds contrite but have not humbled themselves beneath everything on earth. For this reason they have not known. For pride opposes the truth, preventing us from knowing it, and despondency opposes humility, preventing us from perceiving it. For no one knows the will of God from ink, unless they have entered into fellowship with him in spirit. That is, unless a person becomes the gentlest and humblest of all people, as he said: “Whom will I look upon and dwell in, except one who is gentle and humble in spirit and keeps my word?” For this reason, no one knows how to understand Scripture and explain the commandments except someone who has entered into fellowship with God in spirit. For we have all run after service to the body, and not service to the spirit, and there is no one among us who hates his own life and takes up the cross, humbling himself—that is, having nowhere on earth to lay his head. Instead, even the diligent person among us gives alms from his possessions—things that people of the world ought to do and live by. And let us leave everything and walk in the humility and self-emptying of our Lord, which are great commandments, whose nature we are explaining. But we observe the small commandments, which are vegetables and milk, and not the great ones, which are solid food. For this reason we do not know how to distinguish the great commandments from the small ones, or the service above from the service below, or the food that consists of vegetables for the sick, or milk for infants, or what permission has been granted to one person alone but has not been granted to another. Likewise, we do not know through which commandments a person receives the Paraclete, or through which a person is nourished like someone who is sick, or through which a person grows like an infant, or which commandments are addressed to everyone, through which a person becomes blessed by the Father through the pledge of the Spirit.

For the gift of the Paraclete is one thing, and the blessing of a small pledge is another. And we do not know the commandments addressed to each particular person alone, which another person cannot put into practice, or which ordinances do not give a person life when he observes them, but instead lessen his punishment. It is not right to present them either to the perfect or to the righteous. And we do not know how one person becomes greater than another through the Spirit, the Paraclete, or how one sick person is better nourished than another through a diet of vegetables, or how one infant thrives more than another on milk, or how one blessed person becomes greater than another through these commandments addressed to everyone, or how a person serves our Lord bodily, or how a person serves our Lord spiritually, or how one person's punishment becomes lighter than his neighbor's through the judgment of condemnation given to them, in accordance with what they themselves desired in their hardness of heart, and they fell from perfection and from the righteousness that is below perfection.

Our father Adam fell from the rank of perfection and remained in the rank of righteousness, which does not do to anyone what it hates, and just as it wishes people to act toward it, so it acts toward the people who encounter it. But we have fallen even from this rank, for we do to one another what we hate. Everything you do not want your neighbor to do to you, you do to him. And you do not act toward everyone as you want everyone to act toward you. Now I, like everyone else, want people to do good to us. Therefore, by this very fact that we do not do good to everyone, including those who have harmed us, we fall short of righteousness. Now I, like everyone else, hate anyone harming us, even someone whom we have harmed. Therefore, if we have harmed someone, Or to the one who harmed us: we have fallen away from righteousness, because we have done to others what we ourselves hate. And what we want others to do for us, we are unwilling to do for them. But we will explain righteousness in its proper place. Now let us distinguish the commandments: how they do not know how many degrees there are in each of these foods and services, nor how high the highest degree is, nor how deep the lowest degree is. Nor have we understood that there are many places in the Father's house, as our Lord said.

Let us therefore begin to explain what we said above, each commandment in its proper place, as our Lord shows us. For these are the commandments spoken to particular individuals. It was to Abraham alone that God said: “Sacrifice to me your son, whom you love dearly.” No one else can carry out this commandment today without dying, unless someone takes this commandment as a pattern for himself: to love God more than his son, and not to value his son as highly as God's teaching.

Again, it was to Hosea that the Lord said, “Take a prostitute as your wife.” No one today can make use of this commandment and marry a woman who commits adultery with others every day. Even if he does marry her, he marries her only after she has left the street. But the Lord permitted Hosea to marry her while she was still standing in the street, so that through her he might rebuke the Israelites who had prostituted themselves: when they came to judge him for marrying a prostitute, he would judge them and condemn them to death: “If you judge me for marrying a prostitute at the Lord's command, how much more will the Lord condemn you to death, because you have committed adultery, prostituted yourselves with idols, and abandoned the commandment of the Lord your God!”

The forgiveness granted to just one person was that granted to the robber alone, without deeds. No one else is forgiven in this way without deeds, unless he repents. We explain other commandments elsewhere. But as for how this man was forgiven, if you want to understand: the king came to his door without his knowing it; he presented a petition to him, and he forgave him. Our Lord has authority over what is his own, and to you he said, “Repent, and I will forgive you.” Thus he showed the riches of his mercy in that one man, to encourage those who repent and keep the commandments in their repentance: how abundant his mercies are, since he had mercy and forgave without deeds! Here ends the first discourse, on distinguishing the commandments.
The Second Discourse: On Those Who Want to Become Perfect

Now let us distinguish the great commandments through which a person becomes perfect, and separate them from vegetables and milk: those which our Lord and his apostles gave to the perfect, and did not write of themselves and for themselves. It is not that we learned from our Lord and his apostles to write these things for them, from them and to them [?]. But because interpreters today are scarce—hardly more than a few individuals— we were compelled to write them down so that even children might see them, and everyone might struggle to enter through the narrow gate of perfection and inherit, below it, a place of righteousness. Anyone who does not push himself should at least inherit a place below perfection: let him be well nourished on the gruel of the sick, or grow well fed on the milk of infants, or become blessed through these commandments that are addressed to everyone—that is, become righteous. And if he falls away from righteousness, let his good deeds outnumber his evil deeds, so that he may escape Gehenna and live, without slipping and descending into torment. Or, if he does descend into torment, let his torment be eased a little.

To those who wish to become perfect, however, our Lord said this: “If someone strikes you on your cheek, offer him the other one and pray for him, and you will be perfect. If someone forces you to go one mile, go two with him. If someone takes your tunic by force, let him take your cloak too. Love whoever hates you, bless whoever curses you, and pray for whoever abuses and persecutes you. And you are to say, ‘Our Father in heaven, forgive us as we have forgiven.’” For he said, “When you offer your thanksgiving to God, forgive your brother and be reconciled with him, and then offer your offering. Do not judge,” he said, “so that you will not be judged; and do not condemn, so that you will not be condemned. Who,” he said, “appointed me ruler and judge over you? And if I do judge, my judgment is true. I did not come to judge the world, but to teach them humbly, give them life, and be an example to my disciples, so that they too might act as I do.

This is how I teach those who wish to become perfect: a good tree produces good fruit. You,” he said, “must overcome evil with every kind of goodness toward everyone. And I,” he said, “have nowhere on earth to rest my head. Imitate me and remain in my love, just as I,” he said, “have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. By this,” he said, “everyone will know that you are my disciples: that you love one another. I give you a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you. And you are to bless and not curse. Do not,” he said, “call one another ‘madman,’ ‘empty-head,’ ‘fool,’ or ‘loathsome.’ Otherwise you will not attain perfection.”

“Anyone who curses,” he said, “or becomes angry, or has a fault and does not root it out, does not attain perfection. Anyone who does not,” he said, “leave everything, take up his cross, and follow me—that is, follow my way of life—is not worthy of me.” That is, he will not inherit the kingdom of heaven with those who bear the cross. “Anyone who looks back,” he said, “is not fit for me.” That is, anyone who abandons these great, humble, and self-emptying commandments and descends to the lesser ones. “Whoever hates his own life is the one who loves me.” That is, whoever does not love his life in this passing world. “Whoever finds his life will lose it.” That is, he must bring it to an end and make it abstain from the world. “Whoever does not forgive seventy times seven is not worthy of me.” That is, whoever demands an accounting for offenses, even a little, does not become perfect. “Whoever does not wash his enemies’ feet, knowing that they will hand him over to be killed, as I did for Iscariot, is not worthy of me.” That is, he does not become perfect, nor does he become a brother, mother, children, and sisters to me. “Whoever does not go to someone who needs him, as I went to John, who needed me, does not become my disciple.” That is, he does not become great. “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.” That is, when he is rejected before God. “Give to everyone who asks you.” That is, give what you have. If you possess earthly things, give some of them. And if you possess heavenly things, give some of them to whoever asks you. Bodily envy belongs to someone who withholds bodily things, and spiritual envy belongs to someone who withholds the word from someone capable of receiving it.

“Keep praying and do not grow weary, so that you do not enter into temptations and afflictions.” “So that I would not boast because of the abundance of revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan to strike me, so that I would not say that I had grown greatly or had attained my goal.” “Do not worry about what you will eat or what you will drink.” That is, “Do not work for the sake of your stomach.” Those who keep these commandments and are born anew “are like the wind, which blows wherever it wishes.” That is, they are in heaven with our Lord, and there is no compulsion governing them, because they have overcome the outward battle, in that they have no dispute or battle with other people; and they have removed their inward fear, in that they fight only against sin, not against their fellow human beings, even if those people kill them. For this reason, they have rescued their will and their freedom from the one who wants to subject them to slavery. They gaze upon our Lord in the spirit in this world as in a mirror, and when they depart from their bodies, they see him face to face, as from glory to glory. Because they have closed their eyes and stopped their ears against evil things, “they see the king in his beauty in distant lands.”

“Consider everyone superior to yourself, and become all things to all people.” “Anyone who does not follow in my footsteps and enter the houses of tax collectors and prostitutes and teach them as I have shown him does not become perfect.” “Let your humility be known to all people, and greet everyone with a holy and pure kiss.” “Blessed are those who are pure in heart and those who make peace with everyone.” That is, they should not only make peace with their own enemies, but should also reconcile other enemies who are far away from them. In this way they will gain the trees of Paradise above the heavens, from which Adam was commanded to eat and enjoy himself. But he listened to the evil one, who brought him down, and the gates of Paradise were shut in his face until Jesus chose to open them and broke down also the barrier of hostility, reconciled creation to himself, and made peace through the blood of his cross with everything on earth and everything in heaven.

The great trees of the spiritual Paradise, from which those who keep the great commandments eat, are these: faith, meekness, humility, love, hope, truth, and holiness in our Lord; with our Lord they eat and enjoy themselves. This is the conclusion of my words: no one should call anyone a pagan or unclean, as Simon was told. These commandments were given to anyone who wishes to be perfect, along with others like them throughout the whole New Testament. Anyone who wishes to become perfect should practice these commandments and leave aside those other commandments that are vegetables and milk, like a child who leaves his mother's milk as soon as he grows a little stronger. These include: “Accuse your brother in court,” and “Consider him a pagan,” which is contrary to “Do not judge” and “Forgive him however much he wrongs you.” For these lesser commandments and others like them, which are given like milk to infants and like vegetables to the sick, keep a person from ever becoming a grown man or getting well. That is why I have taken care to distinguish them: there are people who wish to become perfect, but the evil one surrounds them and blocks their way with lesser commandments and does not allow them to become perfect, because he makes them think that if they rise above the small commandments, they are sinning. They do not know that if they rise in love even above these great commandments, it is very good for them.

For if someone wishes, he can rise in love not only above these small commandments, but also above these great ones. For our Lord told him, “If someone strikes you on your cheek, offer him the other one.” Let him offer his back as well, and then he rises above the person who offers only his cheek. Let him not demand any reckoning at all for a wrong, and then he rises above the person who forgives seven times seventy. Let him go an additional mile, and then he has humbled himself beyond what Jesus commanded him. For he told him, “If someone forces you to go one mile, go two more with him.” Let him do likewise with these small commandments, come to these great ones, and peacefully make disciples of adulterers, and then he rises above the person who does not eat bread with them or associate with them. Let him teach his brother privately, between the two of them, not to sin, and then he rises above those who judge him and expose him publicly. In this way he rises above the small commandments, stands firm in the great ones, and becomes perfect. Let the person who stands firm in the great commandments, which are humble, humble himself much more than the great commandments require. And look, he was glorified with our Lord and will become greater than the one who stands among them. For one person can become greater than another through the Spirit, the Paraclete, because he humbles himself far beyond what he was commanded. Our Lord also said, “If I, who have neither sinned nor done wrong, and am your Lord and your Master, humbled myself in this way, how much more ought you, who are servants and sinners, to humble yourselves! For I humbled myself before those who did evil to me. How much more ought you to humble yourselves before evil people!” End of the second discourse.
The Third Discourse: On Bodily and Spiritual Service

Even through vegetables and milk, one person becomes greater than another. Through these commandments given to everyone, too, one person becomes greater than another, just as it is in spiritual service: through the great and the lowly commandments, the person who humbles himself more becomes greater. So it is also in bodily service: whoever gives generously, like Abraham, to everyone in need, without asking who is worthy and who is unworthy, but welcomes them as righteous people and prophets, even though they are not prophets or righteous people. Our Lord swore with an “Amen” that such a person would not lose his reward. And he should let his love shine upon the good and the evil, like the Father’s sun upon everyone, good and evil, but especially upon those who build others up and reveal the truth, who belong to the household of faith. For it says, “Do good to everyone, especially to those who belong to the household of faith.” For if he gives to evil people, how much more to good people! And if, for those who have possessions and work, when they are encountered as guests or on the road, you are obliged to welcome them and give them rest, how much more for someone who has nothing and does not work because he is occupied with the teaching our Lord commanded him: “No one who works and becomes entangled in worldly affairs can please the one who chose him.” For our Lord’s servant is always before him, as he said: “Where I am, there my servant will also be, with me and before me.”

For one service is greater than another, just as one portion is greater than another. For the portion of the perfect is greater than the portion inherited by the righteous who come after the perfect. These righteous people fall short in various things because they have not attained all our Lord’s commandments. And they have not done his entire great, acceptable, and perfect will, because they have not emptied themselves and consecrated themselves. But our Lord said to these righteous people, “If you do not attain perfection, feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, bring relief to the distressed, visit prisoners, and meet their needs.” And they took strangers in. Our Lord said to them, “Whatever you do for these people, you have done for me.” “For this reason,” he says, “come, inherit the kingdom.” Have they, then, become completely perfect— these people who are involved in the comings and goings of this world? Or which of those who welcome our Lord in hunger and nakedness are not troubled by shortcomings of one kind or another, because they are occupied with earthly things, and cannot grasp the whole truth because they are occupied with cares? Does the one whom they welcomed, then, wrong them when he says to them, “Come, inherit the kingdom”? For our Lord certainly did not say, “Everyone who does not become perfect will not live.” Rather, he says, “He cannot become a disciple of this perfection that I have shown, nor can he attain that portion from which Adam fell long ago.”

But he inherits the remaining portion that is here, if he is upright in earthly matters, his good deeds are many, and he harms no one. In this way he is righteous. And if he transgresses and does harm here and there, but his good deeds outnumber his evil deeds, mercy is shown to him, and he is delivered and lives. For they do not go to that great portion which Jesus has prepared for the perfect, so that they may be with him in glory that does not pass away, but only those who become perfect and then leave this world without shortcomings. For he says, “As you are found, so you will be led away.” Because the athletes stand in battle and in the contest, striking and receiving blows in it, our Lord said to them: “After you have struck and received blows, if you win and come up out of the contest and receive the crown, and leave this world wearing that crown, your shortcomings will not be remembered against you. Rather, as you are found victorious, so you will be led away, wearing your crowns.” Even though, then, the righteous who do good deeds do not inherit that portion belonging to the perfect, because they have not parted with their possessions and their wives, they nevertheless inherit a portion below it, one smaller than it.

For our Lord said, “Because I was hungry and you fed me, and I was thirsty and you gave me a drink, and I was a stranger and you took me in, and I was sick and was in prison and you came to me, for this reason, come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you.” For the perfect uproot all their shortcomings through the power of our Lord, because they have been patient and sought him. And he quickly grants their requests and fulfills their petitions. For our Lord promised, “I will quickly fulfill their petition.” And indeed, their request continued throughout all the days of their lives, because they kept our Lord’s commandments and overcame their evil thoughts, which fought against them every day, from within and from without. And they persevered patiently in their requests until they overcame and were crowned and received the crown of victory. Then they left this world and went to be with our Lord in that portion which he prepared for them, because it is a lofty rank. And it is prepared for those who have served spiritually in the Spirit, in the great commandments, in the service of the Spirit, and in perfection, and have rooted out all their shortcomings through the power of our Lord, as is written above. But concerning those whose deeds are all evil, the apostle said this: Those who practice these deeds of the flesh have no inheritance in the kingdom of God: sexual immorality, singing, murder, drunkenness, adultery, and theft. And because these people do nothing good, it is clear that they will inherit neither the kingdom nor even their own lives.

But if there is someone who does good things from time to time and occasionally does what is right, the apostle said this: “On that day of judgment he will repay everyone according to their deeds, whether good or evil.” As for my statement that one portion is higher than another, our Lord made both known when he said: “Whoever does not give up everything he has, take up his cross, follow me, and imitate me is not worthy of me.”

Here he indicated the great and exalted place. And when he said, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you,” here he indicated something lower than that first portion. “I was a stranger,” he said, “and you took me in.” Who takes in strangers when he owns no house? As he said: “Free yourself from buildings and possessions.” “I was hungry,” he said, “and you fed me.” Who feeds the hungry when he has stripped himself of everything and owns nothing, as our Lord said: “Whoever owns anything is not worthy of me”? Is it not clear, then, that he is proclaiming an inheritance smaller than that first one? “I was naked,” he said, “and you clothed me.” Who clothes the naked when he has stripped himself of everything and owns nothing? And if there is someone who owns nothing, but is a provider for the poor and bears the burden in our Lord, and that of the rest of the poor— the sick, the naked, and strangers—because he takes from those who have and gives to those who have nothing, that is good and fitting. Yet even this person has not stripped himself of everything according to the word of our Lord, who said: “Do not even concern yourself with your own life, thinking about food and clothing, but give everything you have to the poor in one day or in one month, and take up your cross and follow me.” But even though he owns nothing, if he takes from one person and gives to another, he too remains involved in the taking up and laying down, the receiving and giving, of this world. And he has not stripped himself of everything, as our Lord said: “Rise above the earth and do not be anxious.” And as the apostle said: “Seek the things above, and set your minds on the things above.”

For he ought to have taught the owners of possessions to keep doing good. They themselves, from their possessions, with their own hands, to everyone in need and distress, as the apostle said: “Teach the rich in this world to be ready for good works and to store up treasures for themselves in heaven. And their trust must not be in wealth that passes away.” This, then, is what someone caught up in the concerns of receiving and giving ought to do: He should teach those who own possessions to give to the poor themselves, with their own hands, from what they own. He himself should remain devoted to prayer, petition, ministry, reading, and the word of God. And he should be available and ready for everyone who needs instruction and the word of our Lord’s truth. For our Lord himself and his apostles acted in this way. They appointed ministers for the sick, the naked, strangers, prisoners, and all who were in need, while they themselves were to minister the word of God and prayer. This is how someone takes up the cross, receives the Paraclete, and becomes perfect: by having no involvement at all with visible things. But if he loves these things, he is righteous but not perfect, because he has not been freed from visible things. If, however, those rich people do not see where someone is in distress, he should merely show them where there are people in need. This is better than taking it into his own house and falling into great turmoil, with many people grumbling against him and embittering his spirit, and not allowing him to become perfect. For the person who has been provided for rejoices, while the one whom he has not had the means to provide for— that person complains against him and grumbles, “He has received something but gives us nothing!” And they do harm to the person who involves himself with visible things. Instead, let the perfect giver empty himself of his possessions, and concern himself with people who lack knowledge of our Lord, and with all humanity: how they may live and how they may become perfect. Let him remain devoted to prayer, supplication, and the ministry of the word of God for all humanity and on his own behalf. In this way he will benefit everyone, including himself, through prayer and exhortation to a new life.

For someone who takes up the cross and teaches the word cannot receive from one person and give to another, or buy and sell. He cannot even carry his own burden, unless some matter presses him very urgently. For our Lord said, “Do not worry about your body, what you will wear, or about yourself, what you will cover yourself with.” How can someone who takes up the cross and is commanded not to worry take upon himself the burden of other people’s visible things? The person who takes up the cross, then, instead of taking on visible things, takes on the burden of praying for all humanity, and of exhorting and teaching everyone with humility, both good and bad, and of reconciling them to one another and making peace among them, if they are willing to listen to him. Whether they listen to him or do not listen to him, he is obliged to teach everyone humbly, both the worthy and the unworthy. For this is how our Lord wants him to teach even those who kill him, and to pray for everyone who harms him and everyone who loves him.

There are people who hunger for this visible bread, and there are those who hunger for righteousness and life. And there are those who are stripped of invisible clothing, of light, of life, and of the kingdom. Therefore, people who possess visible wealth clothe those who are visibly naked and satisfy those who are visibly hungry. And those who live in the Spirit and possess something invisible to bodily eyes clothe people who are stripped of clothing that does not pass away, and of light and life, through their good teaching, which they sow in receptive hearing, as it is written: “Rivers of living water will flow from within those who believe in Jesus, keep all his commandments, and do his entire will.” For this reason they satisfy people who hunger for righteousness and true food, and present every person perfect in Christ, just as our Lord had it written for us and taught us about perfection. For he said, “Be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect,” and as the apostle wrote: “This is my labor and my struggle, through the activity that works mightily in me by the power of our Lord: to present every person perfect in Christ.”

These words of our Lord therefore apply to two kinds of people: “I was hungry and you fed me, and I was naked and you clothed me.” For there is someone who thirsts for living water, the water of which our Lord said that whoever drinks it will not thirst. And there is someone who is sick in body, and someone who is sick in conscience; there is someone who is held captive bodily by other people, and someone who is held captive in his spirit by Satan and does not receive the Spirit of the Lord, as it is written. And there is someone who is estranged from humanity, and someone who is estranged from God. There are people who serve those who need bodily things, and there are those who serve those who need spiritual things. These people who serve in the Spirit are very great. Now those who bear the burden of the needy and open the door for others, because they take from those who have and give to those who have nothing, and also those who do good with their own possessions— both these groups, if they keep themselves from every evil and do not do to others anything they themselves would hate, but instead do to others as they want people to do to them—those who live in this way are the ones blessed by the Father, those to whom the Son said, “Come, inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you.” which is below that good portion that our Lord has prepared for those who took up their crosses, freed themselves from everything visible, followed him, and imitated him—our Lord—and his apostles. And all this is because these blessed ones of the Father were unable to take up their crosses, because they did not free themselves from everything they possessed, but occupied themselves with taking up and laying down the things of this world. For this reason they were held back and could not receive the Spirit, the Advocate, grasp the whole truth, and become perfect. For whoever takes up the cross is raised above what is visible. For just as our Lord, when he took up his visible cross, was raised above the earth and everything in it, so whoever takes up his hidden cross is freed from the earth, its work, all its toil, and all its worries. For just as a person is bound to the visible cross while alive, so, while alive and walking on this earth, he is bound in spirit to that hidden cross.

For there are people who are devoid of the pledge of the Spirit, and because the Spirit of God is not in them, they are rejected, as the apostle said: “If the Spirit of God is in you; otherwise, you are rejected.” And there are people who have within them something from God and something from Satan. They do good things through the pledge of the Holy Spirit that is in them, but they transgress and do evil things because of the pledge of sin that is in them. And every day that pledge of the Holy Spirit urges them to turn away from evil things, do good things, stand against the evil one, and overcome him. If they overcome him, they become righteous; and if they further wish to rise higher, they become perfect. But if they remain as they are, on that day of judgment they will be repaid for their deeds, both evil and good; or mercy will be shown to them, and they will be delivered and live. And there are people who have been cleansed of Satan’s pledge and are filled with the Spirit of God all their days and all their hours, as our Lord said to whoever takes up his cross as he did: “Look, I am sending you the Spirit, the Advocate, to be with you until the end of the world.” These people who are like this belong to our Lord at all times, and our Lord is in them. But whoever does not do even one good thing, either with his body or in his heart, and does not even think anything good, is devoid of God and his grace.

For just as evil thoughts arise in the heart from Satan, so good thoughts also arise in it from God. And whoever does evil things and good things has within him something from God and something from Satan. But whoever does every good thing, is stripped of possessions and chaste, and loves everyone, even those who kill him, without falling short, has been made perfect by our Lord and filled with his Spirit. And whoever has been filled with the Spirit of Christ does every good thing and thinks good things about everyone, both the good and the evil, and there is no deficiency in him. And if any shortcoming is found in him, he struggles against it and roots it out, and he rises above evil things even while he is still in the world. And when he departs this life in a state of perfection, he is with our Lord and sees him face to face. For there are people who have within them a little from our Lord, a small blessing. This small share is called a pledge from God. And there are those who have received the gift that is greater than all gifts. This is what is called the Spirit, the Paraclete. Through this they are perfected and are also filled with God, and Christ dwells fully within them. A person who has the Spirit, the Paraclete, within him is therefore recognized by this: people see that it teaches him to love all human beings, including his enemies and those who kill him, and to pray earnestly for them.

For there are great gifts and there are small gifts; there is a pledge and there is a blessing, just as the Lord said concerning Miriam and Aaron that their gifts were smaller than those of Moses, and just as those seventy men who received a share of Moses’ gift were lesser than he. And just as Martha’s share was smaller than Mary’s. Look, the Lord spoke with all these people, and they had within them a pledge from him, but not as Moses and Mary, the sister of Lazarus, had. But whoever does not do even one good thing has received no pledge within him from the Spirit of the Lord, and he is rejected. If, then, we take up his cross in humility and holiness, we are exalted after our humiliation, just as he was exalted after his voluntary humiliation, so that he might be an example for us, and as the apostle said, “Imitate me, my brothers, just as I imitate Christ.” Thus Mary’s share was greater than Martha’s, as our Lord testified about her: “Mary has chosen the good share for herself.” Mary took up the cross, which is humility, [?] the great commandments, and she died to the world and its needs, and lived in our Lord in spiritual things. She served our Lord in spirit, was bound to him, and praised him all day long, as the Spirit said concerning spiritual people: “We have praised you, God, all day long.” And she instructed and taught and made women disciples for our Lord, women who praised and served alongside those disciples who received the Paraclete and served our Lord in perfection. Martha, however, at that time served our Lord by providing clothing and food for him and the company with him, while she had a house and possessions, like Abraham. Although she was righteous in her conduct, she had not taken up the cross.

Therefore no one receives the Paraclete as long as he serves in a bodily way, engaging in buying and selling, with his mind bound to the earth, unless he closes his eyes to the earth’s evils and to all its beauty, which is opposed to perfection. For the perfect person is a stranger to the luxuries of kingdoms and to those close to them. Therefore, whoever has not become perfect is far below the one who has been nailed to the cross and whose hands and feet have been bound, and who cannot occupy himself with earthly things, but looks upward, seeks what is above, and thinks about what is above, where Christ sits in the heights at the right hand of God, and who becomes dead to the world while still alive. For those who occupy themselves with this world and use its resources to provide for the hungry and the naked, while harming no one, are alive, but they cannot receive the Paraclete. Instead, the pledge of the Holy Spirit increases in them. For those who have come to live in the Spirit, our Lord asks this of them: that they be bound to him, continually thinking of him, through the sacrifice of conscience, thanksgiving, prayer, and humility, while worn down, exhorting everyone with discernment, as the Spirit teaches them, so that they may make disciples of people with humility and make everyone servants of God according to each one's ability. Someone who can serve in the Spirit they make a servant of the Spirit; and someone who can serve bodily they teach how to serve our Lord bodily. Bodily servants are those who serve the needy with food and clothing. Servants of the Spirit, however, are those who explain the commandments, teach the true word, and show everyone how to live and how to grow.

Therefore, let no one blame those who have nothing and do not perform visible acts of charity, because this is not their service, nor does our Lord demand it of them. Rather, they are servants of the word and of prayer, just as the apostles appointed seven servants to oversee food and provisions, while they themselves taught the word of God. Even among these providers, anyone who wishes to discipline himself and empty himself comes to the greater commandments and stands in perfection, as Stephen did, who was one of the seven servants. He emptied himself and received the Paraclete, and they killed him while he was teaching the word, not while he was performing visible acts of charity. For a person can make many servants of visible acts of charity, but a single servant in the Spirit, who teaches people the truth and is emptied of the world, comes into being only with difficulty and through much toil. He carries out the greater commandments and teaches people to do the same, and he becomes great. And if he does more than he was commanded, he is greatly praised by our Lord. For our Lord, too, wishes to make these people servants in the Spirit. For our Lord has given these bodily servants an opportunity to perform visible acts of charity and to live through them. It is not because God needs them. For he who feeds everything could himself feed everyone in need, as he does those worlds above, which neither toil nor labor for clothing and food. But they praise the radiance of that majesty and do his will. And God wanted all human beings to praise him in this way, without toil, if Adam had remained upright. But neither are his children upright. We provoke our Creator every day, and our wrongdoing increases.

For those who serve in the spirit are greater than those who serve in bodily matters, just as Simon was greater than Tabitha, who served our Lord in bodily matters. Although she was a daughter of the kingdom, she was lesser than Simon and his inheritance, as shown by his praying and raising her. Nevertheless, at that time Tabitha's service and Martha's were the same, and Simon's and Mary's were the same. For Simon and Mary served our Lord in the spirit, while Martha and Tabitha served our Lord in bodily matters. When Simon raised her and saw that at that time she did not have the strength for the higher service, he took her by the hand and entrusted needy people to her, for her to feed and clothe, so that she would be a daughter of the kingdom below the perfect. For spiritual people deal discerningly with everyone. Whoever pushes himself to rise to perfection, they show him perfection and make him a servant in the spirit, in the service that is spirit and life. But whoever does not push himself and seek this portion, they make him a servant of bodily things—that is, of what is visible, in a visible service. The one who serves in the spirit serves what is invisible to bodily eyes, but is visible to the soul in the spirit, through the spiritual eye itself. Yet it is easy for anyone, if he is willing to push himself, to empty himself, humble himself, rise to the great rank, and become perfect, and then humble himself still more and be glorified with our Lord. The third discourse, on bodily and spiritual service, is finished.
The Fourth Discourse: On Vegetables for the Sick

Now that we have explained the commandments of perfection and the service below perfection, let us now explain the food—that is, the vegetables—that upsets the sick. For just as a sick person is disgusted by every kind of food, so someone whose conscience is sick is constantly disturbed and lax, because of anyone in whom he sees a few shortcomings. And just as that sick person is disgusted by good foods, so a sick conscience grumbles at good conduct. He does not examine the beam in his own eye, but condemns someone who is like himself. He does not rebuke and correct him with compassion, but utterly crushes him with judgment. For this reason our Lord, knowing that the one who judges is himself lax and takes no care for himself, and has no compassion for his brother, said to him, “When you see that your brother has sinned, admonish him with love.” But if he does not listen to you, and you cannot close your eyes to judgment, and you cannot shut your ears so as not to hear evil about your brother, approach him again, just between you and him, and rebuke him. For love covers a multitude of sins, but hatred stirs up judgment. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, and you cannot leave your brother alone, approach him in the presence of one other person. But if he is not persuaded, and you do not keep to yourself, approach him in the presence of two. But if he feels no remorse, and you cannot stop reproaching him, rebuke him before as many as three. But if you do not attend to yourself, and he feels no shame, shame him before the whole church. But if he will not listen even to the church, leave him to his reproach and leave him alone. Enough—go no further. Consider him like the rest of the rebellious pagans, whom you cannot rebuke, and do not speak empty words. Just as you urge a pagan to become a Christian whenever he meets you, so you should also keep urging this brother of yours. Do not become his enemy, lest he be swallowed up by Satan. Just as, with solid food, one person grows more than another who is greatly weakened, so also with this diet for the sick, one person is healthier than another.

Therefore, someone who rebukes his brother privately and, if his brother listens to him, makes him a disciple, but leaves him alone if he does not listen, is healthier than someone who exposes him before one other person. Someone who exposes him before one other person, gains him if he listens, but otherwise leaves him alone, is healthier than someone who exposes him before two. Someone who rebukes and exposes him before three is gentler than someone who judges and exposes him before the whole church. But if malice will not let him leave the other person alone, and he strikes him or drives him away, he falls away from righteousness, because he hates having anyone strike him when he does wrong, yet he strikes someone else who has done wrong. This is the extent of the discernment of those who eat vegetables. But if they too wish to admonish others, as I am writing to them, let them admonish them privately, just between themselves and those people. If those people listen to them, they have gained their brothers. Otherwise, if they refrain from reproaches and judgment, they will quickly advance to solid food. They will become healthy and perfect, and will attend to themselves so that they do not sin. What business do they have judging servants who are not their own? If those servants fall, they fall before their own master; and if they stand, they stand before their own master. Indeed, they will stand, for it is within Jesus’ power to raise them up, just as he raised up Paul. For how do you know whether this person whom you want to persecute and judge is a second Paul?

But listen to me, my brother: do not be harsh with anyone even when you admonish him privately, lest you suffer great harm. Instead, admonish him humbly, gently, and kindly. For whoever wants to become perfect acts as it is written: “If someone is caught in wrongdoing, admonish him in a gentle spirit.” And it says that the strong must bear the weaknesses of the weak and be patient with everyone.

Listen to me, my brother. What I advise you is for your good, and I advise myself along with you: when we see someone who has become defiled, let us speak to him this way, in private: “My brother, blessed are the holy and pure, who see our Lord Jesus and are not ashamed in his presence, and who are delivered from everything evil and abstain from the world and its desires.” When you see someone who is harsh, say to him: “My brother, blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the land of the living.” And say to him: “My brother, if there is harshness in us, let us humble ourselves from now on, and let us become holy and run in the great and humble commandments, so that we may comprehend and know what the height and depth are, and the length and breadth, together with all the saints.” And when you see someone who has no compassion for his fellow human being, say to him: “My brother, blessed are the merciful, for mercy will be shown to them, even if they have many offenses. And because they forgive anyone who wrongs them, steals from them, or commits a great offense against them, the righteous Judge forgives them just as they forgive; and just as they demand repayment, so he demands repayment from them. For that debtor had been forgiven tens of thousands of talents representing his offenses, because he pleaded with our Lord when he, his wife, and his children were about to be sold. But afterward he went and passed judgment on someone who had wronged him. “This is what my Father in heaven will do to you,” he says, “unless each of you forgives his brother’s offenses from your heart,” even if they amount to four hundred and ninety in a single day. Let us recognize that we too have offenses before God, and if we forgive, our Lord forgives.”

And when you see greedy people and plunderers who hunger for gain, say: “My brothers, blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, and not for plunder, oppression, and greed, which is idolatry.” For the whole sickness is this: a person thinks that he is defiled by his fellow’s sins even though he does not sin with him. He reasons in his mind that if he sees someone who has done wrong and committed an offense, and does not judge him or drive him away, he becomes defiled like him. Because of this, someone whose thinking is sick wants to injure the offender with blows, because he thinks that through that person’s death, persecution, or condemnation, he himself is made righteous or pure, or is thereby delivered from other people’s sins, which he thinks cling to him for no reason. For this reason our Lord told him: “When your brother is unwilling to listen to you, regard him like the rest of the pagans, who are rebellious and do not obey.” And just as you do not judge those who are outsiders, do not judge this brother of yours who has rebelled either.

When you see people who are enemies of one another, say, “My brothers, blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.” Peacemakers are those who reconcile enemies in other congregations far away from them, and make peace in their Father’s land. They act as mediators between them and reconcile them through entreaty, humility, and admonition. When they are reconciling enemies, and these enemies say evil things about one another in their hatred, let us turn those words around and say good things instead: “How distressed so-and-so is that he is not reconciled with you! He wants to be reconciled with you, and he says, ‘I was not happy about this hostility. Satan made me stumble, and I insulted my brother, a member of my own body.’” Say this even though that person has not said it, until their anger subsides while they are apart from one another, and they come and greet one another with a holy kiss. And if we do not turn their evil words into good ones—they say hateful things about one another on every pretext— and you, who are a good mediator, go and carry those words to them just as they were spoken, you stir them up, and they are not reconciled.

When you see enemies whose hostility lies hidden within them, say, “My brothers, blessed are those who are pure in heart, for they will see God.” In this way, conduct yourself wisely and humbly with everyone, teaching them and bringing them peace, approaching them in whatever way you see fit. When evil sees that you are so kind to both the good and the wicked, it wails and says, “What shall I do now? I showed him unclean and wicked people, but he looks at them as though they were saints and admonishes them as brothers. Woe to me! What shall I do? I no longer have any opportunity to fight him. For my whole battle was to make a person hate another human being, even on account of his sins; but this man loves sinners as our Lord does. Woe to me! Like him, he condemns me and kills me. But I know what I will do. It is better for me to leave him alone and move away than for him to kill me through humility, like that teacher of his, Jesus.” The fourth discourse, on vegetables for the sick, is finished.
The fifth discourse: On milk for infants.

Now let us speak about the person whose food is milk, namely: “Do not eat bread with adulterers, oppressors, the dissolute, the greedy, or revilers.” He commands the infant not to eat bread with them or associate with them, because he is a child, lest they lead him to do their will, because he knows nothing and is led along like little children. He told him not to live among them until he knows himself, grows up, and becomes a man. Then he sends him to go and make disciples of them, to be a lamb among them, and to turn wolves into innocent lambs. This is why he spoke to him this way. But if this child wants to be better than the other children, to grow quickly and reach full maturity, without evil gaining power over him and striking him with hidden pains as it would a little child, he must watch himself so that he is not ensnared on account of food and led along according to evil's will. He must not be anyone's enemy or publicly expose sinners, but must make peace with them, while not eating bread with them. It was only bread that the apostle said you should not eat with them—not that one should become their enemy or publicly expose them. For someone who makes peace with them and watches himself is better than someone who does not eat bread with them but publicly exposes them.

For by saying, “I do not eat with so-and-so,” he has exposed him, and his listeners know that he has seen something shameful in him and avoids him because of it. But if he watches himself, he should not be afraid to eat bread with sinners. He does not sin, even if they are pagans. For the apostle gave him this command so that he would not be led along according to their evil will, not because he would be sinning. In this way he quickly comes to fulfill that command: “Consider everyone better than yourself.” And if he gains strength and comes to fulfill this command, he will love everyone: insiders and outsiders alike. He suffers no harm, honors them, and regards them as better than himself. Someone who eats bread with them and keeps watch over himself is better than someone who does not eat with them but publicly exposes them with his lips. But if he goes beyond this and strikes them, curses them, hates them, or becomes their enemy, he falls away from righteousness. Rather, he should live peacefully with them as with everyone else, and admonish them. But if they will not be persuaded, they fall into the hands of the wicked judges of this wicked world, and those judges punish them. Otherwise, perhaps our Lord will do for them as he did for Paul, or for the tax collector and the sinful woman.

For you who are angry with someone who does evil—how do you know whether he is Paul, or Zacchaeus, or Matthew the tax collector, or Rahab the prostitute, or that Samaritan woman who committed adultery with many men, as our Lord testified about her, that she had had five husbands besides the one she had in our Lord's time? All these repented and lived. Yet we exalt ourselves above sinners, not knowing whether our end may be like Solomon's, or Iscariot's, or that of the other people who were good at first, but sinned in the end. “Do not rejoice,” it says, “at your enemy's ruin, lest God bring his ruin upon you and have no pity on you, just as you had no pity on your brother.” For it says, “Whoever rejoices in evil will meet with ruin.” For it is not right that our Lord died for sinners, while we hate them. For even when we love them, we fall far short of our Lord’s love. When we hate them, we never see him.

There are also other commandments that are milk for infants, and our Lord spoke them to little children. This one: “Do not take the road to the pagans, and do not enter a town of the Samaritans,” he said. “Instead,” he said, “go to the sheep that have strayed from the house of Israel.” That is, “Go to your own people and preach.” And again: “When you enter a village,” he said, “ask who is worthy there, and stay with him.” “Do not greet anyone on the road,” he said. And, “Whoever does not welcome you, when you leave, shake the dust off your feet. It will be easier for Sodom on the day of judgment than for that town,” he said. But these things that our Lord told them are contrary to these great commandments: “Regard everyone as better than yourself,” and, “When you enter the home of pagans, eat whatever they set before you.” How is this saying, “Enter the home of pagans,” like that saying, “Do not take the road to the pagans”? Our Lord commanded them in this way, although he himself did not ask who was worthy before staying with someone. Instead, he stayed with evil people, so that even the Pharisees grumbled about him: “He is always visiting sinners, tax collectors, and prostitutes, and eating and drinking with them.” “The healthy do not need a doctor,” he said, “but those who are very sick do.” These things are not like the saying, “Go in to someone who is righteous and worthy.”

The apostle too, while he became everything to everyone in order to win everyone over, commanded others not to associate with sinners as he did. How, then, was this, when they themselves associated with people and did not distinguish the good from the evil? But everything that our Lord and the apostle commanded their disciples in this way was, for one thing, because of their weakness, and for another, because of their immaturity. It is like someone who gives bread to an infant and sees that he cannot eat it and is suffering from hunger: he immediately gives him milk, which he has the strength to take, and he nurses and is happy. This is what our Lord and the apostle did. Therefore, because they were immature in the truth and had not yet grown in the knowledge of mature disciples, and were being defeated by debaters, they were afraid to enter the homes of pagans. Paganism was widespread at that time. And those Jews who feared the Lord kept far away from pagans. For when the sinners among them went and entered the homes of pagans, they became like them. The Lord used to kill them because they abandoned him and worshiped idols. And because they had no strength, as soon as they saw the pagans, evil led them wherever it wished.

When the Lord saw this, he commanded them, as little children, not to go among the pagans. For at that time the disciples, because they did not yet know the truth, thought that even someone who went to teach among the pagans was sinning, and that the Lord would kill him as he had killed those people. They exchanged the good one who nourished them for Satan, their killer, and the living image for a dead calf. For this reason they were bound with harsh restraints, like slaves who rebel against their masters. As he said, “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.” As the Israelites said about that evil one who led them astray in the wilderness: “This is the good one who brought us out of Egypt.” They gave the unclean one the name of the Holy One, the Mighty One of Jacob. It is not, then, with someone who loves sinners, admonishes them, and does good to them as though they were better than himself that God is displeased, but with someone who exchanges his truth and loves the wicked because he does what they do.

Little by little, then, he brought them up in knowledge and guarded them from stumbling blocks until they grew up and were filled with the Spirit and no longer stumbled. For it says, “Everyone who is unacquainted with solid food has milk for his food until he knows the truth.” “Do not greet anyone on the road,” he says. That is, “Do not speak with anyone on the road until you reach the place where I have sent you.” Our Lord told them this so that, through a greeting, they would not be led into sin by anyone, or argue or quarrel with some villager while traveling along the road. Our Lord commanded them this while they were still young. But once they had grown strong and mature, he allowed them to become all things to everyone, so that they might help everyone and admonish everyone with the discernment our Lord gave: to speak to each person according to that person’s ability to listen. For no one is held accountable for another’s sins, and no one is defiled by a sinful person unless he acts as that person does. For the apostle said, “Not only those who do these things sin, but also those who join with the people who do them.” When someone sees thieves, adulterers, and murderers and becomes their accomplice in murder or theft or adultery, or takes some of their plunder, or accepts a bribe and then covers up for them, by any one of these things he assigns himself a share with them.

But if he admonishes them privately and does not expose them publicly, because they are his own flesh and blood— just as he himself would hate anyone to treat him that way and expose him when he does wrong, and asks everyone who sees him, “Cover up for me so that I do not die”—he does not sin. Rather, a person should speak like this to someone who does wrong, when he sees him or hears about him: “My son, I will not accept a bribe from you. But because love covers sins, and because I hate the shame of having someone expose me, even if I stumble and commit murder—for this reason, so that I do not fall away from righteousness, since I hate having someone expose me— how could I expose others and become unjust rather than righteous? For this reason, no harm will come upon you through my own hands. For it is written: ‘Harm will come, but woe to the one through whose hands it comes!’ Let us understand that harm does not come upon a person except either through his own hands, bringing it upon himself, or through his neighbor’s hands, bringing it upon him, or when God wishes to test someone or make him victorious through Satan, as he did with Job. It says, ‘Woe to the one through whose hands harm comes!’

You see that evils come through a person’s hands, either his own or his neighbor’s. Now, my son, no harm will come upon you through my own hands, though I have encountered you and seen you. But if it comes upon you, it will be through the hands of someone else who sees you, or through your own hands, because you are committing this offense. But plead with God and make a covenant with him that you will not do anything like this, and he will have mercy on you. For if you do not do this, even if you escape the hands of people who have no mercy, God will bring his wrath upon you, because you cause pain to the heart of a human being who shares your ancestry from Adam. As for me, far be it from me that harm should come through my hands and that I should hurt anyone.” This is how a person should correct his neighbor privately, between the two of them, when he sees him sinning. He does not take his share with adulterers and murderers or join them, but becomes holy and fulfills the law of Christ. For when he exposes him, he does something that he himself hates having someone do to him, and he becomes unjust rather than righteous. Harm comes through his hands, and he receives that woe, for it says, ‘Woe to the one through whose hands harm comes!’

See, then, how you run with thieves and take your share with adulterers when you rebuke your brother or expose him, or when you admonish him. Let us therefore admonish everyone in love, my brothers: with a gentle spirit, the one who sins, so that he will not sin again; and the one who stands, so that he may be strengthened and grow and not fall. So let us not judge or expose anyone and bring harm through our own hands. For it is written that we should not judge, so that we will not be judged. And it says, ‘Become like your Father in heaven, for he is kind to the good and the evil, and sends down his rain upon the righteous and the unjust.’ Perhaps you will say to me, “These things are written for the perfect, and I do not want to be perfect, but righteous.” Do not be angry at what I tell you. If these things are said to the perfect: “Do not judge, and do not let evil come about through your hands,” then consider that these things are not even said to the good: “Judge and expose,” but to the weak, and to people whom evil overcomes and who hate to the point of murder. He said, “When you have reproved him, if he does not listen to you, regard him as a tax collector and a pagan.” Do not be evil and kill him or uproot him like a weed, when you do not know whether he is wheat.

There are people like Paul, the tax collectors, and the prostitutes, who were weeds at first but in the end became good wheat. And which will the Judge forgive you for: violating his command not to uproot the weeds? Or his command that, just as you hate having anyone harm you, you must not harm others? Or this: “Overcome evil with good”? Or this: “Do not judge, so that you will not be judged”? Or this: “Regard your neighbor as better than yourself”? Or this: “Forgive the one who has wronged you seventy times seven”? Or this: “Offer your cheek, and do not resist an evil person”? Or this: “Woe to the one through whose hands evil comes about”? Why should I write more to you? You transgress the whole law of our Lord whenever you harm someone who has wronged you. But if you harm someone who has not wronged you, how guilty you are, and how you dishonor God! For you transgress his law and do not do his will, and he will punish you on the day of judgment. For you do not attain perfection as long as you judge, and you fall away from righteousness whenever you harm anyone. But you who want to be perfect or righteous, leave your case alone: God will judge it. The person who is evil falls into the hands of the evil judges of this evil world, and they punish him. And if he escapes their punishment and does not repent, God will punish him, for no one can escape from his hands. “It is a very fearful thing,” it says, “to fall into the hands of the living God.” For he will not be meek on the day of judgment as he was here.

But, my brothers, so that we may not be judged when we judge, or hated when we hate, or have retribution exacted from us when we exact it, or be accused when we accuse, and be judged by the judgment with which we judge, I advise us to stop judging and instead admonish everyone with love. “If you do not secure justice for yourself, I will secure justice for you,” God said. But if you become enraged, curse, or strike, and do not restrain your anger and remain quiet, God will not secure justice for you. But if you want to be perfect, pray that our Lord will forgive him, and do not become his enemy. For even righteousness, which is below perfection, is not permitted to pray and ask God for evil to come upon whoever harms it. Rather, righteousness speaks like this: Let our Lord act as he knows best. If it is right to demand an accounting, let him demand it; and if it is right to forgive, let him forgive. But perfection prays with all its heart that God will forgive the person who has wronged it. But God, even if the injured person does not demand an accounting, himself calls the offender to account, though the perfect pray that he may be forgiven.

For there is no possibility of someone opposing the truth, railing against and oppressing someone who belongs to our Lord, without our Lord striking him down, unless he first repents, pleads, and begs forgiveness for his wrongdoing; then he has mercy on him and forgives him. And if, after our Lord has forgiven him, he goes and demands an accounting from someone who wrongs him, our Lord in turn calls him to account. For if that debtor who repented before our Lord had his sins forgiven by the master to whom he owed the debt— although he, his wife, and his children were to have been sold, he forgave him— and because he then went back and passed judgment on and oppressed his fellow servant who owed him, that is, someone who had wronged him, and refused to forgive him, God in turn called him to account for his former wrongdoings and had no pity on him, just as he had had no pity on his fellow servant. Rather, I advise that, as long as we have wrongdoings of our own, we should not demand an accounting for anyone else's wrongdoing. Instead, let us admonish ourselves and the person who does wrong, until we move beyond our wrongdoings. And when our own wrongdoings have been wiped away, let us have mercy on our fellow servants, lest, while we demand an accounting, God in turn call us to account for those wrongdoings of ours committed before our repentance, which he forgave us, as he did with that debtor.

For there is no one among Adam's children who does not first sin and then become righteous, because that thought which was sown in Adam on the day he broke the commandment is sown in all his children from their mother's womb. Then, when they become aware of themselves, they struggle and overcome it and become righteous, or they are overcome, incur guilt, and become wicked through it. He said, “Wicked servant, you ought to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you.” He said, “My Father in heaven will do the same to you unless each of you forgives his brother's wrongdoings from your heart.”

Now, concerning the subject we raised above: because of the disciples' immaturity, he watched over them carefully, as with a physical infant whose bodily mother raises him, carefully watching over him and providing everything he needs, so that he may quickly grow without defect, and his lovely, beautiful growth may not be harmed. In this way our Lord raised his disciples spiritually, carefully and beautifully, so that they might quickly become spiritually mature men and attain perfection, and bring many others to perfection and bring captive humanity back from the hands of Satan the destroyer, and prepare for the Lord a perfect people, zealous for good works, loving their God with all their strength and heart, and everyone as themselves. As it is written in both Testaments, which make known one God and Lord of all, who created everything and holds everything, and to whom everything belongs.

For this reason, then, he said to those who were still children, “Ask who is worthy and deserving, and enter his house.” So that their minds would not be harmed and [?], or be robbed and made to stumble by the evil one or by human beings through one of the tricks of error. If our Lord had not acted this way and guided them little by little, as one guides children, they would have stumbled. As we know, after they had received the Advocate and our Lord had ascended, and the disciples had come to know the truth, they spoke the word of God only to Jews, and did not instruct pagans and sinners, so that they would not be taken captive by evil people or by servants of the evil one, until our Lord showed them, after they had received power. He sent Simon a vision and depicted unclean animals in it, which symbolized unclean people. He said to him, “Slaughter and eat.” Simon recoiled and said, “Far be it from me!” Our Lord called out to him three times, “What God has cleansed, you must not defile.”

For if we say that he spoke to him about animals and meat, the apostles did not eat meat, but fasted until the ninth hour and ate bread, salt, vegetables, and olives. This, then, is the meaning of “Slaughter and eat”: “Go, enter the homes of pagans and unclean people, and make them disciples, for this is what God wants, and you will not be defiled.” While Simon was wondering about the vision, Gentiles came in and approached him. The Spirit said to him, “Get up and go with them, and do not hesitate, for these are the animals about which the Lord told you, ‘Slaughter and eat.’ What God has cleansed, you must no longer defile.” Then Simon remembered our Lord, who had said to them as he ascended, “Go to all the nations and make them disciples in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.” Then Simon gained a sound understanding, took courage, and went out to make disciples of the Gentiles and teach them what they should do to live. When he entered Jerusalem, some of those who were circumcised criticized him, saying, “Why did you go to uncircumcised and unclean people and eat and drink with them, something that is not permitted?” They criticized him on the basis of the lesser commandments: “Do not associate with sinners.” Then he brought them to the great commandment—that is, to solid food—saying, “God has granted me this: that I should not call anyone a pagan or defiled.” So he was patient until the children grew strong. Then, when they had become adults, he gave them solid food through the Advocate and made the whole truth known to them. Then they strengthened one another, knowing that these commandments were higher than those.

So the Advocate came, whom the world cannot contain, and whom no one can receive unless he has become a stranger to the world. As our Lord said, the world cannot contain the Advocate, but righteous people of the world can receive the gift of the pledge. So when the twelve apostles had received this Advocate together on that day, fear still lay upon them. For a person is not perfected immediately when the Advocate comes. But when he receives the Advocate, he knows the whole truth and how to live, and then he begins to be perfected. And until the day he leaves the world, he continues to grow. For we know that after they received the Advocate, they were afraid to go among the Gentiles, until our Lord called out to Simon, and Simon called out to his companions: “Our Lord sent us among wolves, not to righteous lambs.” And Paul too, when he saw that because of their fear they were not walking uprightly in the gospel, after they had received the Advocate, admonished them, as is written in Galatians.

I am not saying that they were not perfected, but that it is not on the very day a person receives the Advocate that he is perfected and fear is taken away from him. Rather, when he receives the Advocate, he knows the whole truth. But if someone does not know the truth, he has not received the Advocate. For the apostles knew the truth after they received the gift of the Spirit, the Advocate. Yet there were occasions when some of them were afraid and did not proclaim the message correctly. Then Paul said to them, “You did not receive a spirit of fear.” Then they took courage, gave themselves over to death, and proclaimed the message correctly. And so the Holy Spirit corrected them through one another until they were perfected. When the Advocate comes, a person knows the whole truth. And when he knows the whole truth, then little by little his fear is taken away completely, and then he is set free. And when he is set free, then he is perfected. And when the vessel is perfected and its images have been imprinted, then he grows in love day by day, until the day when our Lord wishes to take him to himself. And his dwelling will be with him for as long as our God exists, who neither passes away nor changes, but remains as he is. And he is glorified and exalted with those who love him forever and ever.

And as for the saying, “Shake the dust off your feet”: this was when they entered a place and its people did not receive them, being deprived of the truth. They grumbled and acted harshly toward them, just as they had wanted to do when our Lord was with them: to bring down fire from heaven upon the village that had not welcomed them, as harsh people do today. But our Lord rebuked them aloud: “Do not think like this again.” He made this concession to those who were immature in the truth: they were not to act harshly, but to shake off the dust and go in peace. As for anyone who would not welcome them, even while they prayed for him, unless he repents, our Lord himself will hold him accountable. But anyone who shakes off the dust and quarrels with someone who did not welcome him is not righteous. The others, however, when they became perfect in spirit, heard this from our Lord: they were to pray for anyone who struck them. How much more, then, should they pray for someone who does not strike them! But woe on the day of judgment to anyone who did not welcome them. But after they had become perfect, people would strike them, attack them, and drive them out through one gate, and they themselves would enter through another and plead with those people to live—not as on that occasion when people did not welcome them and they wanted to burn them. End of the fifth discourse, on milk for infants.
The sixth discourse: On a person who becomes perfect and grows

Let us explain how a person becomes perfect and how he grows after attaining perfection. It is like architects and craftsmen: when they want to build a house or fashion a large container in which the king’s precious objects may be placed, and when they have built the house with dressed stones, decorated it, and covered it entirely with images, and its windows and doors have been adorned, they say to the king, “Look, the house is complete. Consider what you will fill it with.” Then the king begins to fill it with all kinds of good things, day after day.

Likewise, when metalworkers have fashioned a container of gold or silver and made a door and a lid for it, fitted it with hinges, and put on a lock so that no stranger can open it without its owner, then they say to the king, “Look, your container is complete. Store all your treasures in it and trust it.” Then the king begins to put into it, day after day, everything he gains through trade. So too, when a person has humbled himself below everything on earth and has brought his mind low night and day, regarded everyone as better than himself, emptied himself of everything he possesses, and kissed his enemies’ feet, then our Lord sees his humility and sends him the Spirit, the Advocate, and he comes to know the whole truth. And when he knows the truth, then he distinguishes truth from falsehood and fights against Satan. And he overthrows him, as our Lord overthrew him, and frees him from evil thoughts. Then, when he has defeated his enemy, found rest from his burning arrows, and the sores of his sufferings have closed, and the damage from his wounds has healed, and he stands guard over all his limbs, then Christ the King says, “Look, this person is now perfect, as on the day when I formed him.” Then our Lord opens the heavenly gates for him, and he enters and glories in the riches of the mysteries. And just as this king deposits good things every day in that treasury which the architect built for him and the craftsman fashioned for him, so this person, while standing bodily on earth, has his mind in Eden every day in spirit, that is, in Jerusalem above. In this way he grows and flourishes every day, enjoying comfort and delight in the Spirit, until he reaches the stature of the spiritual Watchers. Then our Lord comes and takes him wholly out of this world, just as he took his mind and brought it into Paradise. There he makes his home, in Jerusalem above. First, however, a person keeps all these great commandments that I have written above, and then he is made perfect. And when he has been made perfect and humbled still further through them, then he ascends to that glorious greatness and makes his home there. Such is the life with our Lord of those who have become humble, gentle, and holy, citizens of the city of life, and doers of our Lord’s good, acceptable, and perfect will, as they pray that God’s will may be done among those on earth as it is among those in heaven. Here ends the sixth discourse, on the person who is made perfect and grows.
The seventh discourse: On the commandments of the righteous.

On the commandments addressed to the whole world concerning how people should become righteous. For not everyone compels himself to ascend to perfection. These are the commandments of the righteous: Do not murder. Do not commit adultery. Do not steal. Honor your father and your mother. Have compassion on those in distress.
