Do not commit sexual immorality. Do not give false testimony. Do not plunder. Do not oppress. Do not covet your neighbor’s ox, donkey, house, wife, field, or vineyard. Do not remove his boundary marker. Do not do to your neighbor what you yourself hate. And as you want people to treat you, so treat them. Through these commandments a person becomes righteous, ranking after the perfect. For just as he hates to have anyone kill him, steal from him, or slaughter his livestock, Or enter his field or vineyard, or approach his wife or anything on his land. And if he does not do to his neighbor what he himself hates, he will thus be righteous as he passes along his neighbor’s paths, and does not hurt his neighbor’s heart. In this way he will be righteous before God. Just as he also hates being cursed by anyone, even when he gives offense, and if he goes astray, hates the person who exposes him, and wants to be forgiven whenever he is caught in wrongdoing, whether adultery or theft, or even if he falls into murder, and wants them to forgive him when he asks them, so he himself should act toward anyone who wrongs him through such offenses, and he will be righteous. And just as he wants someone to feed him when he is hungry and relieve him when he is thirsty, and, when he travels abroad, to bring him into shelter in winter and into shade in summer, and to give him whatever he lacks, and just as he wants someone to clothe him when he is naked and give him shoes when he is barefoot, so he himself should act toward others who share his flesh.

For everyone who is a descendant of Adam is our neighbor and shares our flesh. And if clothing a naked person is too difficult for one individual because of his poverty, let five or ten people join together and cover the bodies of their neighbors. Anyone who acts this way falls short of the perfect in this respect: he has not renounced the earth, sanctified himself, taken up his cross, looked toward heaven, and grasped the truth, which is the perfect cross of our Lord. And just as, if he becomes ill abroad, he wants strangers to come to his aid and heal his pains and afflictions, so he too should act toward the strangers he encounters. In this way he comes to those great commandments found in the Torah, on which the whole force of the Law and the Prophets hangs, and through which a person fulfills the entire Law and the Prophets: that you should love the Lord your God with all your heart and strength and with everything you have; and the one following it, which is like it: that you should love your neighbor as yourself—and this means all human beings. You should care for their concerns as you care for your own, helping them as much as you can. For everyone you encounter is your neighbor, whether you do good to him or harm him. For no one does good or harm to someone far away from him; rather, he hates someone at his side and loves someone near him. But if someone has compassion on a person he encounters, he becomes his neighbor; if he harms him, he becomes his murderer; and if he neither does him good nor harms him, he becomes distant from him, just as those fellow citizens of the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho did. Those fellow citizens of his became distant from him, while the Samaritan foreigner who had compassion on him became his neighbor.

Likewise, he also commands everyone to keep away from sexual immorality and carrion: “Do not eat what a wild animal leaves behind or tears apart, as the pagans do.” They must not practice divination or augury, or whisper incantations, for these are whispered in the names of idols. They must not consult magicians, sorcerers, or makers of amulets, because all these practices constitute idol worship. For he said in the holy Law: “No diviner, sorcerer, or maker of amulets shall enter your land.” Therefore we must not do these things, not even if, because we do not do them, we all go mad, our Lord, or suffer pain until our departure from this life; or if everything we have is lost; or if our wives remain barren for many years, like Sarah and Rebekah. For it is because of these matters that we go to deceivers and depart from righteousness. Do we not see how long those of old endured their trials, until the Lord delivered them? For because of our pains we bring in sorcerers, and we do not imitate Job, who endured his trial. And for childbirth and other pains we make amulets, and we do not imitate Abraham and Isaac, who asked the Lord, and he gave them children. And because of madness we practice magic and sprinkle water on the person who has gone mad, and we destroy him. And the Lord holds us responsible for his blood. Yet we are not persuaded or corrected, not even by the man who had a legion of demons in him and lived among the tombs until our Lord healed him. Nor do we imitate his parents, who did not sprinkle magical water on him and destroy him. For if a magician wishes, he sprinkles water on someone who is physically healthy and destroys him. Is this not the same as someone destroying his fellow with an iron weapon, a club, or a stone? For they cause destruction to the extent that our Lord chooses to leave them alone until the day of judgment. For it is easy for them to hire evil spirits to cause destruction at the cost of their own souls. For they give them a soul in exchange for a soul as their wages, and then they cause destruction. And on the day of judgment God holds them responsible for what the spirits have destroyed, and they give the souls they promised them as wages for their labor. For this is the agreement they make when they send them to cause destruction: “On that day we will give a soul in exchange for each soul you kill at our word and by our hand.” Thus sorcerers wield them like swords and kill people. For every soul they destroy, they give their own soul in exchange. They love worldly honor and hate their own souls.

Glory to you, our Lord! How patient you are: you see and leave them alone, so that perhaps they may repent and not go to the fire that is never extinguished. But I speak to you upon whom a test or trial has come from God, whether because of their sins or so that they may repent; or because they do not pray, our Lord leaves them alone and they fall into trial from the evil one.

They are also tried by people who destroy their fellows, or by Satan because they obeyed him. But a test comes upon people from God because he wishes to examine them, to see whether they are steadfast in faith. Or because in this way it helps the person who has become physically ill. Trials come from human beings when they harm their companions because of their hostility, and repay one another with evil, and because of their wickedness inflict terrible injuries on one another. But neither a human being nor Satan can take a soul out of a body unless God wishes to bring about its departure through their hands. For he commanded them, “Do not harm or kill, lest you be held accountable sevenfold on the day of judgment.” God wishes to bring about the departure of human beings, some through sickness and some through fire, or in a well or a pit; some through an unclean spirit, and some through wicked people. God judges people who kill, because he established a law for them that they must not kill, and gave them freedom to do what they wish.

On that day of judgment he will say to them: “In the place where you killed them, I wished to bring about the departure of these people whom you killed. But how could you raise your hands against your own flesh and blood and not fear me, who commanded you not to strike your fellow human beings, but instead to love them and honor them?” Even when a person's soul is departing, if someone sheds his blood or strikes him, he is guilty of the blood he has shed. It is according to God's will that human souls depart through these other means of departure, and God himself wills that it be through a river, or in a pit or a well, or from a high or low roof. How often someone stumbles over a stone and dies! An unclean spirit has no authority to kill a human being, unless God wishes that person's departure to take place through Satan. For if Satan had this authority to take souls out of human bodies, especially if he saw someone who wished to repent and escape from him, he would kill him wherever he had an opportunity to act against him. And if a sinful person escaped again and transgressed the law after repenting, he would destroy him. For as long as someone keeps the commandments and takes refuge in God, he would be afraid to accuse him. These evil spirits that kill through a magician or a sorcerer kill through human hands. Otherwise, then, would the sorcerer and magician not do something else? And would the person who carries the water for them not also participate with them, along with whatever they use for their sorcery, and comes and sprinkles it on a person and kills him, or hides charms for him in a place and destroys him? And see that the unclean spirit does not kill him unless God wishes to take his soul and send it to whatever place he wishes, through whomever he wishes—that is, according to the measure of his deeds. In this way he prepares a prison for it until the day of judgment, when it takes up his body and he rises again with his deeds.

Satan, however, is condemned because he incites rebellion and teaches people evil deeds, and helps them commit them, and teaches them to deny God, of his own free will. For just as people forge a sword and teach one another to hold it in their hands, so unclean spirits teach people to hold them in their hands, and to kill one another invisibly, with an invisible sword just as with a visible sword. And just as an iron sword kills no one unless someone takes it in his hand and kills with it, so too unclean spirits, which are invisible swords, kill no one unless a person takes them in his hands and kills invisibly with them. These spirits allow themselves to be held in people's hands because they know that they make them murderers, children of hell. And people deny God and acknowledge them, becoming their servants in evil deeds and in the hateful will of Satan, who blinds people's minds to the truth so that they cannot see it.

These unclean spirits do indeed exercise power over people of their own will, because people obey them, become their slaves, and transgress God's law, and do not keep his commandments, and corrupt their own limbs. The spirits are tormented within them, sometimes visibly, and sometimes invisibly. But they have power only over those who obey them, as Paul said: “You are slaves of the one to whom you give your obedience.”

If, therefore, you wish to overcome unclean spirits and those people who learn from them and use them to harm their companions, keep the Lord's commandments and take refuge in him until you leave this world, and you will be victorious in both worlds, even if evil people cut off your fingers, one finger each day. But someone who does not endure this brief affliction inflicted by people— how can he possibly endure hell? Is it not better for me to suffer my brief pains and affliction, and for the Lord to deliver me so that I may go to his rest, rather than break his commandment for the sake of health that does not last, and go to that everlasting torment? The children of Adam are condemned for this: they learn from Satan, their murderer, and despise God, who gives them life.

Unless, therefore, our Lord wills that a person's allotted span be completed, he does not die, either at Satan's hands or at the hands of human beings. Even if they cut his body apart in any manner, the person escapes and does not die, even if he has only one hour or one day remaining. Otherwise, consider how people beat their companions until they maim them, yet they do not die.

And consider how robbers fall upon people. Sometimes there are a hundred people, and ten or twenty men kill them; elsewhere there are a hundred robbers, and they cannot kill ten men, because God does not wish to bring about their death on that day. Yet these men are murderers and are accountable for their blood, because it was against their will that those people escaped them.

Nor does God allow wild beasts to kill human beings unless he wishes to bring about their death through animals. For it is written, “I will put the fear and dread of you upon destructive animals.” But wherever he wishes to take away wild beasts’ fear of human beings, they kill and injure people. Anyone who wishes to harm another person but does not succeed certainly sins in his heart, because, as far as he himself is concerned, the evil has been done. But anyone who willingly refrains from evil, repents, pleads with our Lord, and sheds tears before him, and turns away from evil and does good—our Lord welcomes him and rejoices greatly over the sinner who repents, as it is written: “There will be joy in heaven over a sinner who repents.”

Consider also how people fall into wells, pits, and rivers, and from cliffs and rooftops, and how often they are struck with iron, clubs, and stones, yet do not die, because God does not wish their death to occur on the day when they are struck. And how often someone is struck with a fist or a whip, and his soul departs! Is it not clear that this is because God wished his death to occur at that hour? Again, there are people on whom a house falls, yet they do not die; and there are people on whom a small wall falls, and they die. Some are thrown from a city wall and do not die, while others fall from their own standing height, and their souls fly away. Is it not clear that everyone departs according to his allotted span, as it is written: “See, you have given our days a measured span, and our lifetime is as nothing before you”? For this reason we ask you, as human beings who have freedom, for whom a law has been established and a kingdom promised, and for whom Gehenna has also been prepared: let us guard ourselves and restrain our hands, so that we do not strike another person even with a finger, lest his soul depart, his blood be required at our hands, and we descend into Gehenna, into the fire that is not extinguished. But even someone who stumbles and kills, if he repents and remains in mourning and prayer, in humility and remorse of soul, and in tears before the Lord, he forgives him, just as he forgave David when he repented and poured out his soul before the Lord. For David says, “Look, my Lord, at my affliction and my suffering, and forgive all my sin.” And God saw his humble submission and the labor of his pleading, and forgave him and exalted him. But let us truly love our God, and love and honor everyone, so that we may inherit the kingdom promised to us, whose rest never passes away and whose delight never ends, whose banquet never breaks up, whose crowns never wither, and whose bridal canopy is never folded away.

In every trial, let us ask the Lord for help, as it is written: “The Lord heals every pain.” And the speech on the lips of evildoers—that is, sorcerers, diviners, magicians, writers of amulets, charmers, and soothsayers— and he rebukes them and condemns them. But if you want to be healed without sinning, wait for the Lord and plead with him. He will heal you of the many trials brought by human beings and by Satan. If it is right for you to be healed in this world, our Lord will heal you in this world. And if he does not heal you in this world, then this is for your good, and in that world he will give you rest, exalt you, and give you joy, because you waited for his salvation until your departure from this world. Do not become so impatient under the distress of your pains that you go and destroy your soul for the sake of your body's health. Whether your body recovers or not, it is better for you to endure a little temporary suffering than to go to that suffering which has no limit. Even supposing your body is healed by these deceivers, do you not know that your soul becomes sick with a sickness that lasts until the day of judgment, and that there you will be condemned, because you fled from pains and sufferings that last only a short time, and are going to suffering from which you cannot escape, because you have broken God's commandment? But if you have a pain and there is a physician near you, ask him this: “Are you perhaps a sorcerer or a charmer, or one of those who practice the deceitful teaching of error [?]? The Lord, to whose judgment we are going, is a witness against you if you offer me any treatment except simply in the name of Jesus. Otherwise, do not come near me.” Let him assure you that he will heal you in the name of Jesus, and only then let him come near you.

Now this is my advice to those who kill someone who is possessed or has gone mad: if they can withstand his strength— otherwise, let them leave him to live among the tombs until our Lord heals him or takes him away, so that you do not die with the magicians. And because of a lost possession, which today or tomorrow will surely perish or pass away, we go and associate with diviners, and we do not imitate those of old, who used to ask the Lord until what they had lost was found. And if what they had lost was not found, and if it was not found, they still praised our Lord, because he gave and he took away, as Job said amid all his sufferings and pains, the loss of his possessions, and his grief over his children: “The Lord gave, and the Lord took away. Blessed be the name of the Lord.” And he endured the sores on his body until the Lord healed him and delivered him. The Lord recorded Job’s conduct and set it before the whole world, so that people might imitate him whenever their possessions are lost, whenever their bodies are in pain, and whenever their children die, so that they might wait for the Lord as he did and praise his name as Job praised him. But over something worth a hundred minas, we quarrel and kill one another. We are not like the people of old, whose wives were taken away from them, yet they did not fight. Nor did they quarrel when a well of water was taken from them. Instead, they called the place where people disputed with them Esek and Sitnah. They did not fight or abandon righteousness. They did not do to others what they themselves hated, but treated everyone as they themselves wished to be treated.

How is marriage today like marriage in former times? It is not right for the righteous to sing to sin and revel before Satan. And lyres, harps, flutes, four-stringed instruments, cymbals, horns, bagpipes, trumpets, and everything used to make music— God gave these to human beings because they were unable to make music on spiritual lyres and harps. Because they did not know the truth, he gave them visible instruments with which to sing spiritual songs to God. For they did not know how to praise his name with the members of their bodies, which are themselves instruments of spiritual service and music. For this reason, in place of Satan’s songs, he gave them spiritual songs, so that they might sing them with every musical instrument without sinning. Far be it from the righteous to act as our generation does! Indeed, the holy do not use these instruments even to make music for God. How can those who receive the body and blood of our Savior have no fear, when they secretly serve hidden idols? We do not realize that we have uprooted our ancestors’ idols but have not uprooted their practices.

When God calls us to account for every filthy utterance we speak with the mouth that receives his body and blood, and that says, “I loved a prostitute and did [?]”—something God hates— what answer will we give him? What profit do filthy words and obscene verses bring us, along with disgusting songs and lying stories? Do they bring us wheat or clothing? No, only sins and wounds. Therefore, let us turn away from these things so that we will not be condemned with the world.

God has also given us simple medicine: we may pour oil and wine on our wounds, as our Lord, whom we worship, said; or use wax and honey, or a cake of figs, as Isaiah said; or roots that experience has shown us are good for swellings, as the son of Sirach said; or a skilled man who cuts open our sores and cleans our boils. For not everyone knows how to cut into the body without severing its tendons, but only someone who has taken care to learn how to operate. When a bone is broken, he knows how to bind it or remove it. God gave people the knowledge to do these things for one another, because God promised us pain on the day we transgressed his command. As it is written: “Most of our years are toil and pain.” This service is given to anyone who wants to be righteous. Let him serve and not sin and fall from righteousness, as our father Adam fell from perfection.

Let us also beware of divination, and not watch encounters and happenings for omens, lest we share in the practices of idol worshipers. Our Creator also gave us knowledge, on the day we sinned, to make clothing for ourselves and to make skins into shelter for ourselves against winter. And utensils of wood, and utensils of bronze and iron, served our needs in our poverty. But sin led us astray with ornaments and images that are not needed. And so that we would not do our work in its proper season, in summer, and rest in winter and serve our Lord and know his truth, look, sin has enslaved us to toil in summer and winter for wealth and for things that are not necessary, so that we may learn nothing and turn back to the home of life. We do not remember the Lord and his law, not even on the appointed fasting days. Therefore we eat and are not satisfied, and we run to put our earnings into a bag full of holes, and it profits us nothing, as the prophet said. Did the earlier generation, which did not behave this way, not acquire possessions as you do? Or did they not take wives, or eat and drink wine as you do? Yet it is not written that they became debased as we have. Or do you not know that because the people sang and danced in the days of Moses, and did not praise the one who had satisfied them with his good things after their meal, the Lord destroyed them in the wilderness, because they committed sexual immorality and sang in the service of sin, and their corpses fell? Or do you not know that these things were written for our instruction, so that the Lord would not continually destroy us? “Look,” he said, “they have Moses and the prophets. Let them listen to them and act accordingly. Otherwise hell will exact punishment from them, as it does from you,” the righteous man said to that wicked rich man who had not observed the law and the prophets during his lifetime. When he went away and was tormented, he knew that he could have kept these commandments if he had wanted to. His words make this clear: “Send someone,” he said, “to my brothers, for if they wish, they can avoid coming to this torment. I despised rebuke; otherwise I could have obeyed. But let someone from the dead go and tell them that I am suffering like this. Then they will not show contempt as I did, and they will escape hell.” “They have,” he said, “this law”—which today we do not even want to hear and learn. Is this God of the present not the same one as in former times? Or does he not hate these evil deeds? Or is it because he is patient and does not kill us as he killed them, Do you not know that in Gehenna he reminds us of all these things, as he did the wicked rich man? And all that he overlooks [?], because the time for the reckoning of our judgment is near.

Why do we not fast twice a week, as is prescribed for the upright? For the perfect fast every day. And why do we not pray three times a day, and in the morning and evening, as is prescribed for the upright? For the perfect praise him all day long. And why do we not keep God's law and give alms, and pray during them, as is prescribed for the upright? But the perfect observe periods of fasting and prayer throughout their lives and pray continually before our Lord. But when Sunday comes, sin compels us to say, “Our work has been neglected,” so that we will not learn righteousness on that day. And when the time for prayer comes, we say, “Our business has been ruined,” so that we will not bow down to our Creator. And those who wish to rise above the world and become perfect—why do they not undertake periods of fasting and prayer lasting weeks, fasting, praying, learning the truth, and humbling themselves, and after a little while undertake periods of fasting and prayer lasting months, then seasons, and then years, until they grow strong and are lifted entirely above the earth and come to be in heaven, and there pray and serve before our Lord, rather than down below on earth?

This is how God wants human beings to act, each at the level where they stand. They should do good to one another and love their Creator. Whoever can should help those in need with food and clothing. And whoever wishes to leave everything he owns and attain perfection is our Lord's brother, and our Lord takes greater pleasure in him than in thousands and tens of thousands. Whoever does not attain this portion should remain in the uprightness that our Lord commands. He should not do evil and fall even from uprightness and be condemned. For God wants all human beings to live. That is why he gave greater and lesser commandments, so that everyone might run according to their strength. Through the greater commandments a person becomes perfect, and through the lesser ones a person becomes upright. “As I live,” says the Lord, “I do not desire the death of sinners.” For if he desired their death, he would not have established a greater and a lesser law. He says that if they cannot attain the greater law and become perfect, they should at least live through the lesser law and not perish. End of the seventh discourse, on the commandments for the upright and the righteous.
The eighth discourse, on the person who gives everything he owns to feed the poor.

Now concerning what the apostle said: “If I give everything I have to feed the poor, but have no love in me, I have gained nothing”—that is, I have not grown much. And our Lord said, “Whoever gives a cup of water to drink will not lose his reward.” And again he said, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father.” For I was hungry and you fed me; I was thirsty and you gave me a drink; I was a stranger and a foreigner and you welcomed me; I was naked and you clothed me. I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me. Come, inherit the kingdom that was prepared for you. And to those who did not do these things he said: Go away, you who are cursed, into the fire prepared for the Evil One and his angels. I do not know you. Go to your master, because, he says, you did not do these things for me, and because you served wickedness. And again the blessed apostle said: If I know all the mysteries in heaven and all knowledge, but have no love in me, I am nothing. And our Lord said: If you know the truth, the truth itself will set you free. For even if those who have been set free are not perfect, nevertheless, as soon as they know the truth, they are delivered from falsehood and from slavery to sin, and they become righteous and do not come under judgment. But if they have time in the world and advance day by day, they reach perfection.

Then how did the apostle say that they are nothing? And again he said: If I give my body to be burned but have no love in me, I am nothing. What, then, is this that is so much greater than everything else, which the apostle longs for? And our Lord said: Whoever offers his cheek to someone who strikes him and endures it reaches perfection, if he loves the one who struck him and prays for him. Could the apostle be undoing our Lord’s words? Certainly not! He is not undoing them, but building on them. The apostle did not say that these things are not good; rather, he introduces something greater there. Someone, he says, who gives everything he has to feed the poor for God’s sake and empties himself, as he told him, of everything he possesses, but does not have in him that humble love which loves those who kill him and washes his enemies’ feet, and considers everyone better than himself, and looks toward heaven rather than earth, while his mind serves there in the Jerusalem above, and is bound there to our Lord, and goes to someone lower than himself and bows his head before everyone, and whose humility is known to all people, and who blesses when they curse him and bows down before them when they strike him, and goes in among those who stripped him as though they had clothed him, and goes to someone who has harmed him as though that person had done him good, and has grasped the height and depth and length and breadth, and is humbler than everyone, and while doing these things and others like them, considers sinners better than himself, while he is free from anxiety all day long and has nowhere on earth to lay his head.

So the apostle did not say that someone who gives everything he possesses to feed the poor gains no benefit. Rather, he says, he is nothing in the eyes of the person who has emptied himself and has within him this love that performs these deeds. And all this is humility. Yet people can give everything they own to feed others, and become destitute on earth for our Lord’s sake, without attaining this humility. Instead, they love only as much as they love, and are humble toward certain individuals, but not before everyone. For this reason they are far below anyone who attains perfect love, because whoever does not humble himself in this way does not become perfect. And whoever does not humble himself is far below those who are perfect.

There are people who have given their bodies to the fire for our Lord’s sake, while living in faith and righteousness, and many who have wives, business dealings, male slaves, and female slaves, like Abraham and Job. The apostle did not say that they gain no benefit at all, but rather that they are far below the martyrs who empty themselves and are humble like our Lord, resembling the apostles and Stephen. Again, there are people who are sinners and believe in our Lord. Persecution comes in their days, and they are told, “Deny our Lord and sacrifice to idols.” They do not know what perfect love is, but know only faith and baptism. They are burned, thrown to wild beasts, and put to the sword, yet they endure and do not deny the Lord. Do they then have no reward? Yet they do not attain perfection, and they are nothing in the eyes of Stephen and the apostles. Nevertheless, their failings are forgiven, and they do not come under judgment. But although all people are gathered before Christ’s judgment seat, as the apostle said, “We must all stand before Christ’s judgment seat,” some of us come for judgment, while some of us come for glory and to sit on thrones, as our Lord said to those who had carried out his entire perfect will: “You who have left everything and followed me, on the day when I am revealed in my glory, you will sit on thrones and judge the tribes of humanity.” You see, then, that they come before the judgment seat for glory, not for judgment. Whatever condition a person is found in on the day of his departure, in that same condition he stands before the judgment seat on the day of judgment.

Again, there are people who have left everything they owned for our Lord’s sake, who love our Lord and are devoted to him, yet do not possess that love which loves God and other people. Because they have loved our Lord, he reveals to them the mysteries in heaven and all the knowledge of faith, yet they do not grasp the reality of love. They do not grasp the height and depth and length and breadth that love grasps. Instead, they grasp all the mysteries and all the knowledge found in faith, which is less than love—that love which loves everyone and brings everyone to peace. For faith loves our Lord, his friends, and the members of his household. But love loves our Lord, his enemies, his killers, unbelievers, and idols, as it is written: “Regard everyone as better than yourself,” and, “Let your humility be known to all people,” and, “Love those who hate you.” “And you will be like your Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise and sends down his rain on the righteous and the wicked, on the good and the evil.” “And in this way let your love shine especially upon the members of the household of faith.” The apostle did not, then, say that those who knew the mysteries of faith had gained no benefit. Rather, he says that they are nothing in the eyes of those who have attained love and perfection. The eighth discourse is finished, on the person who uses everything he owns to feed the poor.
The ninth discourse: On righteousness and on the love of the righteous and the prophets.

Let us now show that the prophets who lived among that stubborn people had a love that accorded with the yodh and the new covenant, and that they lived according to the will of the Lord Almighty. They did whatever he told them. And when they pursued love and reached perfection, the Lord held them back from perfection, because he would send them and kill his enemies through them. But our Lord, who came into the world, did not come for the prophets or for the righteous, but for sinners, for the lost, and for those who had no hope, to call them to repentance and bring them back to the dwelling of life. For the prophets and all the righteous could receive life or be made perfect through the living and holy Spirit, who is the Lord. But our Lord appeared in the flesh for the sake of the whole world, which was lost, so that he might benefit the whole world, and so that the whole world might learn God's will from God himself and from his way of life. Our Lord's own statement makes this known: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” Our Lord was therefore born for everyone's instruction, so that everyone might clearly learn the truth of his humility and his love, because not everyone is able to hear the Lord's will from his Holy Spirit. His coming was therefore for everyone, so that everyone might learn his humility, kindness, and gentleness, and so that people could not excuse themselves from this love, humility, and patient endurance of suffering. For they see that the Lord of all endured everything before their eyes, for everyone's sake, as an example to all, so that they might marvel and say, “If our Lord endured everything because of our own wickedness, How much more should we ourselves endure for our own wrongdoing than he endured for our sins!

So that both sinners and righteous people may benefit from the good example that our Lord became for everyone, so that everyone may imitate him and both good and evil people may benefit from him. Yet God restrained the prophets in various circumstances even from righteousness, because he needed them at that time, since through them he forcibly subdued the rebellious, as his will saw fit. In this he also restrained them from love—the love that loves one's neighbor as oneself, and our neighbors are all human beings. For he sent them at that time, when there was hostility between God and human beings, to go and kill his enemies, because they stood against the Lord and said, "What is the Lord's renown?" As Pharaoh said, "Who is the Lord to me as king, with Moses and Aaron as his messengers?" For this reason he sent his prophets and killed through them, sometimes with the sword and sometimes without the sword, sometimes with fire and sometimes with hail, and with trials of every kind. In this way the Lord restrained the prophets from time to time from that commandment of love which leads to perfection. For if the Lord had killed them without the prophets, they would have said, "Our idols killed them, and not the Lord." They would have sacrificed their children to their idols to appease them, and would not have known the Lord. For this reason he subdued them through the prophets until they acknowledged that the Lord is God in heaven and on earth, above heaven and beneath the earth, throughout its breadth and length, and that there is no place far from him. For this reason, then, the Lord restrained the prophets from time to time even from love. For they pursued perfection with endurance, as Jeremiah said: "I owe nothing, and no one owes me anything, yet they all insult me." He longed for solitude and said: "Blessed is the one who took up your yoke in his youth, sat alone and kept silent, put his mouth in the dust, offered his cheek to the one who struck him, and had his life filled with disgrace." This was what he sought—this yoke of our Lord Jesus—but the Lord restrained him, because through him he was laying waste to his enemies. "The Lord," he says, "sends me against them by force, and they insult me." David also said: "My enemies and those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head, and I restored what I had not stolen." In this way all the prophets also hoped and waited for the hope that was to be revealed. The rest of the prophets, however, came as far as perfect love, but the Lord did not allow them to become perfect.

There are also instances in which the Lord brought them down even below righteousness, which accords with these two great commandments of love. For righteousness neither curses anyone nor harms anyone. But because the Lord was sending them, they went and cursed and hated his enemies, and they became angry with those who opposed him, and they fell below righteousness. The rest, however, remained steadfast whenever the Lord was not sending them, in these commandments: love the Lord and your neighbors, who are all human beings. And they pursued perfection, resting from anger and wrath, seeking peace and pursuing it, turning away from evil deeds and doing good deeds, offering thanksgiving to God rather than sacrifices, and saying, “An evil heart has departed from us, and we have not known evil.” And Samuel prayed for those who rejected him, and Jeremiah prayed for those who threw him into the muddy pit. Three times the Lord told him, “Do not pray for them,” but he did not listen to him. They treated their own flesh and blood as they wanted others to treat them, but the Lord restrained them, because that was what was appropriate at that time.

And Jeremiah also said, “I restrained myself from going out and cursing them, for I hate to have anyone curse me. The word of the Lord came upon me like fire and burned me, and I could not endure it without cursing them”—until he descended from righteousness and cursed them. What wrong did the prophets do by harming the wicked and transgressing that commandment of righteousness, killing and cursing, although they hated to have anyone curse or kill them, and doing to others what they themselves hated, and transgressing righteousness, when it was the Lord who forcibly made them transgress against their will? For this reason they were blameless in everything the Lord commanded them, before our Lord was born of Mary and brought about humility, harmony, and peace—a covenant better than the first. How intently the minds of the prophets looked toward this covenant! Yet it did not come in their days. For this reason God was not ashamed to be called their God. That is, he was not ashamed to call them his brothers, just as he called the apostles. For this reason he prepared a holy city for them. That is, he brought them to perfection in the sight of the apostles. But today God himself asks human beings to love one another, and not to do to their brothers, their fellow human beings, whatever they hate to have anyone do to them. Otherwise, they will not enter the kingdom.

Again, when our Lord wanted to put the Israelites to death, Moses said in his prayer for those who embittered his spirit every day and insulted him, “If you blot them out, blot me out of your book of life.” See how Moses treated those who sinned: just as he would have wanted the righteous to treat him if he had sinned, interceding for him. Do you see how the righteous pursued perfection? And God said to him, “No! Rather, I will blot out whoever sins against me.” Moses pleaded in his love, for he loved other people as himself. In his righteousness, he wanted someone to intercede for him in the same way if he sinned, until the Lord forgave the sins of his fellow human beings. How are we, who rejoice over one another, like those righteous people who were distressed and prayed for anyone upon whom calamity came because of his sins? But in another place, the Lord brought Moses down below righteousness when he said to him, “Command the Levites to put their brothers and fathers to the sword, because they worshiped the calf and exchanged him for a lifeless calf.” When Moses saw that evil had brought this about, and that it did no good to intercede for them, he did to them what he would have hated anyone to do to him if he sinned. This, however, was at the command of the Lord’s mouth, not by Moses’ own will. And when he put sinful Amalek to the sword, the Lord brought him down from righteousness, and he did what he would hate anyone to do to him and to his fellow human beings. For at that time there was hostility between God and humanity.

Whenever the Jews acted wickedly, God would also bring the Assyrian rod against them and discipline them with it. But since the day our Lord ended the hostility and, through the blood of his cross, reconciled what is on earth and what is in heaven, and made wars cease to the ends of the earth, if the Assyrian rises up, it is not our Lord who rouses him; and if the Roman goes down to battle, it is not our Lord who sends him down. Nor, if a prophet goes out burning with zeal and kills sinners, is it our Lord who sends him. Rather, evil is asserting itself today in all of them. For our Lord made peace, but human beings do not want there to be peace, and they will not be reconciled with one another, as the apostle wrote: “If anyone has a grievance against another, forgive, just as Christ forgave all humanity.” If only they were willing to turn away from evil! Our Lord does not wage wars today as he did in former times. It is human beings themselves who wage war today of their own free will. And whoever exalts himself against another, the Lord throws him down before that person, as he said: “Whoever raises his hand against another will not prevail.” So both sides raise their hands against each other with the sword and are destroyed in this world, and in the world to come they are tormented, because they did not uphold the peace that our Lord Jesus made on earth and in heaven, and because they stirred up those wars that he had brought to an end throughout the earth. And he said to them, “If you thirst for blood, here is my blood for you. Drink and live! Do not drink one another’s blood and die.” They killed him and drank his blood, yet they feel no shame. Look, they are once again drinking their brothers’ blood, something God has hated and rejected from the very first day.

David too pursued perfection: when the Lord delivered Saul his persecutor into his hands, he did not kill him, but repaid him with good for evil. As for David’s command to Solomon to pass judgment on Shimei: It was the Lord who spoke through his mouth, so that through that severe judgment everyone whom Shimei had wronged might be avenged on him and obtain justice for himself. For look: someone who is angry with his fellow remembers death and lets go of his hostility. Would that discerning and righteous prophet, then, have harbored hostility at his death, while during his life, when Shimei insulted him, he forgave him his offense? Would he have been planning all this evil as he left the world? Certainly not! And even if Shimei insulted him, what about Joab, who fought all his battles? Wherever the Lord sent David, Joab went in his place. For the kings and righteous men who arose in Israel did nothing unless the Lord told them to, except when they transgressed the commandment and sinned. What had Joab done to David that he commanded that Joab’s gray head should not go down to Sheol in peace? Rather, this is clear: the Lord brought judgment upon the wicked through David’s word, and through Solomon’s hands the Lord exacted punishment from Shimei, who cursed and wronged that humble, spiritual prophet, and from Joab, who shed blood when the Lord had not told him to. The Lord took vengeance on them through Solomon, just as he took vengeance on his enemies through the holy prophets. But now, since peace has come upon the earth and reconciliation between God and human beings, and God has been reconciled to his creatures through his Son Jesus the Savior, if all human beings feared our Lord, turned away from evil, and set their minds on good, and one or two evil people were found on earth, our Lord would kill those two evil people. No harm would come upon anyone at the hands of good people, and all human beings would be perfect. But today it is we ourselves who are eager to be agents of wrath. We all provoke anger and bring harm upon one another and upon ourselves, until we all perish at one another’s hands. For today the Lord has not told anyone to do harm and be zealous for him as in former times.

Abraham too pursued perfection, making his love shine upon everyone who passed his way, both good and evil. He supplied food and clothing to everyone who was needy and distressed, and he would not let his servants serve them. Instead, he himself stood before them like a servant, and he would say to his servants, “Give alms in your tents out of your earnings.” He imitated our Lord and washed the feet of strangers, both good and bad, although our Lord had not written a law for him. He looked to God, who makes his sun rise on the good and the bad, on the ungrateful, on Sodom, and on those like her. He became a law of love to himself and made his love shine on everyone. He gave away his possessions for the needy, and when they took his wife away from him, he bowed down before them. He humbled himself before them, greeted them, and called them “my lords” because of his love for them. On another occasion, God brought him down from the love of the perfect—a man who loved both the good and the bad—and sent him as he sent the prophets. He went and destroyed wicked kings who had encroached on what did not belong to them. So that he would know that the Lord had sent him, he met him after he had pursued many nations with a small number of men, and said to him: “Your reward is very great, because you went at my word and returned at my word, and you did not greedily seek the plunder.” Melchizedek also met him with bread and wine and blessed him because he had kept the commandments.

Elijah also pursued perfection, fastening his belt with love and kindness. He became a messenger of peace and ran many miles ahead of Ahab, his enemy and persecutor, who thirsted for his blood and searched for him in every kingdom to kill him, although Elijah had done nothing wrong. Rather, the Lord had compelled him to do these things. For he testified as he offered the burnt offering, saying, “Answer me, Lord! Answer me, so that all the people may know that you are God, and that at your word I have done all these things.” It was therefore because of the wrongdoing of the people and the kings who denied God that he destroyed them through the prophets. For Elijah prayed, and rain came down; and he ran to honor the wicked king, so that the king might enter his house with honor. You see that the prophets desired life and honor for the world and its kings, while those people denied God and wronged the prophets.

Elisha also pursued perfection when he fed his enemies and gave them something to drink, just as he wanted his enemies to do for him. After they had been released, he sent them back to their master in peace. On another occasion, the Lord brought him down from righteousness and love, and he did to those boys something he would have hated anyone to do to him if he did wrong. To those who wanted to kill him, he did good in return for evil, as is fitting for someone who seeks perfection. But as for those boys who laughed and said, “Go up, bald man!” he did to them something that love and righteousness do not do. Rather, it was Elisha’s own will when he fed his enemies, but his killing the boys was the Lord’s will. There is, then, a case in which the Lord brought the prophets down from uprightness and from love; and the rest were running after perfection. And if it happened that they were overcome in one place or another and departed from uprightness without a commandment, the Lord rebuked them, and it became known that they had erred; and they washed away their faults, went up to love, and were made firm.

And Abel ran after perfection, bowing his head before his killer, and he did not depart from love and from uprightness and strike him with anything with which he would have hated anyone to strike him. And Adam showed his truthfulness when he did not demand vengeance for Abel from the hands of Cain, because he wished that people would forgive him whenever he sinned. For in this way he had found relief, in that the Lord forgave him on the day he erred and did not kill him.

And each one of them in his generation acted thus: they endured wrongs and did not do evil to those who wronged them, because they hated that anyone should do evil to them, and they did not do to others anything that they hated; and as they wished people to do to them, so they did to everyone, both to the one who did them good and to the one who did them evil, whenever the Lord did not compel them by force to do evil to his enemies. And they waited for peace to come in their days, and to be perfected and completed by the Spirit, the Paraclete, and so to depart from the world. But God did not wish at that time to make peace, because human beings did not wish to confess him. Therefore they saw from afar the peace that was to come through our Lord Jesus Christ, and they greeted it and longed for it. And our Lord promised them: “That perfection which I will bring about when I come, I will give it to you, as one sends the Paraclete to the apostles; you too I will perfect, because you waited for me and ran after the perfection of the heavenly Watchers, that from which Adam your father had fallen. I will raise you and your father Adam up to the height from which you fell.” And with this all the prophets and the righteous were comforted, and they all fell asleep in faith, in love, and in uprightness, without having received their promise. And our Lord said to his disciples: “Prophets and righteous men waited to see the peace that you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. But if people had confessed me and I had made peace in their days, they would have been like you.”

For the Lord destroyed the erring nations through the prophets, so that they would fear him and confess him of their own will; but they were not persuaded, because of their accursed will, and they all fell by the sword, until our Lord was revealed and overcame them by the force of his love and his humility. He persuaded them through his humility, and they acknowledged that the Lord is God; and what is on earth and what is in heaven were reconciled. Yet some of them rebelled even against the love of Jesus in their hardness of heart. But our Lord said to his chosen ones, “I promised the prophets that I would come and make them perfect.” For all those who were not made perfect remained so, not because they were less capable than you of becoming perfect, but because there was no peace in their days. For this reason, justice brings it about that they too are made perfect. For this reason the apostle said that we have no advantage over them. He foresaw that they would not be made perfect without us. As for the advantage he spoke of, it is as though he were saying, “We are the first”: he hastens to make us perfect before them, rather than them before us. The perfect of today are the image of the apostles, which is a great gift. But the prophets and the righteous of old, those who were made perfect after they departed from this world, in the sight of the apostles, were made perfect for this reason: because they had pursued love and perfection in this world. A person ascends from righteousness to love, and from love is raised to perfection.

As for all the rest, anyone who is not made perfect in this present time and then departs from the world is not made perfect in that world. Rather, everyone inherits according to their course, from perfection downward: teachers who teach many, and the strong who bear the sickness of the sick and bring peace to many, and everyone according to how they are found in generosity in giving, cheerfulness in showing mercy, and diligence in leadership, or in the calmness of a love that loves without disturbance; and so each person in their own rank. But if someone empties themselves and is made holy, they receive the Paraclete and are made perfect. The apostle showed that God placed the perfect in the church, after them prophets, and after them the strong, teachers, builders, and helpers, and after them gifts of healing. He showed that one rank is higher than another. For it was about these present-day gifts that the apostle said, “God placed them in the church.” For the prophets of old and the apostles enjoy delight together in the kingdom, according to our Lord’s saying that the sower and the reaper will rejoice together: these are the prophets and the apostles. And all who are made perfect and depart from this passing world rejoice with them.

But now that our Lord has come and reconciled through the blood of his cross what is on earth and what is in heaven, people too have been persuaded through the prophets, through our Lord and his apostles, through teachers, through the strong, and through those who encourage others; and everyone has said that the Lord is God, whether sincerely or insincerely, whether in truth or in wrongdoing. Our Lord has been proclaimed today throughout creation, which acknowledges the Father, or acknowledges the Son, or the Spirit, whether they hold these beliefs rightly or wrongly. But they do not say, like those accursed people of old, “What is the Lord’s reputation?” For this reason the Lord has made peace with them in this age, even though they are not pure in faith. This lasts until the coming judgment arrives and the Lord Jesus repays everyone according to their deeds and their faith. So the Lord Jesus does not need anyone today to be zealous for him and use that zeal to punish someone who acts wickedly. For the Lord himself disciplines today those who sin against him, because all the nations have come to know that there is a God in heaven who puts to death and gives life. So the Lord does not need anyone today as he formerly needed the prophets, because the wicked did not understand either who was killing them or who was giving them life. For if the Lord had killed them without the prophets, they would not have known whether the Lord was killing them or their idols. They would have thought that their idols had killed them, and there they would have offered still more prayers. And when the Lord gave them life, they would have thought that their idols had given them life, and would have loved them still more. The discipline would have been futile: they would not have known who was disciplining them or why they were being disciplined. Blessed is our Lord Jesus, who through the compelling power of his love rescued them from the sword of the idols.

So God does not prevent anyone today from attaining love and perfection. Let us therefore pursue love, because if someone leaves this world today without being perfect, our Lord will not perfect them as he did the prophets. And if someone today does not walk in the footsteps of our Lord and his apostles, they will not go to be with the prophets. For after the prophets had left this world, our Lord perfected them before the apostles’ eyes and raised them to the place of perfection— them and all the righteous who, like them, had pursued perfection. But the compelling power of Jesus’ love led all creation and turned it toward the knowledge that there is a God in heaven, who created them and who sustains them.

This message also deeply stirred creation, and it turned back: they heard that the Son of God had died for sinners so that they might repent and live. All the worlds were shaken because the one who gives life to all had died for the beings he had formed. The nations heard of God’s care for them, and they trembled and understood that he had died for their sake. They were alarmed and consulted one another: “With what spirit [?] will we go to the one who formed us, whom we forgot, and who died in our place, while we do not obey him? What punishment will we deserve? Or how will his mercy rest upon us unless we repent?” With this thought the nations repented and turned back— those who had not been willing to be persuaded through the prophets.

For it is one thing when people hear that a son of Adam died for his fellow human beings, and another when they hear that the Son of God died for what he had formed, and for his servants. For it is no great thing for human beings to die for their fellows, in keeping with their lowly nature, compared with the Lord, whose nature is above death, dying for wicked human beings. For this reason people were captivated by this love and loved him.

Now let us speak again about the love of our fathers, whose love and humility we ought to imitate. Abraham and Isaac pursued perfection: when their wives were taken away from them, they neither quarreled nor fought. When their water supply was taken from them, they did not quarrel or become enemies of those who took it, and they joyfully endured the plundering of their possessions. They were not bound to either their possessions or their wives as they were to the love and affection of God. And if the Lord had told them, “Separate yourselves from your wives and leave your possessions,” as he told the apostles, they would have done his will, just as they did his will when he told them, “Leave your land and your family’s household, and go where I tell you.” For they loved him and loved other people, even though they knew that people were plundering them, wronging them, and taking away their wives. In order to fulfill the command of the one they loved, and to go and honor those who loved them, they went joyfully. Even their sons, whenever he asked them to sacrifice them, they would joyfully sacrifice. For love for him was firmly planted in their hearts, and they did his will in everything he commanded them. And if he had chosen to tell them, “Leave your wives, your children, and your possessions, and come, go and proclaim me wherever I tell you,” it would have been easy for them to leave their wives in chastity in their own lands, and their children alive, and their possessions and everything they had among their relatives, and themselves go wherever the Lord sent them. That would have been much easier than what he told them: “Go, with everything you have.” For their wives were forcibly taken away to be dishonored before their eyes, and their children to be sacrificed before those who loved them, and their possessions were plundered every day while they watched with their own eyes and endured it, because of the hope of the truth that is to come. But the whole reason the Lord kept them from renunciation and bodily chastity was so that they might also be an example to everyone who marries in this world, so that they might conduct themselves as they did.

Jacob also pursued perfection, humbling himself before his brother Esau and giving way to anger until Esau’s fury subsided. When his anger had subsided a little, Jacob sent him the message, “I am your servant,” through the gifts he sent him. When Esau drew near to meet Jacob, Jacob bowed down to the ground before him seven times. Esau's hostility subsided, and he threw his arms around Jacob's neck, kissed him, and was reconciled to him. Where is our humility today? Which of us humbles himself like this before his enemy, bows down to him, and wins him over?

Joseph too pursued perfection, repaying his brothers with good for evil: they had sought to kill him once and twice, but the Lord rescued him from their hands. They sold him into slavery, and he endured great suffering because of them. His feet were bound in stocks, and he himself was put in irons, as it is written. He repaid them with every kind of good for their evil deeds. He bore them no grudge and did not become their enemy. It is also written elsewhere that, when he did good to them in Egypt, they repaid him with evil and conspired against him to kill him. He endured these evils like a good worker and did them no harm. Instead, he did them good, triumphed, and overcame all the evil with good deeds. When Israel had died, they came to plead with him, saying, “Our father gave us strict instructions as he was dying: ‘Tell Joseph my son: Forgive your brothers' wrongdoing.’” For they thought that Joseph bore them a grudge and hostility, and that he had refrained from harming them only because of his father. Then Joseph raised his voice with sobs and tears and said to his brothers, who were his would-be murderers, “Do not be afraid of me, for I am under God.” They knew that he loved the Lord, as his fathers had, and kept his commandments. For just as his mercies are abundant, so those who love him also abound in compassion. For just as he makes his sun rise and sends down his rain on the good and the evil, so those who love him also make their love shine on the good and the evil. And because people exalt themselves and hurt their brothers' hearts, and stand against God's commandment, he casts them down in one place after another, in this world and also on the day of judgment. But if we are upright, God is kind and good, from everlasting to everlasting. The ninth discourse is completed: On the righteousness and love of the righteous and the holy prophets.

The tenth discourse: On the benefit we gain when we endure evils while practicing good deeds. And on fasting and the humbling of body and soul. By this same saint. May his prayers help us all. Amen and amen.

It benefits us, our brothers, to endure evils while doing good, because Satan stands against us. Whenever we do what is good, he schemes against us to bring suffering upon us, so that we will not do what is good. For whenever we do good to strangers or to our brothers, he brings his disciples, wolves in the likeness of lambs, and troubles us in the guise of our brothers, so that we will neither welcome strangers nor do good to our brothers. But let us not be afraid, turn back, or be deterred from any good deeds, because if we persevere, the Lord will overthrow him before us. He cannot tempt us all the time.

“Pray,” he said, “that you may not enter into temptation.” But if he frightens us through troubles or afflictions, and we flee from good deeds, this is precisely why he struggles to frighten us: so that we will not do what is good, and will leave this world without fruit. For nothing from this world accompanies us except the good deeds we do, our fasting, and our constant prayer.

Let us therefore set our departure before our eyes and see what goes with us from this world to that world. For look: in this world we are unwilling to go even to a small mountain or a nearby place without provisions, where a person can buy and sell, and can work and make a living. For if here, where a person has a hundred opportunities, he is unwilling to travel without provisions, how will he go to that world? If nothing goes with him from here, no one will give him anything there; instead, they will call him wicked. Yet we are unwilling to humble ourselves in our hearts and bodies, so that in our hearts our humility and submission to God may be known, and in our bodies our humility and submission may be revealed to everyone, as it is written: “Let your humility be known to all people.” For if someone greets people in his heart and bows the head of his heart, but does not bow his head and his heart before them, his humility is known to God alone. His humility is not known to people, and he does not teach them. And if he greets people outwardly with his lips and bows his bodily head, his humility is known to people, and it is people he pleases, not God, because the Lord is served in the heart, while people are served through visible things. But if we wish to practice and teach and be called great, let us wash and cleanse the inside as we do the outside, and the outside as we do the inside. Let our bodies and souls be alike, united in fasting, prayer, and humility. Let our bodies fast from foods and delicacies, and from all the vanity of clothing and the luxuries of life; and let our souls fast from ugly words, quarrels, envy, jealousy, curses, anger, hostility as well, and everything evil and similar to these.

For gluttony harms bodies when they are healthy, and ugly words and everything evil harm the soul. That is, if the soul is harmed, the body is harmed; and if the body is harmed, the soul is harmed. For the inner person is not without the outer person, nor the outer without the inner. But if you want to become perfect and pure, pursue righteousness of heart and body, and purity, humility, and peace of heart and body. For soul and body gain victory through one another, and through one another they are defeated. Together they are glorified, together they are disgraced, and together they find rest on the day of our Lord: those who have kept his commandments in their bodies and their souls. But let us humble ourselves before God and before other people, just as we see that our Lord and all his heralds humbled themselves and were exalted because of their humility. They bowed down before their enemies, and Israel bowed down before the one who wanted to kill him. He humbled his soul and body and bowed down before him many times. And just as our Lord humbled himself in his body and his spirit in order to teach us, so the prophets and apostles humbled themselves in their bodies and their souls. That is, in their bodies they fasted from ornate clothing and from all pride, and in their souls they fasted from foods and from every luxury. He says, “Do not worry about your bodies, what you will wear, or about your souls, what you will eat. The soul,” he says, “is worth more than food, and the body more than clothing.”

But as for those who are occupied here with the labor and profit of this world, the Lord commanded them to fast from the bonds of wickedness and the fetters of deceit, to set the oppressed free, and to fast from injustice and exploitation, from violence, sexual immorality, usury, haughtiness, and pride, and not to do to others anything they themselves find hateful. They were not to be sealed with foreign names, but to do everything in the name of Jesus and to place a seal over every illness. He commanded them to do to everyone what they wanted everyone to do to them. He says, “Break your bread for the hungry, bring strangers into your house, give clothing to the naked, and do not neglect your own flesh and blood. When you do these things,” he says, “then trust that the Lord will set you upon the stronghold of the earth, satisfy your soul with rich food, and cause to dawn for you your salvation like the light. Your righteousness will blaze like a torch, and the glory of the Lord,” he says, “will overtake you, and his salvation will dawn upon you.” This is the fast that the Lord commanded those who give alms. As for the solitaries—that is, the merciful who harm no one— our Lord commanded them, the first and the last, in this way: to fast from every luxury, saying through Paul, “It is good for us not to eat meat or drink wine.” And he says, “Be careful that your hearts are not weighed down with indulgence, drunkenness, the cares of the world, and anxious thought. of wealth. And take care, he says, not to become preoccupied, because it is the nations of the earth that seek all these things. But he commanded the nations as follows: Take care not to acquire possessions unjustly, or to build sinfully, or to build as though you would live forever, or to acquire possessions as though you would live forever. And do not live luxuriously in the world, because, he says, the present form of this world is passing away.

God could have made everyone in the world rich and healthy, settled in their own homeland and free from need. Instead, he made some rich, some poor, some strangers, and some sick. Through those who have nothing, he tests those who have possessions, to see whether they have compassion for their own flesh and blood, and whether the rich look after the poor, the healthy after the sick, the clothed after the naked, and those settled in their homeland after strangers. If they do this and have compassion on those who have less than they do, the weak find relief through the strong, and the strong are made righteous through the weak. But if they do not do as our Lord commanded, showing compassion to those who have less than they do, he sustains the weak according to his mercy, and they live in poverty in this world. But those who showed no compassion will have neither fruit nor righteousness on the day of our Lord. For Lazarus suffered during his life in this world, but he went to the other world and found rest. But woe to the rich man who went without provisions, for he will not fill his belly with the rich fare of the new world.

My brothers, look after strangers, the needy, the weak, the destitute, and the sick. Let us prepare provisions for ourselves for the long journey and for that great world, so that, when those who do good enjoy themselves and rest, we will not be tormented and afflicted opposite them. But if we want to give ourselves over to food, we argue that it is not what enters the stomach that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth is what defiles a person. And if we want to neglect prayer, we argue that we should please our Lord in our hearts. And if we do not want to make an effort to go to church, we argue that our heart is a church. And if we want to adorn ourselves, we say that we should mourn inwardly: God does not desire these outward things. And if we prefer not to give relief to anyone, whether naked or poor, we say that we should practice righteousness within ourselves and attend to our own sickness.

Evil teaches us all these things so that we will grow lax and make no effort with either our bodies or our souls. But while making us think that we are serving in our hearts, it makes us serve with neither our hearts nor our bodies. For no one practices righteousness in his heart without also practicing it with his body, because the lips speak from the heart’s abundance, and the body follows the heart’s thoughts. Just as the heart is humble, so too the body becomes humble. And if we also want to acquire possessions and build, we say, “We possess without possessing; we have things, but our minds are not attached to them.” Then let someone ask you for that possession of yours, and let me see you give it to him without being attached to it. Or if someone takes it from you by force, are you not distressed over it, or do you not take him to court, or become angry with him and become his enemy? Woe to us, for we live in falsehood and deceit. Liars resemble demons, for everyone who empties his heart of land and possessions also physically gives them up. Then if a possession is acquired without being acquired, and a building is built without our being attached to it, theft, too, is committed without being committed, and evil deeds are done without being done. Let us also say that we ourselves are heaven and earth and everything in them, that we ourselves are Paradise and Jerusalem, so that we will not even long for or devote ourselves to that glorious place which the world cannot contain, and to that Father's house which belongs only to the children who have kept the commandments in their bodies and souls, and have become holy in heart and body: they enter there. But who, then, sowed this laxity among human beings? This is sin's trick, and this teaching that encourages such laxity has the tastes of death hidden within it.

But we did know this: no food defiles, and someone who eats is not thereby defiled. Rather, his body grows heavy, becomes pampered and proud, and falls behind in the race toward perfection. Someone who adorns himself is not defiled, but he becomes boastful and conceited and is brought down from the race toward perfection. And between self-indulgence and boastfulness, pride, and arrogance—things that do not come from love— error slips in, and a person grows fat and kicks, just as the Israelites kicked. First a person forgets that he is a member of the covenant, and a little later he forgets to serve God, just as the Israelites forgot the Mighty One who redeemed them. After he has grown fat on wealth and luxuries, then he becomes defiled. For he does not become defiled immediately when he becomes proud and indulges himself, but little by little. For through a few good deeds of fasting and ascetic discipline, righteousness increases along with humility. And through evil deeds, luxuries, and extravagance in food, he becomes defiled little by little.

But our Lord and the apostles, when they emptied themselves, emptied themselves completely, and they fasted fully in their bodies and souls. For they never said, “We are fasting,” while they were indulging themselves and growing proud. Nor did they say, “We are emptying ourselves,” while possessing things, or, “We are building,” while not building. Let no one lead us astray from the way of life of our Lord and his apostles, nor from the fast that the prophets observed. While lying on each of their sides for three hundred and sixty days, they took upon themselves the guilt of sinners, for forty days at a time and for all the days. And the fasting of the apostles, who fasted continually, both they and the prophets, was so that they might be an example to us. And our Lord fasted so that he might be an example to us in his fasting and his prayer. Who would not hear and tremble, that the one who forgives debts and pardons sins fasted and pleaded because of our own wrongdoing? How much more, then, should we ourselves fast and plead because of the wickedness of our souls and because of the trials and adversities we have in this world, and because of the inheritance we have in that world, so that we may go and receive it by the grace of our Lord, with our faces unveiled before his face, because we have kept his commandments. End of the tenth discourse, on the help we receive when we endure evil while doing good, and on fasting of the body and humbling of the soul.
The eleventh discourse, on listening to the Scriptures and on when the Law is read before us.

Just as we distinguish between foods for the body and know which is good and which is bad, which is unclean and which is clean, and we know that some foods contain deadly poison, and we take care to distinguish one food from another, so also with the Scriptures whenever the scribe reads: if there is someone to explain them to us, well and good; otherwise, let us not be at a loss. Rather, let us distinguish the commandments of perfection from those concerning vegetables and milk, gentle commandments from harsh ones, and great ones from minor ones, and those by which a person does not live when he keeps them from those by which people live when they keep them. When the Law says, “Love the Lord your God more than yourself, and your neighbor as yourself,” say, “This commandment is for me.” But when it says, “An eye for an eye,” and “Hate your enemy,” and things like these, say, “These are not for me, but for the harsh and the wicked.” [?] For our Lord laid down gentle commandments for the gentle, so that they might become still more humble and be made perfect, as I wrote above. And when David says, “I hated those who hate you, Lord,” say, “This is not for me.” It was the Spirit who willed this and spoke against the Lord’s enemies, so that they might hear, be afraid, repent, and live. But when he says, “Who is the man who desires life?” and “Come, children, listen to me, and I will teach you the fear of God; keep your tongues from evil and your lips from speaking deceit; turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it; refrain from fury and refrain from anger,” and “Put an evil heart far from me, and I have not known evil,” say, “These are the commandments for me, through which I become gentle and humble in spirit.” And the same applies to things like these in all the prophets and apostles, as the apostle said: “Choose for yourselves the gentle things from among the harsh ones, and in this way you will be made perfect.” And when the Apostle and the Gospel are read, all these commandments for the perfect, which I selected for you above: Keep pursuing them and others like them, and rise above those that are vegetables and milk and are not addressed to the same person.

Do you want to become perfect? Run after the greater commandments. Otherwise, bear in mind that if you assign these greater and lesser commandments to the same person, he cannot possibly keep them together: unless he abandons one, he cannot keep the other. And see how the words of Jesus become opposed to one another. So that you may know that they are addressed to two different people, our Lord said, “Do not judge.” And he said, “Put the person to shame before the whole church.” If both are meant for you, which of them do you stand by? If you judge, you fall short of that greater commandment, “Do not judge.” And if you do not judge, you stand condemned by that commandment, “Put him to shame before the whole church.”

Again, our Lord said, “Forgive your brother seventy times seven if he sins against you in a single day.” And again he said, “Regard him as a pagan.” If they are addressed to the same person, which of them do you stand by? The one that says, “Forgive him seventy times seven,” or the one that says, “Regard him as a pagan and withdraw from him”? For by saying, “Forgive him,” he told you not to separate yourself from your brother. Thus the greater and lesser commandments clash, because they are not addressed to the same person, but to everyone according to their strength. For example, the commandment, “Do not associate with adulterers,” clashes with the one that says, “Be everything to everyone.” These commandments, then, about not judging anyone and loving everyone, are addressed to the strong. They are addressed to those of whom he said, “We who are strong ought to bear the infirmity of the weak, visit them every day, and admonish them gently.” And these lesser commandments are addressed to the children and the immature, whose consciences are offended, as Paul said: “Someone whose conscience is sick is greatly offended when he sees someone whose conscience is healthy, when he eats with pagans and admonishes them, just as our Lord admonished them.” It is like the way the Jews took offense at Jesus, saying, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.” “To the pure,” he says, “everything is pure.” That is, someone whose heart is pure from Satan thinks no evil of anyone, but only good things. Someone whose conscience is mixed with Satan, he says, thinks impure things about people.
