Again, he commanded the healthy, “Do not become a stumbling block to the sick while they are recovering, otherwise they will die, and you will be sinning against Christ, who died for them.” Again, the apostle told those who are healthy to regard everyone as better than themselves. But to the infant he said, “Do not eat with adulterers,” so that they would not make him like themselves while he was still immature in the truth. Which of these commandments does someone follow who says that they are addressed to the same person? The greater one or the lesser one? The greater one is: “Humble yourself, and regard your brother as better than yourself.” And the lesser one is: “Do not eat with adulterers.” If you keep the greater one, you receive a blessing from God. But if you hold to the lesser one, most of the world becomes unclean in your eyes. Satan makes even the clean appear unclean in your eyes, because you give him room to gain power over you. So if you keep the greater commandment, you rise above the lesser one. But if you hold to the lesser one, you fall short of the greater one. Again he said, “Become all things to everyone,” and, “Do not associate with adulterers.” That greater commandment stands opposite the lesser one. The greater one says, “Become all things to everyone, and admonish everyone.” And the lesser one says, “Flee from someone who is sick, and go to someone who has strength.” For he said that the lame should not be overturned. He sends all the sick to the strong, and the strong to the sick, since it is fitting for the strong to bear the sickness of the sick. To someone who cannot teach even himself, he says, “Do not go to the sick, but to the healthy,” so that the sick do not go to one another and die because there is no one to care for them. So if someone does not distinguish why these things were said, he neither helps nor receives help.

But the Spirit has written wisely: the sick are helped without realizing it, while the healthy person knows which commandment is his. And because our Lord said, “Whoever sets aside one of these lesser commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least,” you are not setting aside these lesser commandments when you follow the greater ones. Rather, you grow beyond that lesser commandment and follow the greater one. So when someone becomes a grown man, does he abolish milk because he no longer drinks the milk of infants? Certainly not! Infants drink it, while he does not touch milk. So too, when a spiritual infant grows strong and comes to something greater than milk, he likewise [?] to solid food, the food of those who are vigorously trained to understand and distinguish the ministry above from the one below. “As infants in Christ,” he says, “I gave you milk to drink.” Come now to solid food—that is, from the lesser commandments to the greater ones. And just as sucking milk is a torment for a grown man, bread is something that chokes an infant. Thus the lesser commandment stands in opposition to perfection. For anyone who never rises above the command, “Expose your brother before the church and regard him as a pagan,” does not attain perfection. Instead, approach the command, “Forgive him seventy times seven, and regard him as better than yourself.” End of the eleventh discourse, on the meaning of the Holy Scriptures.
The twelfth discourse: On the hidden and visible ministry of the church.

My brothers, since we believe that there is a hidden self-emptying of the heart, which leaves the earth and rises to heaven, it is right for us also to empty ourselves physically of our possessions and inheritance. Then we keep the commandments of the one who gives life to all. And we know that there is a hidden prayer of the heart for anyone who is bound to our Lord and meditates on him continually. Let us also pray with our bodies as well as our hearts, just as Jesus knelt and prayed in body and spirit, and the apostles and prophets prayed in the same way. Let us not be people lacking understanding, who will not be persuaded by their fathers. Let us not lose our spiritual fathers and acquire fathers according to the flesh who are not trustworthy and who lead us astray from the truth of our Lord and his heralds. And since we know that there is a hidden fast of the heart, a fast from evil thoughts, let us also fast outwardly, as our Lord and his heralds, both earlier and later, fasted. And since we know that the body becomes a hidden temple and the heart a hidden altar for worship in the Spirit, let us be diligent at this visible altar and before this visible temple, so that, by laboring in these things, we may live forever and ever in that great, free church in heaven and at that altar which is adorned and raised up in the Spirit, before which the angels and all the saints minister, while Jesus serves as priest and hovers before them, and above them and on every side of them. And since we know that the perfect are baptized in Jesus Christ and are washed in a hidden way, let us believe and affirm of this visible baptism that it is of the Spirit, that it brings atonement, and that it forgives the sins of anyone who believes in it, is baptized in it, and does good deeds.

For it was not in vain that our Lord and his heralds, both earlier and later, established the church, the altar, and baptism, which are visible to bodily eyes. Rather, it was so that through these visible things we might come to be among those things in heaven that are invisible to eyes of flesh, with our bodies becoming temples and our hearts altars, and so that we might depart and enter while still in this visible church, with its priesthood and its ministry, so that they may be good examples for all people who, within it, imitate the vigils, fasting, and endurance of our Lord and his heralds. Let us practice and teach these things. Then, when we live in great humility and honor all people, great and small, that church in heaven and that altar in the Spirit are revealed to us, and we offer thanksgiving upon it through the prayer of our hearts and the supplication of our bodies, while believing in this visible altar and holding firmly to this priesthood that ministers at it. That everything in this church is arranged in the likeness of that hidden church. But if we are divided and despise this visible church, this visible altar, and this visible priesthood, and this baptism that grants forgiveness, our body does not become a temple, nor does our heart become an altar and a stronghold of glory. Nor are that church on high, its altar, its light, and its priesthood revealed to us. There all the saints who are pure in heart gather, dwelling in its glory and exulting in its light, because they do not despise this blessed nurturer, who gives birth every day, raises good pledges, and sends them to that great church on high. This church is visible, seen by everyone, with its altar, its baptism, and its priesthood. Our Lord established it, for our Lord and his apostles prayed in it, baptized in it, sacrificed his body and blood in it, and truly served as priests in it. It is truly a church and a blessed mother, for it nurtures all the children. And the body and the heart in which our Lord dwells, because of the Spirit who dwells in it, is truly a temple and an altar. For our Lord dwells there, as it is written: “Your bodies are temples of the Lord,” and, “Christ dwells in your inner person.” For everything good began to exist from that church in heaven, and from there light dawned for us in all the ends of the earth. The church on earth, its priests, and its altar came into being in its likeness. Following the pattern of its ministry, the body ministers outwardly and the heart serves as priest inwardly. They imitate it and follow it as they strive within this visible church. For this reason, that church is greater than all, and it is the mother of all the baptized, especially because it is our Lord’s own face that shines in it, and he himself gives light in it.

This church, its altar, and its baptism give birth to people as infants, and they drink milk until they are weaned. Then they come to the training and knowledge of the body and the heart. They make their bodies temples and their hearts altars, and they eat solid food that is better than milk, until they become perfect and truly eat our Lord, as he said: “Whoever eats me will also live because of me.” And when they have eaten true food, as the apostle said, “True food belongs to the perfect, to those who are vigorously trained to know what the height, depth, length, and breadth are,” then they reach that church on high, and it perfects them. They enter that city of Jesus our King and serve there in that great and glorious palace, the mother of all the living and the perfect. Let us therefore not despise the visible church, for it nurtures all the children. Nor let us despise this church of the heart, for it strengthens all the weak. Let us long for the church on high, for it perfects all the saints.

All three churches and their ministries have life, but one glory surpasses another. But whoever departs from the ministry of this church and does not reach the church of the heart and the church on high, He leaves this world without sins, and it is well with him; his good deeds also accompany him. And whoever dies in the church of the heart is still more excellent. And whoever [?] in his heart to that church in heaven and then dies: Blessed is his spirit, for he becomes perfect and goes to see our Lord face to face. When someone devotes himself to this visible church, he comes to be in the church of the heart and in the church on high. It is like someone being baptized in visible water: through it he is baptized in fire and in the Spirit, which are invisible. And it is like someone who, when he believes, loves; when he loves, becomes perfect; and when he becomes perfect, reigns. But without this visible baptism, no one is baptized in fire and in the Spirit. And without this visible church, no one comes to be in the church of the heart and in the church on high. For if someone separates himself from it and worships on a mountain, he has become guilty or gone astray. Rather, wherever he is, let him be certain that there is life in it, and let him not break his covenant.

For just as a nurse who raises an infant teaches him to eat bread, which is better than milk, so this visible church teaches its children to eat something better and far greater, through which they may grow. For it is not that the woman raising the infant has no food. Rather, the infant is too weak for food, and milk is what he needs. Nor is the Spirit that ministers in the visible church weaker than in the church of the heart or in the church of the spirit, because one Spirit ministers to all three. But human beings are very weak, and unless she raises them like infants, they cannot receive solid food. Or what nursing mother is there who has many children, some thirty years old and some thirty days old? Can she possibly set the same food before them? If she sets only one kind of solid food before them, the thirty-day-old dies, while the thirty-year-old grows. And if she sets out only milk, the thirty-day-old lives and grows plump, while the thirty-year-old suffers and dies. For this reason, our Lord and his heralds, who are the guides of everyone, command the thirty-day-old: “Do not eat with adulterers, and do not associate with the sexually immoral, the dissolute, those who curse, or anyone whose deeds are evil.” But to the thirty-year-old they say: “Take on the sickness of the sick, and become all things to everyone. Do not call anyone a pagan, defiled, or evil, even when he is indeed such. Regard everyone as better than yourself, and in this way you will grow.”

They commanded each person what was appropriate for him. For if the thirty-day-old goes to the house of evil people, he is lost. But if the thirty-year-old goes to the house of evil people, he brings them back; and even if they do not turn back, he himself is not lost, because he has become a mature man in the Spirit. And likewise they also command the person whose nature is immature and who is not concerned to work and then eat while exerting himself. The apostle, however, was not concerned about the bread, but that, while idle from visible work and not knowing how to do hidden work, he should not learn frivolity, falsehood, and deceit, and fall into worldly storytelling, joking, laughter, and improper talk, and forget that he is a Christian. But to the person who is mature in understanding and attentive in heart, and knows how to do work that is not visible, our Lord and his heralds say: “Do not worry about your body, what you will wear, or about your life, what you will eat to sustain it. Instead, seek the things above and set your mind on the things above.” For a person like this can guide people, bring them peace, admonish them, and teach them to please the one who gives life to all, and put an end among people to improper talk, unprofitable stories, unwanted joking and laughter, ugly words, and evil deeds. Because of this conduct and this benefit, our Lord does not allow this person, who helps everyone, to work the land. For he says to him, as he did to Simon, “If you love me, tend my flock, my sheep, my ewes, and my lambs for me.” This person who tends Christ’s flock cannot go and drive a plow and cultivate the visible earth. Instead, he gathers, tends, and brings peace to the flock entrusted to him, and his face will be unveiled on that day before the one who commanded him, “Tend my flock, my ewes, and my lambs for me.”

Blessed is the person who has entered that church in heaven, in which our Lord shines openly, just as this visible sun shines upon this visible church and upon these bodily temples. For this sun often sets upon these, but the light of the face of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ never departs from that church above. For although our Lord is everywhere, he is seen openly in that church in heaven. But only those who have humbled themselves and become gentle and kind toward everyone, and have struggled and waged war against evil spirits alone, and have cleansed their hearts of their evil thoughts, as the apostle said: “Your struggle is not against human beings of flesh and blood, but against rulers, authorities, evil spirits, and Satan the destroyer.” Those who have struggled against Satan and defeated him are counted worthy of this church in which our Lord shines openly, which is above everything, and they receive that light of his glorious face. For our Lord said, “Blessed are those who are pure in heart, for they will see God.” For although there are other blessings and other places, for each person according to their deeds, yet to that great place only those who have been cleansed of evil deeds and contemptible thoughts are raised up, and they see him. They are glorified with our Lord Jesus and receive blessings from his priesthood. “Who,” it says, “will ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who will dwell on his holy mountain?” This is the church in heaven. “The one whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure,” it says, “will receive a blessing from the Lord and righteousness from God our Savior,” who is our Lord Jesus Christ. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen. The twelfth discourse, on the hidden and visible worship of the church, is finished.
His thirteenth discourse, on the conduct of the just.

Justice deals honestly with what belongs to her and does not touch what does not belong to her. She claims the principal of what is hers. She takes no interest and has nothing to do with bribes. She acquires property righteously and buys and sells as is fitting before God. She does not lie, nor does she borrow anything she lacks. She claims back only what she gave, without stipulated interest, even if a hundred years pass. She does not do to anyone what she herself hates. Just as she wants someone to treat her kindly whenever she is in need, so she meets everyone's needs, as far as she is able. If someone wrongs her, she states her case before one person, then before two, and then before three. If he will not agree to repay what belongs to her without interest, then she speaks before the whole church. If he will not agree even before the church, she entrusts her case to God and lets the matter go, while still speaking with him and not grumbling against him. She does not approach him to insult him, nor does she bring a complaint against anyone who harms her. She is not permitted to strike or curse, lest she depart from the law. Nor is she permitted to hope that God will bring harm upon that person, whoever he may be. For he said, “Do not rejoice at your enemy's ruin, lest twice as much come upon you.” This commandment was spoken to someone who harbors enmity. Justice, however, has no enemy, unless someone unjustly chooses to become her enemy. Nor is she permitted to call anyone another name to distress him, whether “idiot,” “Raca,” “fool,” or “ugly.” Instead, if she can, she addresses him with honorable names. Otherwise, she does not give him insulting names, but calls the person by his own name.

Justice honors the parents who brought her into the world, and they hear no harsh word from her. She honors the elderly and asks after their well-being. She honors the priests and listens to their words. She goes to them and gives her priests the firstfruits of all her produce, the first portions of her dough, and the firstborn of what she owns. She brings these into the Lord's house and does not begrudge the support of the priests who bury her dead, visit her sick, and teach and build up her living. On Sunday she sets aside some of her earnings in the Lord's house for the needy, because they come to our Lord's house. On the appointed fasting days, she brings what she saves to the Lord's house. She takes care to go and pray at the appointed time and to see whether there are needy people there, so that she may relieve them and receive a reward from our Lord. She loves those who love her and does not hate those who hate her. If someone hates her, she keeps very much to herself, making peace with him and with everyone. If she does not say good things about someone, neither does she say bad things. If she is not someone's friend, neither is she his enemy. If someone is dishonest and in distress, and she knows that he will not repay her, she gives him freely as much as she can afford. If someone's intentions are evil, she keeps to herself and does him no harm. If she can, she does him good. She does not spread a bad report about anyone to harm him. She makes peace among the brothers, honors the whole congregation of the Lord, and gives everyone the honor due to them. She honors old men and old women, and it is good for her and for the deaconesses. She herself is honored by them as she deserves.

She takes one wife, without songs, obscene words, or commotion, and worships the Lord, his Son, and his Holy Spirit. She is not dissolute, drunken, boastful, or unjust. Rather, she endures injustice and speaks the truth. She does not look enviously at anyone who lives comfortably, nor does she quarrel in the fellowship of righteousness. The wife gives her husband the love she owes him, and he gives her the same. They provide relief for everyone who is distressed or a stranger, with whatever they can. Wife and husband agree together, or man and man, or woman and woman. They clothe the naked, as our Lord said. They open their door to strangers on days of cold and heat, and they have compassion on others as on themselves. In short, they treat others as they themselves want others to treat them. They know that they do not want anyone to harm them, and they themselves do not harm others. The righteous have appointed observances of fasting, and observances to keep, during which they learn the law of the Lord their God and give alms. In short, on a day when they rest from their work, they either pray and fast or give alms. Otherwise, why are they resting? The righteous have hours of prayer, to worship the Lord their God three times a day: once in the morning, in the evening, and at midnight, as it is written: “They shall rise and give thanks to you for your righteous judgments.” Such is righteousness. This is what God commanded Adam on the day he left heaven and loved the earth.

But the love of righteousness does not withhold from anyone anything it has, whether food, drink, or clothing, but gives generously to everyone, both good and evil. By evening it reconciles anyone who is angry with it, if the angry person can be persuaded. Otherwise, it entrusts the judgment to our Lord. He asks his neighbor privately for what he owes him, and does not expose him before the congregation. If someone steals from him and he catches him, he takes back what belongs to him and lets him go without humiliating him. If the thief has nothing, he still lets him go without humiliation, and does not insult anyone who wrongs him. In every dispute, he swears only by yes and no. He does not lie, practice divination, tell fortunes, perform sorcery, or practice magic. He does not make use of familiar spirits or soothsayers, nor does he make spells or amulets. He lives blamelessly and gives alms from his own possessions. He does not envy or imitate a man who does wrong and prospers in his ways. Even halfway through his life, he can consecrate himself and become pleasing like Enoch, if he wishes. For after Enoch fathered Methuselah, he consecrated himself and did not taste death. That is, if he empties himself of everything he owns, he becomes like Enoch when he takes up the cross.

Whoever walks in this righteousness and this love while living in his home with his possessions and his wife, follows the conduct of the righteous people of old. And if he wishes to become perfect, he empties himself, consecrates himself, leaves everything, binds himself to our Lord in heaven, and becomes dead to the needs of the world. He rises to these great commandments, receives the Paraclete, and knows the whole truth, as our Lord makes it known to him. He is quickly made perfect and takes up the cross. But if he departs from the world in that righteousness and that love while still living with his household, and excels in righteousness, he inherits a portion below that of the perfect.

Those who act this way and keep these commandments of righteousness are admirable, while they engage in buying and selling, having married one wife, as is fitting for righteousness and for life in the world, and doing good to everyone, just as they themselves want everyone to do good to them, according to what each has the means to do. Whoever has a good word should give a good word to anyone who needs it. Whoever has food and clothing should give food and clothing to anyone who needs them. Just as they themselves do not want anyone to harm them, so they should not harm anyone. Just as they want everyone to forgive them for their words and deeds, they too should forgive those who do wrong. Those who are like this rank after the perfect. If they wish to leave everything and empty themselves, they quickly come to know the whole truth and are made perfect. But if they depart from the world while they are righteous, they rank after the perfect.

But the love of perfection owns nothing beyond its clothing and food for the day. It desires nothing that comes from the earth and does not toil over earthly things. Instead, he flees from everything on earth and possesses none of the things of earth. Instead, he teaches and benefits everyone through the word of truth and certainty, and in love he becomes everyone's servant. That is, he admonishes one person, teaches and loves another, honors everyone, and prays for everyone. In this way he becomes a servant and gazes at our Lord in heaven all day long, and he cannot do any bodily work without being greatly distressed in his mind if he works in this passing world. Instead, he is nailed to the cross. All his limbs are bound against doing evil and set free to serve every kind of spiritual good. His mind is bound to our Father in heaven, and at every moment and in every place he gives thanks and praise to him. The love of perfection is not permitted to fail to love everyone and pray for everyone. The perfection of the apostles speaks in this way: “We wanted to die and bring the wicked and sinners to our Lord, [?] by force, so that they might praise him.” Because the love of perfection is greater than that of righteousness, the perfect wanted to die so that sinners might live. Someone who is like this rises very high. Such a person knows, as it is written, that whoever loves our Lord loves everyone more than himself. He is the one who knows the truth according to the will of our Lord Jesus.

The love of the prophets, however, was guided by what the Lord told it, and it walked as he commanded it. But our Lord commands the love of the apostles to regard everyone as better than itself. The love of the prophets, however, loved where the Lord told it to love, and hated where he commanded it to hate. The prophets wanted to love everyone fully and become perfect, but the Lord held them back from perfection. He did this by sending them to kill the wicked, his enemies, through them. The love of righteousness, however, is not permitted to give to the good and withhold from the evil. Instead, as God commanded, one must love one's neighbor as oneself—and one's neighbor is all humanity.

But righteousness, the kind that is properly complete in its knowledge and its deeds— some of its practices are mingled with the love of perfection. It falls short of perfection because it has not emptied itself and been sanctified, and because it loves and takes pleasure in concern for bodily things. It does not dwell and take pleasure in the joy of spiritual things, nor does it become rich, radiant, joyful, and grow in the holiness of God's wisdom, rejoicing and taking pleasure, being nourished and living spiritually. The love of righteousness is not permitted to call people insulting names. But she calls those of distinction “my lord” and “my lady,” the elderly “my father” and “my mother,” her companions “my brothers” and “my sisters,” and children “my son” and “my daughter.” If they do not wish to address everyone this way and be righteous, let them call each person by name. They must not give anyone offensive names, distressing that person and committing sin. For it is the Evil One who teaches people to call one another names. Here ends the thirteenth discourse, on righteous conduct.
The Fourteenth Discourse: On the Righteous and the Perfect

The righteous do not commit adultery and are not condemned; the perfect, however, do not lust and suffer no loss. The righteous do not plunder, defraud, or oppress, and they do not seek what is not theirs. The perfect, however, do not acquire possessions, build, or plant; they do not inherit land, and they do not work for food and clothing. Instead, they live by grace in poverty. The righteous do not swear oaths, but say “yes” and “no” in every matter. The perfect, however, say only, “As our Lord wills,” so that they may not transgress and suffer loss even through a “yes” or a “no.” The righteous keep themselves separate from the earth’s evil, but not from its possessions, its good things, or participation in its life. The perfect, however, rise above the entire inheritance of the visible earth, all its evils, all its possessions, all property, temporal marriage, and all its desirable things. The righteous distinguish unclean animals from clean ones and eat of them; the perfect, however, rise above both clean and unclean animals. The righteous build and acquire possessions, but not as though these were forever, and they live in the world as strangers. The perfect do not build or acquire possessions, and their minds do not remain on earth. The righteous distinguish good people from evil people and have compassion on them; the perfect regard them as superior to themselves. The righteous uproot anger and find rest from it; the perfect, however, do not merely find rest from anger, but also love their killers and everyone else, and pray for them. The righteous reclaim what is theirs wherever they have lent or bought, without interest or additional charges. The perfect, however, do not borrow or possess anything beyond meager food and humble clothing.

The righteous rebuke without becoming angry; they admonish only with gentleness and teach with love. The righteous feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and rescue those in distress, using their possessions and property. The perfect, however, give away all their possessions in a single day to the needy and distressed, take up their cross, and follow their Lord in spirit. And they serve him in spirit, loving all people and praying for them. The righteous have one or two doors in heaven, and they knock on them five times a day. But for the perfect, all heaven is a gateway before them, and they gaze there all day. They give thanks and praise to our Lord and advance from glory to glory in the Spirit. They see our Lord in their hearts as in a mirror. The righteous receive their inheritance on this side of the city of the perfect. But the perfect are with our Lord in Eden and in the Jerusalem above, because they have become like him. The righteous cannot do the whole will of our Lord unless they attain holiness and empty themselves. But the perfect do it and are with our Lord. The righteous do not now know all the ways of our Lord unless they attain holiness and empty themselves. But the perfect both act and hear the voice of our Lord, as he said: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me, and they do not recognize the voice of a stranger.” The righteous praise God with trembling and turn away from evil. But the perfect comprehend the height and depth and length and breadth, together with all the saints who have been made perfect, have attained, have overcome, and have ascended to the Jerusalem above. It is the perfect who reach Zion and the Jerusalem in heaven and the spiritual paradise. The righteous barely reach a point far short of them, and are far below the perfect.

The righteous are not shaken and do not stray from our Lord’s commandments concerning righteousness. But the perfect excel and rise above them, and bring back all who have gone astray. Whoever is pure in heart sees our Lord. Whoever is not pure in heart cannot see him, but inherits the place appropriate to him. The righteous do not curse anyone or call anyone empty-headed, foolish, or contemptible, and they do not lie to anyone. But the perfect honor and bless everyone, and teach everyone not to lie to their neighbor. Each person is exalted according to his course, his measure, the contrition of his mind, and the extent to which he humbles himself. As for the rest, everyone is repaid in that world for what he has done in this world, whether good or evil, according to his deeds, whether good or evil. As the apostle said: “We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive in his body repayment for what he has done.” One person’s punishment is harsher than another’s. Another deserves to be shown mercy because he has shown mercy, and he escapes punishment. But whoever obeys the word of our Lord, whether concerning righteousness or perfection, does not come into judgment. But even if he comes, it is to be glorified before the judgment seat of Christ in the sight of the whole world, or to judge sinners, as our Lord said: “Whoever obeys my words has passed from death to life.” But the spiritual person—that is, the one who knows the truth and has been made perfect—judges everyone and is judged by no one.

Blessed are you, Lord Jesus Christ! How upright you are, and how good you are! Your greatness cannot be fathomed, and your grace cannot be measured. Everyone finds you according to how he seeks you. And as he compels his inclination to keep your law, so he rises; and the more he humbles himself, the more he will be glorified. End of the fourteenth discourse, on the righteous and the perfect.
The fifteenth discourse, on the sexual impulse that arose in Adam.

Now let us explain this sexual impulse that arose in Adam: how it arose in him and when it is taken away from his children. After he sinned and was condemned, and a law lower than the first was laid upon him, God permitted him, in that very law, to have sexual relations. And because he preferred to be bodily rather than spiritual—that is, earthly rather than heavenly— the impulse of desire then arose in him, because Adam wanted sexual intercourse, through the teaching of the Evil One, who cunningly contrived to bring him down from the holiness of the angels and make him resemble the animals. But Adam had already entertained these things, which the Evil One had taught him, before God permitted him to have sexual relations, while there was no desire in him. And Adam and Eve believed that everything the Evil One had taught them would happen. For if God had not had mercy on Adam, in the downfall into which the Evil One had cast him—he wanted him to become a satan like himself and to bring him under his power. Blessed is the Good One, who has opened a door to everyone who repents.

First, then, Adam and his household accepted the evil thought and longed for the beauty of the earth. “The woman saw,” it says, “that the tree was desirable to eat from and a delight to the eyes,” just as today we know that gold, silver, possessions, clothing, and earthly luxuries are desirable. These were what they first desired, in the hope of becoming like their Creator, through the deadly counsel that the Evil One put into their ears. Their minds pursued these things, for there was no desire in them that would make them long for sexual intercourse. Yet they chose it willingly, because the Evil One directed their attention to the beasts. This is why David said that the human being, in his honor, did not understand that he was holy like the angels and at peace like the heavenly beings, but looked at the animal and wanted to resemble it in mating and sexual intercourse. There was no desire or impulse in them to have intercourse until they were persuaded by the Evil One to become earthly and acquire toil and earthly wealth. After cursing them, God permitted them to have sexual relations and to toil, and desire and the flow of semen arose in them, because they sinned and transgressed his commandment, hated holiness, and loved sexual intercourse. It was not that they actually felt desire for it, but rather that they hoped, as they were told, to become great like God. Let us show from this that there was no desire in them—in Adam and Eve—before they sinned.

For it is written that Adam and Eve were naked, but their nakedness was not apparent. That is, they were like nursing infants who are undressed and do not know what nakedness is. In this condition they feel no shame at an indecent thought, for if they knew, they would cover themselves. Who, then, is the man or woman who can stand naked before the other without desire being aroused in their hearts, while seeing that they are naked? Who but those whose hearts are pure of desire and who are holy in their hearts and bodies, as Adam and Eve were before they sinned? For this reason our Lord said, “Unless you turn and become like these children, you are not like Adam in his original creation, before he transgressed the commandment of his Maker.” Before they sinned, Adam and Eve were naked like nursing infants. Because desire was not aroused in their hearts, they were not ashamed, just as nursing infants are not ashamed. But once they sinned and sin came into their hearts and induced them to desire intercourse, they saw that they were naked. That is, they came to know the shame they had not known before. And just as Adam and Eve desired intercourse only after sin had come into their hearts, and God permitted them to mate, and sexual discharge and desire for intercourse arose in them, so today, when Adam’s descendants struggle— those who love holiness and have put sin to death in their hearts through humility and love— then they leave bodily desire behind, and it departs from them, and they rise to the desire for God. Then God commands that desire be removed from the heart and sexual discharge from the body completely. Then the holy become like children, as our Lord said: “Unless you turn and become like these children, you will not be as you were before you sinned, in that purity in which I created your father, so that he would not transgress my commandments. And if you do not become like this,” he says, “you are not worthy of me, to be perfected and glorified with me.”

Nursing infants do not lust, judge, or worry, and they are free to cry at any time. But we who have been purified judge and worry, and we are not free to weep at all times for our Lord because we are separated from him. For our Lord said that those who have been found worthy of that resurrection are like the angels of God and cannot die. That is, he says, “Those who know my words and keep them become like angels.” How, then, can we say that desire is not removed from human beings? Is there, then, desire in the angels, whom our Lord said you would be like? And if you say that it is in that world that we become like angels, But let us listen to what our Lord said: “As you are found, so you will be treated.” For insofar as you are more excellent in that new world. And if you say that there are people in whom desire remains until they leave this world: Does desire, then, remain in them on that day of judgment? That is not what I am saying. Rather, if someone does not become like the angels— those who have no fleshly passions or bodily desire—while in this world, he will not be like them in that world, as our Lord said.

Our Lord promised: “Whatever you ask, you will receive, and there is nothing you ask while believing in me that will not be yours.” Why, then, do we not ask our Lord for this very thing: that we may become like the angels, without passions and without bodily desire, and live according to the perfect will of our Lord? Perhaps you say to me, “I would be glad to ask him and have him grant me this request,” which is a great gift, given through love, prayer, fasting, and humility. But we ask and do not receive because we do not do the perfect will of our Lord, since we do not keep these great commandments of his, nor do we love or humble ourselves as our Lord humbled himself. For this reason he does not grant us our perfect request, but only when we become dead to the world and condemn our bodies and put them to death because of the sin that lives in us, until we kill it. “Those who have put on Christ,” he says, “have crucified their flesh in opposition to all their desires and passions, and then they put him on.” Do you see how the people who put on Christ condemned their bodies, and did not allow them to rejoice and find rest in the comforts of this world, its luxuries, and its pleasures? Then their bodies died to sin, and they put on Christ. For this reason he said: “If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness.”

Paul said that foods do not bring us before God, because those who lived by them gained no benefit. Instead, they forgot God after they ate and indulged themselves, and the Lord’s anger rose against them. Do you see how foods and luxuries do not allow us to stand before God? It was with this hope, then, that the evil one instructed Adam and his household, saying: “In this way you will become great like God, and only then will it be possible for you to be fruitful and multiply and do whatever you wish, as the Creator did.” And Adam chose to rebel and to be persuaded to become like the animals in their mating. Adam did not know that they would have been fruitful and multiplied if they had kept the commandment, just as he had brought forth Eve through the word of our Lord, without desire. Yet even they could not have done anything without the word of our Lord. But they thought that what the evil one had said would happen apart from our Lord. In this Adam sinned and acted foolishly: he was persuaded by the evil one’s advice. He could not accomplish anything in practice apart from the Creator. Instead, he was brought low and left the paradise of the kingdom. And perhaps you will say, “Since, then, he could not actually accomplish anything apart from the Creator, why did he drive him out and shut the gate of paradise so that he could not enter it?” For was his offense a small one, that he wanted to become his Creator’s opponent, take his stand against him, and defy him, imagining that he would become like him and confront him with force? For had he not thought, “I have no regard for him,” he would have feared his command and obeyed him. But even without lust he became defiled, and they became involved in what the evil one had put into their ears. For as soon as they were persuaded and gave him a hearing, the evil thought, the taste of death, entered and became fixed in their hearts. And if you say, “But the organs were there as though intended for sexual intercourse,” if you do not desire sexual intercourse, the Creator made these organs for you to urinate through.

So keep his commandments today, as he told you, and come to that perfection which Adam lost. And see, he takes lust away from you when you attain that state from which Adam fell. And when you have become holy, without lust, you see that these organs are for urination, not for sexual intercourse, because lust no longer enters your mind when you have become holy, and you do not desire sexual intercourse, just as a dead person whose soul has been taken away does not desire it. But you are the same way: your free will too obeyed the evil one, and you desired it as Adam did. Your Creator gave it to you in anger, as he did to Adam. He is angry because we abandon the holiness of the angels and make ourselves like animals. Yet he has mercy on you as he did on Adam, and you practice righteousness and live even while engaging in sexual intercourse. And if you say, “Why did he make male and female?” go and reproach him for making male and female. He will tell you, “It would not have harmed you at all if you had not wanted to be like an animal rather than like the angels.” For, it is said, the human being looked at the animal and wanted to be like it, and hated the holiness of the angels, that is, in the hope of rising above the angels and becoming like their Lord. And the Watchers were distressed over Adam’s fall and over the wrath he received from the evil one. At that time there was hostility between those above and those below, because Adam had despised his Creator’s word. So too today, when we keep our Lord’s words, those above are reconciled with us. But once Jesus was revealed, he made it known to anyone who wishes to become like Adam at his original creation. For before our Lord’s coming, the kingdom of heaven was restricted, because it had not been revealed to everyone. Only a few individuals constrained themselves, humbled themselves, did God’s will, and reached him. That is, look: today it is revealed to everyone who loves it.

So after Adam and his household abandoned heaven and loved the earth and visible things, and transgressed the Creator’s law, God came and rebuked them, had mercy on them, and established another law for them after they had transgressed the first. And God permitted them to have sexual intercourse. Then the stirring of sexual desire arose in Adam and Eve, and then, at the end of all his wrongdoing, he had intercourse. For it is written that after God rebuked Adam and allowed him to acquire what he loved, Adam left Paradise and cultivated the earth from which he had been taken. He had intercourse with Eve, and she gave birth to Cain. But there is one kind of desire and another. The desire for intercourse is one thing, and the desire spoken of in ‘Do not covet anything belonging to your neighbor’ is another. Likewise today, when Adam’s descendants love heaven and abandon the earth and everything in it, and withdraw their minds and bodies from passing gain, and their mind humbles itself, just as it knew how to exalt itself, abandon heaven, and inherit the earth.

So when they empty themselves and humble themselves, just as they exalted themselves in the beginning, then the stirring of desire is uprooted from them. For just as God permitted desire to exist in them only after their mind came to love the earth and everything in it, so also today, when they abandon the earth and everything in it, look toward our Lord in heaven, and attain what Adam lost, and know what truth is, and height and depth and length and breadth, then they are freed from the stirring of desire. God cuts it off from them, and they become like the angels in heaven, who do not lust. For the apostle said, ‘I say these things: just as you prepared your bodily members as weapons for sin, so prepare yourselves to give ear to righteousness.’ And now, just as we know how to abandon heaven and inherit the earth, so let us abandon the earth and inherit heaven. And look, we overcome the incitement of evil, because evil has mingled even with lawful intercourse: adultery of its own, and it added fornication and something worse still than fornication, something God hates, so that Adam’s descendants might fall away even from righteousness. Therefore those who empty themselves of earthly things, look toward their Lord in heaven, and worship their God, and love everyone, become holy and dwell with our Lord in the highest heaven. And those who carry on dealings in the world, buying and selling, acquiring possessions justly and doing good to the needy: When they harm no one, they are righteous, ranking after the perfect. For human righteousness does not harm anyone who harms it, but forfeits its possessions and flees from evil, just as Isaac abandoned his father's wells of water when people quarreled with him. He named them Sitnah and Esek because they quarreled with him and made trouble for him, and he moved away from there. And just as Abraham and Isaac gave up their wives without going to court or quarreling, but God judged their case.

Those, therefore, who do good and act uprightly here and there, but sometimes harm someone, have remained constant neither in righteousness nor in wickedness; they practice both. Thus today we see people whose deeds fall below those of the righteous, who themselves rank below the perfect. The righteous are those who practice good things without harming anyone. As for those whose deeds are half good and half evil, even though they are disciplined, God shows them mercy, because they themselves showed mercy to other people. As for those whose good deeds are fewer than their evil deeds, God is not unjust so as to forget their deeds: just as he repays them for their evil deeds, so also for their good deeds. But those who have done neither good nor evil, and have neither benefited nor harmed anyone, neither descend into Gehenna nor inherit the kingdom. They are given greater honor than those in Gehenna and dwell in a place appropriate for them, and our Lord does for them whatever he wishes. But just as they harmed no one, so they withheld their mercy from everyone. They observed the saying that whoever does harm is tormented, but disregarded the saying that whoever does good inherits eternal life. Thus they deprived themselves of delight and kept themselves from torment. Righteousness, however, is this: to be upright in one's own affairs and to do good to everyone as far as one is able, without harming anyone. This ranks after perfection, because it has not emptied itself of earthly things and has not attained the height and depth and length and breadth. But those people who have neither benefited nor harmed anyone dwell between those who are tormented and those who are in the place of life, just as in this world they were between those who do good deeds and those who do evil deeds, and neither did good deeds with the former nor evil deeds with the latter. And that these things are so is shown by the fact that there are many places in the Father's house.

For our Lord said, “Whoever is dishonest in a little is dishonest in much, and whoever is faithful in a little is faithful in much.” But anyone who does not distinguish the meaning of this saying either acquits all creation by it or condemns all creation by it. Except for those who are made perfect, who do not fall under it, because they have cast off all their shortcomings. Nor do those who act wickedly and are devoid of all good things fall under it. Neither do the upright fall under wrongdoing, but they do fall short of the perfect. And because they have not emptied themselves and become holy, they have been unable to do the perfect and acceptable will of God. But because the perfect are complete, and there are no shortcomings in them, not even a little since they became perfect, and the wicked have not become righteous even a little since they became wicked, these are outside the scope of this saying. But everyone who has a little righteousness or a little wrongdoing is included in this saying. It does not allow him to rise above, nor does it allow him to descend to the wicked. So those who argue that our Lord has only one place of life and that there is only one Gehenna— where do they place these people who are a little sinful and a little righteous, since our Lord’s saying does not allow them to ascend to the highest height, the place where there are no shortcomings, and does not allow them to descend to Gehenna, the place where there is no life? For unless someone casts off all shortcomings and loves all people, good and evil, he does not reach the rank of perfection. For whoever lacks one thing is less than the perfect. Everyone, then, is repaid according to his deeds. For someone who commits a hundred murders is not equal to someone who commits one murder. Rather, if the latter gives one life, the former gives a hundred; and if the latter suffers one punishment, the former suffers a hundred. And do not say that they are punished equally. Rather, when the punishment of the one who committed one murder is finished, then, after him, the other suffers a hundred further punishments.

But all the prophets, the upright, and the righteous who attained perfection and died before our Lord’s coming while they were not yet perfect— he made them perfect in the sight of the apostles, as Paul said: “They were not to be made perfect without us.” For neither was the Paraclete, who teaches humility before everyone and love toward everyone, sent to them as he was sent to the apostles. They waited all their lives for peace to come in their days, but it did not come. For they knew that the Savior would come into the world, through the Spirit that was in them, and would bring peace to all. To Adam too, when he wept and pleaded and begged for mercy, he had promised, “I will come and make perfect those who pursue love and perfection”—the perfection from which he had fallen. Therefore, because there was no peace in their days, they were not made perfect, because the Father and Lord willed to bring about reconciliation through the suffering and cross of his Son. And if the whole world had wished, before his coming, to become like Moses and Elijah, our Lord would have allowed them to become perfect, and he would not have needed to undergo birth and the shame of the cross. He would have broken down the barrier of hostility caused by transgressing the commandment, while sitting in heaven in the glory of his majesty, and the prophets would have been spared the sword of unbelievers and the wicked and would have become perfect. “If,” it says, “the first covenant had been without fault”—that is, perfect— why would a second covenant have been needed? For through the later covenant the Lord broke down that ancient barrier of hostility. Yet the righteous people of former times who walked according to our Lord’s word were without fault.

But the perfect do not marry, cultivate the land, or acquire possessions, and, like their teacher, they have nowhere on earth to lay their heads. The upright and righteous, however, made use of the earth, and in some cases they reached perfection when they emptied themselves and became holy. And when some of them lived in virginity, they advanced very greatly, but they did not become perfect, because the Lord held them back even from righteousness when he sent them to kill his enemies. Nevertheless, all these died in righteousness and faith and did not receive what had been promised to them. And he foresaw something greater for the apostles than for them. The apostle said that without them they would not be made perfect. So our Lord made these people, who had departed without being perfect, perfect in the sight of the apostles, because he himself had held them back from perfection. For this reason he showed no partiality and made them perfect in the sight of the apostles, and God raised them up after he had made them perfect. And they appeared with him in the cities above, both they and the apostles. But as for the rest of the righteous, whom the Lord had not held back from perfection as he had held back the prophets, but who themselves wished to remain in righteousness, they are like the righteous people of today and not like the perfect, since they were not made perfect like the prophets whom the Lord made perfect with the apostles, because they did not pursue love and perfection as those prophets did.

But when the apostles departed from their bodies, from this world, they were with our Lord. And when Jesus made the prophets perfect in the sight of the apostles, they entered and lived with them in the cities above and rejoiced with the apostles in the company of our Lord, because our Lord himself had held them back from perfection, since that was fitting at that time, as it is written: “After our Lord’s resurrection, some of the righteous who had died rose up and appeared in the cities above.” But today, anyone who wishes to go to the prophets will not become like the prophets unless he follows the way of life of the apostles, because the Lord greatly exalted the prophets and righteous people who pursued perfection. After he had perfected them; and God has not permitted his servants today to conduct themselves like the prophets. But this is written in the Gospel: some of the righteous who had fallen asleep rose and appeared in the cities above with our Lord. It did not say all of them, because our Lord did not raise the bodies of all the righteous with him from the dead, but those who had been striving after perfection. He brought them up with him to show those above and those below the resurrection that is to come, and the glory prepared for the bodies and souls of all who have fallen asleep and who fall asleep in the love of our Lord, and of all his heralds, earlier and later. For it was fitting that their bodies and souls should be perfected together, just as the apostles were perfected while clothed in their bodies.

And so that you may know how Paul said that before our eyes all the prophets, the upright, and the righteous who did the perfect will of our Lord are being perfected, yet did not receive what was promised them, he said this: “You who are perfect have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, to Jerusalem in heaven, to the hosts of myriads of angels, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the upright who have been perfected, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant.” By this he showed that a transformation also takes place in their souls, since he showed that they had been perfected. And that the prophets and apostles are with our Lord today, Paul also made known when he said, “When we depart from the body, we will be with our Lord,” until that day of judgment comes, and the bodies of all the perfect rise in glory and are swallowed up in the light of their spirits. And they are glorified with our Lord forever and ever. For just as they suffered with him, so they are glorified with him. “If anyone suffers with him,” Paul said, “he will also be glorified with him, just as he was dishonored with him.”

But if someone today observes righteousness and attains it, our Lord’s coming is revealed to him—how it took place— as well as the way of life of the apostles. He discerns the commandments through which the apostles were perfected, and he also knows those through which he may give life to the world. And if he also adopts this way of life of the apostles, he receives the Paraclete and is perfected. He goes to the prophets and apostles and becomes great there, in proportion to how he made himself small here. And if he humbles himself still more, the Lord reveals himself to him in this world. He hears the voice of God and distinguishes the voice of God from that of Satan. And when he knows the whole truth, he recognizes our Lord’s voice as distinct from Satan’s. But if someone remains in that righteousness of the people of old and does not leave the earth as the apostles left it and abstained from the whole world, he cannot receive the Paraclete, nor is the whole truth revealed to him, nor does he hear the voice of God as the prophets did. But he had within him the pledge of the Holy Spirit, and he knew how the apostles had abandoned the earth and fasted from the world: And how they then received the Paraclete he cannot comprehend. But he knows the power of these commandments of righteousness: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart, and other people as yourself”; and this: “Do not do to your neighbor anything hateful to you”; And just as you want people to do to you, so you too [?] that people should do to you: So you too must do to them. And he knows that all righteousness is contained in these four commandments. He also knows that these sayings, “An eye for an eye” and “Evil for evil,” were not addressed to him. He does not put them into practice, and he leaves this world in righteousness and is gathered to the place of the righteous.

People should also know this: everything that our Lord said to them—to the prophets—at that time, when they were not perfect, was because he was holding them back from perfection at that time, and because he knew that they were going to become perfect, together with the rest of the righteous. Today, he does not speak openly with a person because that person is not perfect. Until that person reaches perfection and he knows that the person can listen to him, he does not speak with him. As he said: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments, and I will love him and show myself to him. I will reveal to him what concerns me, and he will comprehend the power of my mysteries as I shine upon him.” As for his speaking with those righteous people who were not going to become perfect: because the path had not yet been trodden by the footsteps of our Lord, he therefore spoke with them at that time, to show them, so that they would not perish or stray from the way in which they ought to have walked at that time. Today, however, the ways of life of the righteous are written down before our eyes, and the path of our Lord and his apostles has been trodden for us. There is no need for God to speak openly with anyone, unless it is right for God to call him to his path. As for the rest: until a person comes, enters into the commandments of our Lord, walks in them, and advances toward reaching our Lord’s house, like that son who squandered his possessions, then he goes out to meet him and welcomes him, like the kind father who welcomed his repentant son.

As for someone who can hear from our Lord, our Lord himself calls him to enter his path. And as for someone who cannot hear from our Lord, a person belonging to our Lord who is perfect shows him our Lord’s path. If someone can hear from our Lord, he reveals his truth to him from the beginning of his discipleship. But if he delays and has not revealed himself to him, that person should know that he can hear the truth from someone who is fully mature. There is also someone who, of his own free will, can hear our Lord’s word from letters written in ink, and humbles himself and calls upon our Lord Jesus until our Lord answers him and shows him what his perfect and acceptable will is. For not everyone is able to be called by God, and not everyone can hear from the Spirit. For this reason it is written that there are believers whom our Lord called and made. There are others whom someone called to our Lord, and there are others who humbled themselves, sought, and persisted boldly in their humility, until they satisfied our Lord, and he revealed himself to them and showed them what his acceptable and perfect will is. And that this is how a person first proceeds on the way of our Lord, either through a human being's call or through a person's humbling of himself, and that our Lord then reveals himself to him, David clearly explained: “Shall I walk blamelessly in your way until you come to me?” And again he said, “My soul thirsts for you, the living God. When shall I come and see your face?” And, “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments, and I will come to him—I and the Father and the Holy Spirit.” You see how both sides move toward one another, until a person's mind leaves the place of evil and reaches the place of peace where our Lord dwells. And just as the son left the place where he had been tending pigs, and then, when he reached his father's house, his father went out to meet him and welcomed him, so, when a person leaves the earth in his mind—the place where a person tends evil things through the desires he acts on—and hungers, as it is said, for righteousness and holiness, no one gives him anything unless his mind journeys upward to heaven, the peaceful place of his father's house, where the hired workers have righteousness and good things in abundance. So, when the penitent journeys and arrives there in his mind, the Merciful One goes out to meet him and says, “This son of mine went away from me and tasted death, and now he has come to life and returned.” Then he satisfies him with the holiness for which he hungered and clothes him in perfection, the finest robe of the highest rank. While he stands bodily on earth, his mind is in heaven every day in the Spirit, and our Lord speaks with him there as a father with his son. And he supplies others with heavenly riches, the food of the Spirit, instead of enduring his hunger here, when he had become fleshly and was looking toward the earth, without knowledge and truth, seeking to fill his belly with life here. And no one would give him anything. That is, he wanted to know even the right ordering of this world, or how he was created, for what purpose he was created, and why he had been made a slave to sin; but no one revealed it to him. And the one who was hungry then and had nothing—that is, who knew nothing— now teaches others things they do not perceive and brings them back to the house of life.

Therefore, if a person is married and lives in the righteousness of the righteous, the pledge of the Holy Spirit is in him. And if he rises above marriage while living in the righteousness of the righteous, he grows still further beyond marriage. And if someone who is married rises higher, let him rise from marital union to the apostles’ way of life. He becomes greatly perfected, receives the Paraclete, and hears the voice of God. And if virginity attains the apostles’ way of life, it becomes greatly excellent, receives the Paraclete, is perfected, and hears the voice of God. And if married life is sanctified and becomes much humbler than bodily virginity, it rises above it. But if it surpasses it only a little in humility, it becomes its equal. But if bodily virginity exists in the Spirit, empties itself, and becomes humbler than all, no one among human beings surpasses it. Yet married life that has likewise become humble and been sanctified in the Spirit walks beside it, though lower than it.

But if someone from a higher rank in that world appears among the ranks below him, they become as nothing in his eyes. And if someone from the lesser ranks appears among those above, he becomes as nothing among them. It is fitting for everyone to struggle to keep the commandments in the place that our Lord has prepared for him according to his measure, so that he may become great in the eyes of the great ones in the new world of our Lord Jesus Christ, the King of all ages. To him be glory. Amen. The fifteenth discourse, on the course of married life, is finished.
The sixteenth discourse: On how a person rises above the great commandments.

On how a person rises above the great commandments. On how a person rises above the great commandments through love. If you wish, then, listen to me, and I will show you how you can grow and rise even above these great commandments. Our Lord said to you, “If someone strikes you on your cheek, offer him the other.” Give him your whole body as well, and you have risen above the person who offers only his cheek. He said to you, “If someone forces you to go one mile, go with him another two.” Go farther than he told you, and you have risen above the person who goes as he was commanded. And he told you to forgive the offender seventy times seven. Do not demand an account of any offense at all, and you have risen above the person who forgives only seventy times seven. He said to you, “Do not judge, so that you will not be judged.” But you must not expose your brother to shame, and you have risen even above the person who offers only his cheek. For he told you not to call anyone “Empty-head,” “Madman,” “Vile person,” or “Fool,” so that you will not be condemned to Gehenna. But whoever calls someone “Fool” or “Empty-head” is liable to judgment before the assembly all day long. Because he called his brother empty, he himself became empty all day long. With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged. And if he calls him that tomorrow, he likewise becomes empty. And if he keeps calling him that until he leaves this world, He lacks understanding, and he does not gain complete understanding until he uproots these shortcomings, as our Lord said.

But one sin differs from another, and one punishment in hell from another. Everyone is judged according to their deeds. But you, call someone your own age “my brother” or “my sister,” and someone younger than you “my son” or “my daughter,” and those older than you: “My father” and “my mother”; and those who are priests, “my lords and my patrons”; and holy men and women, “my lords and my ladies.” Give honor to whom honor is due, love to whom love is due, and reverence to whom reverence is due, with respect and diligence. In this way you rise above the earlier and the later law; that is, you are with the Lord of the laws. But if you call someone “my brother” or “my sister,” regard that person as a brother or sister. Do not make your words a lie. You are not permitted to harm him, even if he harms you. And if he forgets, you must not forget that he is your brother in love. And as for someone you call “my lord” or “my lady,” remember that you are that person's servant by your own choice. If that person harms you, do not resist, but bear with that person as with a master. And as for someone you call “my son” or “my daughter”: Remember that they are your children in affection. Bring them up, care for them, and love them as much as you can. And if they forget that they are your children, you must not forget that they are your children, and you must not neglect them. And as for someone you call “my lord and my patron,” remember that he offers offerings and prayers on your behalf and on behalf of all humanity. And because of their deeds, be reconciled with them and submit to them.

And he also said, “When you pray, say: Our Father in heaven, forgive us our debts, for we too have forgiven our debtors.” Forgive your brother, and then pray. Say in your prayer, “Forgive me, my Lord, for I have forgiven the one who owed me a debt. And forgive those who have wronged me. I ask this of you, ashamed that I became angry at all.” In this way you rise above the commandments, great and small, and above the Law and the Prophets. And you attain to our Lord—that is, to his way of life, through which you go to him and to his apostles. But if you attain to these great commandments, it is easy for you to go beyond them. If you refrain from saying “empty-head,” you immediately say “my brother”; and if you refrain from saying “fool,” you immediately say “my son.” And if you refrain from saying “idiot,” it is easy for you to say “my beloved.” And if you forgive seventy times seven, it is easy for you to forgive absolutely everything. And if you become reconciled and then pray, it is easy for you never to become angry again. And if you wash your enemies' feet, it is easy for you to kiss them. And if you offer your cheek, it is easy for you to offer your whole body. And if you go two miles, You may also go as far as you wish; and if you give your tunic, you can give your cloak as well. And if you reach the commandments themselves, you will rise above them, and then it will be easy for you to remain so and grow.

At first you are constrained, but in the end you find freedom. For he said, “I will keep your law forever and ever, and I will walk in freedom.” But he said to you, “Love your brother more than yourself.” “By this,” he says, “you will know what love is: someone laying down his life for his friend.” “And if your love for me is true,” he says, “lay down your lives for your brothers.” But if you love the wicked who hate you more than yourself, you are far greater than someone who loves his fellow more than himself and his enemy as himself. In this way you rise even above the great commandments and are glorified with our Lord. For whoever carries out these great commandments becomes perfect. And if he does more than the great commandments require, loves, also humbles himself greatly, and suffers with our Lord, he is glorified with him, because he looks to him in spirit and suffers with him, as he said: “I have set you this example, that you should wash the feet of your brothers and of those who betray you.” Kiss the feet of those who betray you, and see, you have risen above someone who washes the feet of those who betray him.

Our Lord called all human beings his friends: both his enemies and his friends. He loved them more than himself, so that he laid down his life for them. Whoever becomes his disciple should do likewise, as he did. And if your teacher, who is without sins, made himself sin, which commits the sins of all sinners, consider yourself something worse than sin, and then you will judge no one. For if you say, “No one is more guilty than I am,” but you are found judging someone or reproaching him, you have exalted yourself above him, and your deeds do not match your words. Act in this way, and you will be found with our Lord. And because you consider yourself sin, you do not judge sinners; and because sin commits the sins of all creation, your sins cannot be measured. And because your sins cannot be measured, do not judge someone whose sins can be measured. “For if I,” he says, “your Lord and teacher, made myself sin in my humility, how much more ought you to humble yourselves?” For, it says, “He who knew no sin— he made him sin for your sake.” That is, he made himself so and humbled himself, to be a model for us to imitate. And if our Lord, in his humility, greeted women, we ought to bow down before men and women. For as for that child whom the Lord told us to be like, our Lord said we should be like a child nursing on milk or a humble weaned child. Where can you find a child who passes judgment in the village, or who knows who the adulterers or thieves in it are? Thus adulterers do not even hide from the children whom our Lord told you to become like, because the children do not know how to expose them. Nor is impurity apparent to their minds. Otherwise, bring a child into a house where there are adulterers and thieves, and say to him, “Go in and see what is inside.” See that he does not look at them with evil intent, neither if they are naked nor if they are committing adultery. Let us too be children with regard to these evil things, but mature in knowledge, love, and humility.

I will therefore explain to you what you should take from children and what you should leave behind. When you see a child who is not worried about his clothing or his food, say, “This is mine.” And when you see that he does not desire a woman and can weep at any time, say, “These things are mine: I will be without lust and will weep at all times.” And when you see that he does not judge and does not recognize wicked people and adulterers, say, “These things are mine.” But if you see him cursing, getting angry, doing harm, or striking someone, say, “These things are not mine.” Do not imitate him in these things. For your mind is not so childish that it should follow evil things like that child, who curses when someone tells him, “Curse!” And when someone tells him, “Strike!” he strikes and gets angry, because sin is born along with him: it is cunning, while he is childish. But you must overcome it and uproot it, and be a child when it comes to involvement in evil, as he said, “Be children with regard to evil things, but mature in knowledge.”

I will also explain to you about the fool. When you see a fool who despises himself and owns neither a house nor a wife, nor property, nor any clothes apart from what he is wearing, nor food except what he needs each day, say, “These things are mine, and I will imitate them.” And when you see him speaking in his foolishness with everyone, and making it a rule for himself not to become angry, so that he will not be disturbed; and the worldly sage who has become foolish through wisdom, and the philosopher who despises what is visible, say, “These things are mine. This is the foolishness of the apostles.” When you see him casting spells, reading omens, committing sexual immorality, practicing divination, or worshiping idols, say, “These things are not mine.” Even the fools of the world live in their foolishness and do not distinguish between those who insult them and those who honor them. They speak early in the morning with the very person who struck them in the evening. Imitate them in this way: like a fool, go to those who insult you and speak with them, and honor those who honor you. Look at the fool who, in his foolishness, does not distinguish good people from bad people. In the same way, love both the good and the bad, even though you know who they are. And when you see him behaving foolishly—if someone tells him, “Go commit adultery, or steal, or curse,” and he does so— do not imitate him in such foolishness. For it is out of the cunning of earthly wisdom that someone tells you to be a fool, not out of heavenly wisdom. Do not be like these cunning wise people, looking at the wicked and judging them. Rather, be like these fools, looking on and overlooking their follies; and like someone with heavenly wisdom, admonish them to repent. Do not judge them like someone with earthly wisdom, so that they die at the hands of wicked people. Imitate the goodness of God, and do good to everyone. But do not imitate him in repaying everyone according to their deeds, because you are not self-existent and above the law as he is. For if he does not secure justice for the oppressed, who will? Do you want to be like him? Make a creation of your own, as he did. Do not be a god within his creation, lest he overthrow you as he did Satan.

But the law has no authority over the person who pursues love in the Spirit; rather, that person is above the law. So do you want the first law not to judge you? Do not sin with your body. And if you want the later law not to condemn you, do not sin in your heart by harboring an ugly thought about another person. And if you want to be with the Lord of the Scriptures, love your Lord and love every human being descended from Adam, and then you have fulfilled the law.

For it says, “The goal of the law is love arising from a pure conscience and faith free from confusion.” People have abandoned these commandments and forgotten truth and purity of heart. “The letter kills you,” it says, because you do not know how to distinguish its commandments and draw love from them for yourself. But our Lord Jesus gives you life when you share in fellowship with him. Christ dwells in the humility and love of the humble, and to them he reveals his mysteries. And if you wish, come to this rest and taste this sweetness. See when you were at rest: when you were judging everyone, or now, when you forgive everyone and love them? See when the power of sin over you begins to be broken: when you are hostile toward those who share your faith and toward religions, or now, when you love all human beings, good and evil, and have no enemy except Satan, and have no struggle against flesh and blood, the descendants of Adam, but wage war against evil spirits, the forces of sin? Abandon wealth, injustice, and everything that passes away, and keep away from it as from an enemy. Let all people and our Lord appear to you as beloved friends, relatives, fathers, and masters; and in your love be their servant, son, brother, friend, and heir.
Let us therefore be this way, and let us pray for all human beings, from Adam until the end, that they may live and glorify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the perfect Trinity.

For the Lord is my witness: if all human beings who have existed and who will exist among Adam’s descendants were to live, from the beginning until the end, and if each one of them had ten thousand mouths, and each mouth ten thousand tongues, And for each tongue, ten thousand words; and for each word, ten thousand praises; and for each praise, ten thousand acclamations. They are too few to give thanks and praise for the kindness God has shown to human beings, whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. And human beings are too small for the places of rest prepared for everyone according to their deeds and their measure, and according to how they have disciplined themselves, humbled themselves, and suffered. And even if they rise still higher than the apostles and than the example of humility our Lord showed them, they are far too small for what our Lord has prepared for them. “I consider,” he says, “that the sufferings of this time and the race run by the perfect are not equal to the glory and beauty they are to receive: what no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart—what God has prepared in the heights for those who have loved him, abandoned everything that passes away, and loved what does not pass away, so that they may be with him in the kingdom and be glorified with him, because they suffered with him and did not acquire anything that passes away while with him, so that the service of the Spirit might not cease within them. They did not undertake earthly work and abandon heavenly work from the day they came to know him.
