What is prepared for the righteous and for those who do good is also glorious, and that whole world is glorious and excellent for whoever enters it. But one glory surpasses another. There is one that rises like the glory of the sun, another like that of the moon, and another like that of the stars. And there is one who inherits a great and hidden glory, surpassing that of the sun, the moon, and the stars. “The glory in heaven,” he says, “is one thing, and that on earth is another; the glory of the sun is another, and that of the moon is another, and that of the stars is another. And one star,” he says, “surpasses another star in its brightness.” “So it is,” he says, “in the resurrection of the dead”: one person's glory and brightness surpass those of another. But that glory in heaven is what our Lord spoke of: “What the fleshly eye has not seen and what has not entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who have loved him and kept his words”—something far more excellent and glorious than all glories. Those who become perfect and attain it are those who humble themselves, make themselves holy, empty themselves of this world, and gaze in their minds upon their Lord in heaven as in a mirror, imitating him in all his acts of humility. And when they depart from this world, they are with our Lord. The sixteenth discourse is ended: On How a Person Rises Above the Great Commandments.
The Seventeenth Discourse: On the Sufferings of Our Lord, in Which He Became an Example for Us

On the sufferings of our Lord, in which he became an example for us to imitate him: if we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him. So when you read the New Testament, distinguish the sufferings from the miracles, and suffer as our Lord suffered, so that you may be glorified as our Lord was glorified. That is, you suffer with our Lord, because even today, whenever you suffer, He suffers with you, as the apostle said after our Lord had suffered and been exalted: “If we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him.” Is it not clear that our Lord suffers with us in secret? He was tested, but he did not put an end to our trials, and he suffers with those who suffer and are tested. You see how he suffers in secret, as our Lord himself said: “Whoever insults you insults me, and whoever honors you honors me.” For he had suffered openly before that time of which Paul spoke. But to say that our Lord comes again and suffers openly—this no longer happens. Rather, if we give ourselves over to sufferings, our Lord is faithful to suffer with us in secret. So when you read that our Lord cleansed lepers, opened the eyes of the blind, straightened those who were bent over, and strengthened the paralyzed, relieved those suffering from dropsy, healed the sick, made the lame leap like deer, and loosened the tongues of those unable to speak, these are signs that our Lord performed for those who did not believe, so that they would believe. But those who believe do not need signs. Instead, they need sufferings, so that they may be perfected, suffer, grow, and be glorified. So if you believe that Jesus is God, you do not need signs, and you should not investigate how and why. Instead, come to suffering and love, and then it will be revealed to you how and why these things happened. “If anyone thinks he knows anything,” it says, “he does not yet know anything as he ought to know. But whoever loves God knows this.” You see that it is through love that a person knows everything. But since you see that our Lord performed signs that human beings cannot perform, if the matter seems objectionable to you because of his lowliness, because he does not seem like God, know from his signs that he is the Lord. Understand that he himself is not thus contemptible and lowly, but is teaching you to humble yourself and be despised like him, so that when you have humbled yourself like him, you may be exalted as he was exalted. Understand, then, his sufferings from his signs.

These are the sufferings of our Lord: he offers his cheek to the one who strikes him, speaks peacefully with him, and prays for him. If you restrain your impulses, pray for the one who strikes you, and make peace with him, you suffer with our Lord and are glorified with him.

Another suffering. Our Lord acts as a servant and washes the feet of the one who sells him, hands him over to death, and becomes a companion of his murderers. Our Lord seats him and stands before him like a slave, and washes the feet of this enemy of his before washing those of his friends. For the lowest of the disciples was Iscariot the thief, and Simon was the chief. He began with Iscariot and finished with Simon. So if you know who those are who hand you over and sell you, and who the companions of your murderers are, and you restrain your impulses and seat them, wash their feet, give their feet priority over the feet of your loved ones, and do not let them know that they are your enemies, Just as our Lord did not expose Iscariot, but said, “One of you is Satan,” and, “The hand of the one who betrays me is with me in the bowl,” so that his disciples would not stumble and say, “How could he say, ‘I am the Lord,’ when he does not know who will hand him over to death?” and go astray when these things happened and our Lord was physically absent. But as for us, no one blames us, and no one stumbles because you do not expose those who betray you. And see: our Lord did not expose him, but did make it known that he knows everything. You too, when you know that your murderer is eating with you among many others, even if you say, “My murderer is eating with me,” do not say his name and put him to shame. And see how much our Lord’s disciples pressed him to tell them his name, yet he told them only with great reluctance, when that confidant of his pressed him—the one who had entered his confidence before his companions, whom our Lord trusted as someone after his own heart. And only with great reluctance did he tell him secretly, until Judas himself said, “It is I.” He exposed himself, though our Lord did not expose him. When you treat those who sell you and betray you in this way, then you truly suffer with our Lord and are greatly exalted.

Again, another suffering: our Lord healing the ear of the man who took up a sword and came to kill him. If, then, you compel yourself to do good to someone who wants to kill you, in this way you are made perfect.

Again, another suffering: our Lord saying in prayer, “Father, forgive these people who covered my head, struck me with a reed, and slapped my cheeks in mockery, and gave me vinegar and gall to drink with fury and curses, and stretched me out on the cross in anger, and pierced my hands and feet in hatred, and stabbed me with a spear in hostility.” You too, if you restrain your inclination and say, “My Lord Jesus, forgive these people who have done evil things to me, as they did to you yourself, Lord of both worlds,” you are greatly glorified with our Lord.

Again, another suffering: our Lord saying to his disciples, “Come, let us go to those who stoned me yesterday and teach them gentleness.” They said to him, “Our Lord, the Jews were seeking to kill you.” He said to them, “Come, and do not remember in the morning any evil they did to you in the evening.” And his disciples imitated him and said, “Let us go and die with him, so that we may live with him.” If, then, you die with him, you will nevertheless be raised after a little while and be beyond death. For anyone who undergoes these sufferings is hard-pressed even to the point of death.

These are the sufferings, along with others like them. If you bless whoever curses you, love whoever hates you, pray for whoever persecutes you, and forgive whoever wrongs you seventy times seven in a single day. This concerns what our Lord said: “Do not be angry at all with anyone who sins against you.” But if you are not convinced that he told you to forgive all these offenses in a single day in order to keep you from becoming angry at all, and you therefore intend to become angry with the offender once these four hundred and ninety offenses are complete, keep counting from morning to morning, night and day. And if your fellow human being commits four hundred and ninety offenses— which is the total of seventy times seven—if you find that the offender has committed all these offenses in a night and a day, you are allowed to be angry with him. But if you do not have even five or ten to hold against the offender, has it not become clear that our Lord has forbidden you by this saying to become angry with the offender? This is what it means: when you have loved him, repaid him with good for evil, washed his feet, and prayed for him, then you become perfect, when you give yourself to someone who wants to kill you and profit from you, and you become all things to everyone, and you make disciples of sinners and prostitutes, and you do not recoil from the unclean and the wicked, or from those who have the rust of sin in them, and you heal everyone who comes into your hands, like a good physician.

If you suffer in this way, blessed are you, for your heart is being purified and you see our Lord. For this is what Stephen did, and he said in prayer for those who drove stones into his brain: “May this sin committed against me not be counted against them.” Do not think that our Lord alone prayed for his killers. All the apostles also said these things to those who were gnashing their teeth at them: “Men, our brothers, listen and live! On God’s behalf we beg you to be persuaded.” Even while they were being killed, they prayed for their killers, just as our Lord had done before their eyes. And when they were taking them outside the city to kill them, they would stand and urge them to live, and then give themselves over to them to be killed. And when they hung them on crosses, even as they were crucified they continued to exhort and teach them. Glory to our Lord Jesus Christ, who suffered apart from them, while they suffered with him and in him. That is, he suffered alone and became an example for us, so that we might imitate him, suffer with him and in him, and walk as he did. Glory belongs to him, and blessed are they. Our Lord, do not deprive us of you or of their company, but let us rejoice with you and with them in your presence.

But if you want to know these mysteries, do not stop praying and asking everyone, and do not despise anyone, for perhaps the very person you despise knows the truth and will explain it to you. And be humble and bow down before God and before all people. Be like a man traveling to a distant country or to some city, who looks down on neither a child nor an old man, nor a lame person, nor someone whose face is ugly, nor does he look down on a woman. Instead, he asks everyone he meets to direct him to where he wants to go. So too, you who want to go to the city in heaven, do not look down on any of the lowly and despised, but keep asking humbly, until you find someone who shows you the heavenly road, so that you may go to the home in heaven and enter the presence of God, who gives you joy. The seventeenth discourse is finished, on the sufferings of our Lord, through which he became an example for us.
The Eighteenth Discourse: On Tears in Prayer

Understand, then, my son, what I am saying. There are tears caused by sorrow, and there are tears caused by joy. As our Lord said, “You will weep and mourn and be sorrowful, while the world rejoices. But after a time your tears will turn to joy.” For there is someone who weeps over his sins, and he does well, as it is written: “Sorrow for God's sake is repentance of the soul that leads to life.” And there are people who have overcome sin, turned away from sins, and done good things, and they weep with joy because of their love for their Lord, who showed them great kindness, freed them from slavery to death, and made them free people, because they humbled themselves and kept his commandments. As David said, “This is the day the Lord has made. Come, let us exult and rejoice in it. O Lord, save us! O Lord, deliver us! Let us exult and rejoice on this day of our salvation.” And when a person has been freed from slavery to death, he serves the Lord with joy and not with sorrow, as David explained: “Serve the Lord with joy, and enter his presence with praise.” And again he said, “Serve the Lord with fear, hold fast to him with trembling, and kiss the Son, lest he become angry and you perish from his way, for in a little while his anger will blaze, and all the wicked will burn. But blessed,” he says, “are those who put their trust in him in this world.” He saves them, and then they depart from it and are made perfect in the love of our Lord Jesus. They are glorified with him on his great and fearful day.

Now, concerning the tears I spoke of: there is someone who weeps for his friend because he loves him and is far away from him. So if someone is far away from his friend, he weeps for him, either because of his love or because of his sorrow. But when someone sees his loved one, he weeps as he meets him, and his tears flow over his loved one's neck, and everyone near him sees him. Is it not well known to everyone that these are tears of joy: when someone sees a loved one whom he had not expected to see, he weeps, his tears flow, and he sobs? So too, people who sin and are far from our Lord and his righteousness weep in sorrow, like someone who is far from his friend, grieves for him, and weeps. These people too grieve over their sins because they fear our Lord’s judgment, and they weep so that God may have mercy on them and forgive them. And if they turn away from their sins and become righteous, they draw near to our Lord, and their tears turn to joy. And when they are without sins and are freed from sin, they weep before our Lord with joy, just as someone sees a loved one whom he had not expected to see, throws his arms around his neck, and weeps over him with sobs and tears of joy. So we too ought to strive to be without sins and ask our Lord to free us from sin, as Paul said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death, except the grace of God that is in our Lord Jesus Christ?”

Therefore, let us leave behind everything visible, because it is passing away, and let us turn away from outward sins. And when we have put an end to all our visible sins, let us stand in battle against the sin that dwells within us, namely, these evil thoughts that sin fashions within the heart. Let us run with strength in the contest set before us, and let us struggle in prayer, as our Lord did before us and showed us, for with a mighty cry and many tears Jesus offered supplication to the one who saves him from death. And he was heard and made perfect. Our Lord teaches us these things so that, when we are without manifest sins, we may enter the struggle of prayer, just as our Lord said and just as he did. Paul said to the brothers in our Lord: “Epaphras struggles for you in his prayer.” Now our Lord cried out mightily and was in anguish in prayer, and his sweat became like drops of blood, and he shed many tears, to show us that, when we are without outward sins and manifest transgressions, we should offer supplication and prayer. But until we suffer anguish in prayer as he did, shed tears as he shed them, and cry out mightily as he cried out, we are certainly not freed from the sin that dwells in the heart or from the evil thoughts it devises within us. For this is indeed fitting for men who are in Christ: that they raise their hands in every region and every place, without anger and without evil thoughts, and shed tears in their love for our Lord and their longing for him, wondering when they will go and see him face to face, as it is written: “Blessed are those who are pure in heart, for they will see God”—indeed, in this world, as Paul said: We see our Lord with the eyes of our hearts as in a mirror, but in that world, face to face.

The heart, therefore, is not purified unless hidden sin has ceased within it, and the evil thoughts concealed and buried within it through the power of the sin dwelling in it have come to an end. Sin is not uprooted from our hearts, nor do its evil thoughts and its fruits cease, unless we pray as our Lord and all his heralds prayed. When we pray to the Lord in our hearts, let us rejoice joyfully, from our lips inward. We rejoice inwardly, when our hearts do not condemn us for sin, and when our faces are unveiled before our Lord because we have kept all his commandments. We rejoice as David said: “Let my heart rejoice in you, Lord, and in those who fear your name. I will give thanks to you, my Lord and my God, with all my heart, and glorify your name forever, because your grace toward me has been great, and you have rescued my soul from the depths of Sheol.” You see how God delivered our fathers from the power of Sheol, and how their hearts rejoiced in the Lord and in those who fear his name. As Mary also said: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior, because he looked upon the lowliness of his servant.” You see how she rejoiced inwardly in spirit and was glad in her mind because she had found grace and mercy before the Lord.

Let us, therefore, be a law to ourselves and pursue perfection. When we hear the word of truth and mercy, let us be good soil for it, so that it may send out shoots within us, take root in our souls, sprout, and yield fruit, thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold. Let us not be thorny soil and choke the seed of truth, and ourselves be choked off from life on that day of our Lord’s judgment. Nor let us be the soil of the evil one’s path, which does not allow anyone to bury good seed in it: a bird comes and picks it up, and it does not sprout. Likewise, let us not be hard, so that the word of life cannot enter us or take root within us, and the evil one snatches the good seed from our soil. Nor let our minds be far from knowledge, like shallow soil whose seed is scorched and does not flourish in the sunlight. Let us strive to bear fruit, lest, when the children who do our Lord’s acceptable and perfect will shine in the sun— the new sun of righteousness—we ourselves be scorched by that sun of mercy, with healing on its wings. When, therefore, we have heard the word calling us to follow the way of life of our Lord and his heralds and become perfect, let us be a law to ourselves, imitate them, and say: “Why do we not become like them, since they too were like us?” Let us listen to Paul when he says: “I despised everything visible, and counted as dung all the gain that remains here and does not accompany me to that world of truth and glory.” “Become like me,” he says, “because I too was like you.” You see that, if we wish, we can become like Paul. End of the eighteenth discourse, on tears in prayer and the distinctions between them.
The nineteenth discourse, on discerning the way of perfection.

Give me, then, the ears of your mind, you who wish to become a solitary and are eager to go quickly to the city of our Lord Jesus. I will show you how to go straight to the city of our King, if you have the strength to travel as I show you. For the ascents that I am marking out for you to climb are difficult. But there are also many paths that lead away from the straight road, which take you on long detours around many mountains, and day after day you are delayed, until the day of your departure comes and finds you on paths that turn this way and that, because you did not know how to travel straight along the road to that city. And if during your lifetime you do not seek out and learn that road, and travel eagerly and reach that city, you will not be able to go there once you have left this world. For the end of your road is perfection, and its beginning is when you begin to uproot all your shortcomings. For just as with the road to these visible cities of this world, if there is no one to direct you to cities you have not seen and do not know, the paths branching off their roads lead you astray, and you wander around for a long time without reaching the place you want to go, so it is also with that hidden road leading to that hidden city, from which many paths branch off in every direction. And if there is no one who knows that road leading to that place to guide you and point out to you all the paths that lead away from it, you cannot travel straight, and you fall behind in the swift race toward perfection, and you leave this world without being perfect. Nor will you then be able to be with our Lord in his city and his kingdom in that world, and you will not enter that city of the saints.

Now these paths that lead away from the perfect road leading to that place where our Lord is seen face to face are not evil. Rather, our Lord and his heralds made them branch off that great road for the sake of infants and the weak. And this is because the ascents are difficult, confined, and narrow, which a person encounters on that road leading to that city. It is so confined that above it is very high, and below it is very deep. If you turn aside to one side, there is fire; and if you turn aside to the other, there is a great expanse of water. If someone falls down below, he is broken; if someone enters the fire, he is burned; and if he falls into the water, he drowns. And it is high above, and the ascent is difficult and narrow. But if you want to go to that city, you must compel yourself to climb and ascend to that great height, without turning aside to the right or to the left, or down into the depths, so that you do not perish. Instead, climb straight up, so that you may quickly reach that great and glorious place. I will explain to you these wonders of the difficult ascents, of fire and water and the great depth. If you have believed the words of Jesus and made a covenant with him to obey his words and keep his great commandments, from that moment, whether in body or in spirit, you have come to this path of the commandments, and you are entering these ascents. If you wish to climb them by confirming your covenant with Jesus, and to see him and receive from him what he promised you— for he said, “You will enjoy yourself with me at the table of the kingdom”—unless you humble yourself like a servant before all people, good and evil, you cannot climb these ascents and complete that path which leads to the place where our Lord promised you would enjoy yourself. And if you turn away from your covenant, you fall into a great depth that leads down to Sheol. And if you transgress his commandments, you go to Gehenna, which is fire. And if you deny him, you are choked like Iscariot in hidden, suffocating waters, which are the teaching of the Evil One.

But listen to what our Lord said: “Narrow is the path that leads to life.” How much narrower, then, is the one that leads to perfection and surpassing glory? Again, Ben Sira said: “Humble yourself below everything on earth, for if you have committed yourself to the fear of God, you have committed yourself to every trial.” “But humble yourself,” he says, “below all people, and endure affliction for a short time, so that you may go to rest that does not pass away. Do not break your covenant, lest you go to affliction that has no end.”

Now our Lord and his heralds provide paths that turn off to either side from that height which rises straight upward, not so that the strong should be held back and fail to ascend, but for the weak and for children, who cannot climb these ascents while they are young and weak. For this reason he provided them with paths that run along the lower slopes of these ascents, beside them, so that they may travel alongside the path that rises to the height while they grow stronger and mature, so that they may have the strength to climb that narrow path and these ascents, and not become afraid and turn back altogether, or falter because of their youth and weakness and fall into that great depth, or slip to one side and perish. And because the hardship of these paths is not as great as that of this great road, people therefore love them, not knowing that unless they come to this narrow road, they will not enter that city of great rest. But let us not allow our illness to linger and our growth to be greatly delayed. Instead, let us make every effort to recover and grow, and let us come and enter the road traveled by vigorous men. For as long as we stroll along paths that are easy for us, we are trapping ourselves. Unless we come to this narrow road, we will not become mature.

The paths are the lesser commandments, given like milk to infants and like vegetables to the sick, because they could not receive the greater commandments, which are solid food for the mature. That solid food, it says, belongs to those who train strenuously. You see how the sick and infants cannot climb these ascents. “And I, my brothers,” he says, “could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to infants in Christ I gave you milk to drink.” “Come, then,” he says, “to solid food. When I was an infant, I behaved like an infant, following the lesser commandments. When I became a man, I put away my childish thinking.” That is, he says, “I left the easy paths, which are the lesser commandments, and became a man and reached maturity. Imitate me, my brothers,” he says, “as I imitated Christ and reached maturity.” You see that he cannot show them how to ascend to that height while they are young and sick. Instead, he showed them these paths, the small commandments. And now, once they had grown strong and recovered, he called them, saying, “Come, walk on the straight road,” which is the greater commandments, for it is the mature and strong who eat this food and travel this great road.

And we—how long will we remain children? Will we not recover from illness and grow from childhood into manhood? “One person,” it says, “has faith to eat everything, but the one who is weak eats vegetables.” Was the apostle speaking, then, about these visible foods? Look: someone who eats everything is of little standing among the solitaries, and is not as virtuous as they are. Indeed, the apostle himself instructs us that it is good for us not to eat meat or drink wine. Our Lord also warns us: “Do not let your hearts be weighed down by eating meat, by drunkenness from wine, and by the cares of life.” Is it not clear that Paul called the person whose conscience is weak and whose understanding is limited “weak,” and that he does not call the person who fasts and eats bread, vegetables, and salt “weak”? For if someone fasts and prays, a person who lives this way is virtuous. But he reproaches anyone who does not keep the great commandments and calls him weak. But, he says, there is someone who has the strength to hear, accept, and keep all the commandments, and to distinguish the great ones from the lesser ones. And there is someone who cannot even hear these great commandments, because his understanding is immature or his conscience is weak. The great commandments are those ascents I mentioned; otherwise, he accepts the lesser ones, which are those paths I mentioned, and walks along them until he grows strong and becomes healthy. But if he dies and leaves this world while he is still on the paths, he will be in the place of life and will not perish like someone who turns back from that narrow road and falls into the great depth of Sheol. Even if he walks along these paths that our Lord and his heralds opened up, which are the lesser commandments, which were spoken for the sake of children and the weak, he will be in that place of rest and will successfully attain life, even though he does not enter that great city and that place where our Lord is seen face to face, unless he comes and climbs these ascents, which are the great commandments and counsels.

As for the way of life of the prophets and the old covenant, he has explained to us above how we should listen to the writings of the prophets and the law of Moses. But now we ought to follow the Spirit, submit to her, and look to the new covenant, which is Jesus Christ, and imitate him. For he became the founder and perfecter of our faith. For look, the apostle said that he made the covenants, the first and the last, into one covenant. And by his commandments he abolished the law of those commandments that were not required, so that, he says, through both these covenants, which he made into one gospel, he might create human beings anew. Before Christ came, he says, we were under the law, which was over us like a guardian over God's household. Just as, he says, a guardian oversees the household of a great man until the heir grows strong, but when, he says, the heir whom the master of the house left behind becomes a man, the members of his household are no longer under the authority of guardians or household managers, so too, he says, we who are God's household, for as long as this new covenant was hidden, were under the law of the old covenant as though under guardians. But now that the heir of the household has been revealed, we are not under guardians, but under the authority of the master of the house, who is the Son, Christ, in the new covenant, who is our Lord Jesus Christ. Just as the affairs of an heir in this world are placed under guardians as long as he is a child, and when he becomes a man, he claims and receives from the guardians the inheritance his father assigned to him, so too, as long as Christ was hidden, his servants and the members of his household were under guardians. But now that he has been revealed, like an heir who has grown up and taken his father's possessions from the guardians and household managers, those who belonged to him also recognized that they had their master, and they ran after him and took refuge in him. It is he who freed us from the yoke of slavery to sin and from the heavy burdens of the old covenant, and harnessed us to the gentle, light yoke of the new covenant and its light burdens. For he took those great commandments of the old covenant, on which the whole force of the Law and the Prophets depends, and established them in the new covenant. He gathered together its entire force, from first to last, and placed it in one new covenant. Let us explain and see what force of the Law and the Prophets is fulfilled in these two commandments, and combine it with the force of the new covenant. Let us walk on the road that our Lord Jesus opened before us, and go to that place from which our first father departed.

From now on, my son, stand firm in the new covenant, and let it be greater in your eyes than all the covenants, in keeping with its greatness, because in it God's acceptable and perfect will is fulfilled in spirit. Paul also wrote: “Woe to those who regard the covenant of the Son of God as that of any ordinary person.” They insult the Spirit of grace by putting our Lord's covenant on a level with anyone else's. For those covenants were sealed with the blood of speechless animals, but this one was sealed with the speaking, pure, and holy blood of the third, our Lord Jesus Christ. Love the new covenant, then, so that it may show you the straight road that comes from it, along which a person quickly reaches the city of the saints and that place where the perfect rest: those who walk according to the great commandments that I am explaining to you, so that you may follow them directly and swiftly.

This is the perfect road: whoever does not break free from his entire family cannot manage it. But this is the path that turns you aside from it: live with your parents and honor them while their minds are bound to earthly things. But what he said—“Live with your parents and your leaders, and honor them”—was for children who are themselves also bound to earthly things. Thus it is good for them to be with their parents, honor them, and live through them.

This is the perfect and straight road: regard everyone as better than yourself. But this is the path that runs alongside it for infants and the weak: if there is a brother who is sexually immoral, abusive, greedy, or a drunkard, do not, it says, even eat bread with such a person. So that the infant and the sick person should not fall from this commandment, which is a great ascent, the Spirit laid out this path for him, so that he might walk alongside this ascent until he grows strong or recovers, and then come and climb it properly. As the apostle said, “Come now, since you have become adults, to this solid food.” For if he had allowed infants and sick people to regard sinners as better than themselves, they would have mingled with them, done what they did, and fallen from the great height of that ascent, the ascent of that great commandment. Instead, he diverted them a little toward the lower slopes of the ascent until they grew and recovered. That is, he separated them from among the wicked until they received power from on high, so that they would not go among the wicked without strength and perish. That is, so that they would not climb that ascent without strength, slip, and fall from it.

This is the perfect way, in which the strong are made perfect: “Blessed are those who make peace with everyone, for they will be called children of God.” And, “Let your gentleness be known to all people.” But this is the path that diverts you from it: “Do not greet anyone on the road.” And, “Discipline those who do wrong.” This is said to someone whose conscience is weak and whose understanding is immature, lest the child fall and be harmed through a greeting, or, because the wrongdoer is not disciplined, someone else like him become arrogant, and someone who is going to imitate him become lax. So when an immature person has offered a greeting in a place he does not trust, he should pass on quickly and go to a place he trusts, and remain close to the strong person who teaches him, so that he does not take liberties and become lax with someone he does not know, not knowing whether that person is truthful or deceitful. For this reason he forbade the infant to greet others, so that they would not take him captive where he was unaware. He should therefore make peace with all people, good and evil, but he should give his companionship and obedience only where he has trust and experience, and knows that they will bring him up properly and establish him firmly.

This is the perfect way: “Bless the person who curses you, love the person who hates you, and pray for the person who mistreats and persecutes you.” But this is the path that diverts you from it: “Regard someone who will not listen as a pagan and a tax collector.” This is said to the weak person: he should regard someone who will not listen as a pagan, rather than strike and kill him.

This is the perfect way: “Do not worry about what you will eat or what you will wear.” But this is the path that diverts you from it: “Work and eat your bread, and do not be a burden to anyone.” This is said to someone who wanders about, because he does not labor at heavenly things through fasting, prayer, keeping vigil, and humility. He told him, “Work, even at earthly things, and give alms.” Do not be completely idle in both of these, lest evil gnaw at you and you become a deviser of every kind of evil.

This is the perfect way: men who have not taken wives and women who have not married men are like angels and cannot die. And he says, “Whoever does not leave his wife, his children, his family, and everything he has on earth is not worthy of me.” But this is the path that turns you aside from it: “What God has joined together, you must not separate.” This is said for someone who does not discipline himself and subdue his body. For it is better for him to marry rather than become corrupt through adultery and sexual immorality, because he does not humble himself and fast from all foods while he is alive and his body is young, and because he does not persevere in prayer and guard himself from everything evil and every hateful word, and make himself someone who blesses rather than curses, someone humble rather than proud and harsh, and a person of peace rather than hostile and quick-tempered. For this reason he also succumbs to bodily desire, becomes corrupt, is overcome, and acts wickedly.

This is the perfect way: a virgin who does not marry a man and a man who does not take a wife— they please our Lord in body and spirit. But those who marry please one another. But this is the path that turns you aside from it: “Marriage,” it says, “is honorable, and their bed is pure.” Again, this is said for someone who does not restrain his body from foods and persevere in fasting and prayer. For he knows that someone who indulges his body and neglects spiritual work is overcome by desires. It is better for him to marry rather than become dissolute and corrupt.

This is the perfect way: “Seek the things above and set your minds on the things above.” But this is the path that turns you aside from it: “If anyone does not work, he must not eat.” Again, this is said about the wanderer and the person preoccupied with needless matters, who slanders and devises evil, does no spiritual work, and does not ponder truth in his heart, so that when no one feeds them, they work on the land, and occupy themselves with this passing work and cease from evil deeds, slander, and needless matters.

This is the upright and perfect way: “Offer your cheek,” it says, “to the person who strikes you, and pray for him.” And it says, “Release others, and you will be released; forgive, and you will be forgiven.” But this is the path that turns you aside from it: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven.” Look, my son, and see how he tells the perfect person, “Pray for whoever harms you,” and he prays. And he commands the leaders, “Bind the offender and remove him from among you, but do not beat him.” But they cannot bear with him, and they beat him and sin. For when they bind the offender so that he may be disciplined, and so that others may be afraid and not imitate him, they do not sin. Nevertheless, they fall short of perfection as long as they hold positions of leadership. For when they beat him, they sin, because they turn aside even from the righteousness that comes after perfection. But this was said to the leaders: Through this word, which binds offending people in heaven and on earth, they are to restrain everyone who rebels against the church’s righteous way of life.

This is the perfect way: if someone forces you to go one mile, go another two with him and make peace with him. But this is the path that turns you aside from it: someone who behaves like this is to be separated from you, so that you do not associate with him. This was said to children, so that they would keep away from evil people and not themselves be drawn into their evil will.

This is the perfect way: possess nothing on earth. But this is the path that turns you aside from it: The person who used to steal should work and acquire possessions, so that he may have something to give to the needy and may live. Everyone knows this: It is far more beneficial for someone to work, acquire possessions, and give alms than to steal and grieve his neighbor’s heart, be condemned at the judgment, and suffer punishment in the end. And if he is caught in this world, he is beaten and dies, or he is stripped completely, imprisoned, and condemned at the judgment, here and there.

This is the perfect and upright way: whoever wishes to be great in the kingdom of heaven should make himself less than everyone, and honor everyone like a good servant who honors his masters. But this is the path that turns you aside from it: Because you have not understood our Lord’s word, you say that the leaders of the nations are their masters, and you have forgotten that saying of our Lord: “Whoever is your leader must be your servant.” Nor have you understood that he said: “Leadership among you must not be like that of the nations, whose leaders make themselves lords and rulers over them. Instead, honor one another as servants.” Yet you have exalted yourself like the kings of the earth, who have no fear of God in their hearts or before their eyes, and who go headlong on their way, mercilessly judging and condemning the people under their authority, condemning without pity, and killing without restraint, without mercy, and without fear of our Lord. Thus they act wickedly and descend to the depths of Sheol and to the bottom of the pit of deepest Gehenna. And you act brazenly, you who have been called a disciple of Christ, who in his love became everyone’s servant, and was beaten but did not strike back, and loved his killers and prayed for them because of his abundant mercy and his boundless humility. to teach us to imitate him. And you say this without trembling: that you imitate the rulers of the nations, because of whom the whole world under their control cries out, as they plunder it and kill its people without mercy? If these are the things you want, you are not Christ’s disciple. Leave our Lord’s church, join the kings of the nations and their nobles, carry out your evil desires, and act wickedly. For Christ’s law is far removed from these things and from anything like them. It strives entirely to advance good and beautiful things, love and humility, to give everyone life and make them great in the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, the mighty and valiant Lord.

This is the perfect way: when the bridegroom has been taken up, the disciples should fast continually, with diligence of heart and body. But this is the path that leads you astray from it: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of his mouth and what his evil heart devises defiles a person.” Foods themselves are not defiling; rather, a person indulges himself, goes astray, and becomes defiled through luxury, through desires that lead to error and death, and through sinful deeds. This—if someone keeps himself from foods that are unclean according to the law, while indulging in other foods that are clean to his conscience, living extravagantly, and filling his heart and mouth with evil thoughts and ugly words— was said so that he would know that unless he cleanses his mouth and heart, he is unclean even while abstaining from what defiles his conscience. For it would have been better for him to cleanse his mouth and heart and eat, rather than fast while unclean. That is: without fasting, prayer, humility, and love, a person cannot be cleansed.

This is the perfect way: let no ugly word come out of your mouths. But this is the path that turns you backward, so that you do not reach what the way promises: when you want to imitate our Lord and call people a brood of vipers: “How do you do what is good, when you are evil and children of the evil one?” Or when you imitate the Spirit who spoke through Paul and call people fools and lacking in understanding. For he has not given you this authority as your own. For our Lord is not subject to the law, and the Holy Spirit permitted Paul to call people such things. But our Lord called people these things to let them know that he is their Lord and has authority over them, and to let them know that he will judge them at the end, and that he humbled himself willingly to give his disciples an example to imitate. This was so that people would not reproach them and say, “Just as our Lord was humble in his words and conduct, Thus he is meek on the day of judgment. And because they would sin without fear, our Lord instilled fear in his hearers through his words and said: “Woe to you who show favoritism, for on that day the King will say to you: ‘Depart, you who are cursed, into the fire prepared for the Evil One and his servants.’” Yet in his conduct he was meek toward everyone. But even if it had pleased our Lord not to humble himself in his conduct, and to tell everyone, “Be humble in your words and also in your conduct,” who could have given him orders? Can something made find fault with its maker? No. Human being, do you dare to find fault with God’s commandment and say, “I do as he did”? Then create creatures, raise them, and nourish them as he does. Our Lord, then, has authority to put to death and to give life. He who is above all authority humbled himself. And wherever he spoke a harsh word, it was because it was right for him to speak that way at that time before his hearers. But he commanded us, “Let no foul word come out of your mouths.” We, then, as obedient servants and as people under authority, should speak with propriety and humility, as our Lord commanded us, so that he does not justly put us to death for transgressing his commandments.

This is the perfect way: forgive the offender four hundred and ninety offenses, even if he offends against you in a single day. But this is the path that turns you aside from it: if he does not listen to you before the church, let him be separated from you, so that you do not associate with him. This is said because of the hot-tempered and because of the lax, so that the hot-tempered do not commit wrongdoing in their anger, and the lax do not become emboldened in sin because no one rebukes them, and so fall into wrongdoing. But when they are separated, both sides have peace: the former, so that they do not commit wrongdoing in their anger when they see the offenders’ insolence; and the latter, so that they do not fall into wrongdoing through their laxity when they see that no one rebukes them, disciplines them, or warns them not to fall into these things.

This is the perfect way: “Blessed are those who are pure in heart, for they will see God.” But this is the path that turns you aside from it: unless he tells you, “I repent,” do not forgive him. This, however, is said for someone who is stubborn and does wrong, so that he may humble himself, turn away from the evil way, and say, “I will not do such a thing.” Then let him be forgiven, and let it serve as a warning and a discipline for others, so that they do not become insolent or lax. This, however, belongs to leaders, not to the perfect. The perfect do not seek leadership. And if they hold leadership and attain perfection, they give up leadership; then they can become perfect. For the perfect teach everyone with humility and cannot make demands on anyone by force, as leaders do. But leaders, in each place over which they have authority, are permitted to demand everything that is rightfully due, and to discipline, as duty requires, anyone who rebels against his companions, and to remove him from their midst until he repents. For this reason he says, “Speak and press your claim.” Those who pursue lawsuits and accusations cannot become perfect, peaceful, and gentle. The upright, however, if they wish, can attain righteousness through these lesser commandments and fare well on that day of our Lord. But they cannot carry out the perfect will of our Lord, because, as long as they hold on to accumulated possessions, they cannot leave these lesser commandments and come to the greater commandments, through which our Lord’s perfect and acceptable will is accomplished, and eat the true food and become perfect through sufferings, humility, and service in the Spirit.

This is the perfect way: if you remember that someone holds a grudge against you, go and be reconciled to him. Then come and pray and say this: “Our Father in heaven, forgive me as I have forgiven, and do not lead me into temptation.” And, it says, “Love covers sins.” But this is the path that leads you away from it: when you have rebuked him privately, between yourself and him, and before three people, and he has not listened to you, expose him before the whole church. Remove the wicked person from among you, so that he does not stand with you in prayer. This is said concerning those who wrong others, those who commit offenses, and those who resemble them. Our Lord instructs the person who has been wronged and the head of the church: when you have rebuked the wrongdoer and offender privately, between yourselves and him, and before one, two, and three people, and before the whole church, and he has not been persuaded, that person is rebellious. “Let that matter go,” he says, “and forgive that offense. Do not bring ruin upon yourself. You will not become poor because you let that matter go. It will benefit you not to seek redress for that offense, and our Lord will judge your case. Remove him,” he says, “so that another person like him does not become bold and become a wrongdoer and offender like him.” From now on, as for anyone who does not fear our Lord, keep away from his sins and his ruin. Exclude him from your congregation too, without blows and without chains. Our Lord will exact vengeance on him unless he repents, feels shame and remorse, and turns away from his evil deeds.

This is the perfect way: become everything to everyone, and teach everyone, so that you may win everyone. But this is the path that leads you away from it: do not eat bread with adulterers. This, however, is said concerning someone whose understanding is immature, lest he associate with adulterers on the pretext of eating bread, and they make him sin like themselves. In his immaturity he is led along, taken captive, and lost.

This is the perfect way: whatever house you enter, proclaim peace over it and pray for its inhabitants. But this is the path that leads you away from it: if someone does not welcome you, shake your dust off against them in anger. Ask who is worthy; enter and proclaim peace there. If that is how it is, we love only those who love us, and we fail in that swift race toward perfection. But this is said to disciples who are immature, so that they will not rise up and shout or be harmed by words. As those disciples said there, while they were still immature and far from perfection: “Our Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down and burn up these people who did not receive us?” And our Lord rebuked them: “Do not say such a thing. Instead, love your enemies, those who hate you, and those who kill you.” This is why he permitted them to shake off the dust.

This is the perfect way: do not call anyone unclean or defiled. As Simon said: “God has given me this: that I should not call anyone unclean or defiled.” But the path that turns you aside from it is this: do not associate with sexually immoral people. But this is said to children, so that in their childhood they will not approach sexually immoral people, lest those people corrupt them, until the power of the Spirit is in them, and their minds grow and they become perfect. Then they are permitted to become all things with everyone.

This is the perfect way: you must bear the sickness of the sick. And, it says, “Let the lame person not be turned aside.” But the path that turns you aside from it is this: do not go along the way of the Gentiles. But this is said to children, so that they will not enter the homes of Gentiles as long as they are infants in the knowledge of the truth, lest those people cause them to stumble, or they become shaken and suffer great harm.

This is the perfect way: our Lord calls tax collectors and prostitutes and turns back all sinners and those who are lost. But the path that turns you aside from it is this: keep away from every brother who conducts himself wickedly. But this is said to children, so that they will keep away from the wicked and follow the strong and the perfect, until they grow strong, receive the power of the truth, and become perfect. Then they are permitted to be lambs among wolves.

This is the perfect way: “I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.” But the path that turns you aside from it is this: do not enter a town of the Samaritans. This is said to the less advanced, so that they will not go in among everyone until they receive power from on high. And once they stand perfect in Christ, they are permitted to be with everyone and to go to whomever they wish. For as long as they are less advanced, they should walk after the perfect, and not turn aside from their teaching until they establish them as perfect in Christ. But because the perfect are complete in every matter of truth and are without fear, they therefore do not say, “This place is ours, and that one is not ours.” Or, “This man belongs to us, and this one does not belong to us”; and they make their claim about everyone. Because our Lord’s truth always prevails in them, and they do not follow any human teaching or word, they are therefore free to associate with everyone. For their understanding has authority in perfection and truth and is complete in the knowledge of our Lord. Therefore they become everything to everyone, knowing how to instruct each person in whatever way will help them. The leaders, however, each have their own place, where they are to discipline people mercifully, as is fitting. And where it is right, they are to distinguish, as duty requires, what benefits the congregations in each place, and what helps the children, the sick, the wrongdoers, and the rebellious. For the perfect, because they travel through many places, speak a word to each person in whatever way will help them, and then move on to another place. But as for the leaders who remain in each place, if they do not rebuke these people and discipline them, the rebellious rebel again. The wrongdoers commit sin again, the sick grow weak, the children stumble, and the oppressors become careless. The plunderers grow arrogant, the oppressed blaspheme, and those who have been plundered cry out. Let us therefore understand, my brothers, what belongs to the leaders, and let us not take it upon ourselves, we who are perfect or who seek perfection. You leaders, too, understand the conduct of perfection. Do not complain about us, blame us for what belongs to us, hate us without reason, or persecute us without cause, on account of the ministry in which it is right for us to walk: to go to everyone, and to admonish and teach everyone with love and humility. This is the ministry that our Lord Jesus taught us and showed us in his own person, and revealed to us in his grace and mercy.

This is the perfect way: “Let the weeds grow with the wheat, until I clear them away at harvest, lest you uproot the wheat along with the weeds.” For you do not know which is a weed, because weeds are transformed and become wheat. But this is the path that leads you away from it: “Separate those who sin from the congregation, so that they do not stand among the wheat, lest the children imitate them and the sick stumble because of them.”

This is the perfect way: “If you love only those who love you, and greet only your brothers, what righteousness is there in that? Even tax collectors, pagans, and sinners do the same. Instead, love those who hate and persecute you, and extend your greeting abundantly to the good and the evil. Then,” he says, “you will be like the Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise and sends down his rain upon them equally.” But the path that turns you aside from it is this: love your neighbor and your acquaintance. And whoever does something for one of these who are called by the name of discipleship to Christ, he says, will not lose his reward. Paul explained this: “Do good to everyone.” “But if,” he says, “you want to do more for the members of the household of faith in Christ, you are free to do so, and what you do for Christ’s disciples is very excellent.”

But this is the perfect way: these humble and great commandments of love, and those that resemble them, are greater than them, or are like them, are stated in the New Testament for those who wish to become strong, so that they may train themselves with all their strength to understand and remember, together with all the saints, what the height, depth, length, and breadth are. And they were able, through strength, to climb these ascents of that narrow, confined, and steep way, which leads up to that city where the saints live with our Lord Jesus, the King of praises.

But these paths that run alongside this way are the lesser commandments, given to infants like milk and to the weak like vegetables, because, as long as they are children in their understanding and weak also in their consciences, they cannot attain these great commandments of love and perfection. For this reason, our Lord and his heralds laid out paths for them in the New Testament through these lesser commandments and through those that are smaller than them or like them, so that they might walk in them alongside this great way until the infants grow up and the weak become healthy. They are to grow up earnestly, he says, and become healthy quickly, and enter this great way of the great commandments, travel along it, and ascend by it to that city of the saints. For as long as they are children and weak, they cannot climb these great ascents, and it is beneficial for them to walk on these paths alongside the way, rather than turn back and perish altogether, or slip and fall into that immense depth and go down alive to Sheol, because they have no strength: some of them are children, and some of them are weak.

But love, which loves everyone and which the apostle exalts above all the good gifts, is acquired through these great commandments. And that perfection which our Lord said is like the angels is brought to completion on this confined and narrow way. This way of the great commandments goes to our Lord’s house and enters his bridal chamber. But these paths of the small commandments do not reach our Lord’s house or enter his bridal chamber. Instead, they stop in the places of life on this side of our Lord’s bridal chamber. But those who travel on that perfect way rejoice in our Lord’s joy and are glorified with him, as it is written: “May I rejoice in your joy and glory also in your inheritance.” But those who travel on these paths remain in the places of life prepared for everyone according to their deeds. And they do not enter into this joy of our Lord, nor are they glorified with him. Nor do they see him face to face in the bridal chamber of his glory and in the joy of his presence. But look at what I am showing you: how infants and the sick lack the strength for this road, and how paths have therefore been opened up for them.

Tell someone whose understanding is immature, “Go, serve our Lord with fasting and prayer, learn his truth, and set others right too. Once you have set things right, do not worry about food and clothing.” Then you will see how earth and heaven disappear before his eyes, and he says to you: “If I do not work, I cannot live, can I?” And tell someone who is sick and suffering and has not yet gained strength: “Go, be reconciled with those enemies of yours who have cruelly harmed you.” And see how he slips and falls from this ascent if he tries to climb it. For when he goes to be reconciled, and that enemy of his says something hateful to him, he cannot bear it. And when he becomes agitated and quarrels with him, he certainly slips and falls. Even if he does not fall into the lowest depths of Sheol, he falls among the crags along this ascent, is broken, and can hardly get up. Or he refuses altogether to be persuaded by you to go and be reconciled. Out of fear, he does not climb this ascent, not even a little way, because his legs have no strength owing to the severe sickness he has, which torments him because he has not asked our Lord and has not yet received power from on high with which to be reconciled with his enemies, as the apostles asked and received. He has not yet recovered enough to stand on his feet, pour water into a basin, and wash the feet of those who mock him and betray him, as our Lord did for Iscariot. And because he is suffering from severe sickness, when someone strikes him and throws him down, he cannot stand on his feet, look up to heaven, and say like Stephen: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, do not hold this sin against this man who has knocked me over and thrown me down, and now wants to kill me.”

You see that infants, because they are immature, cannot bear the force of these great commandments, nor can those who are sick climb these difficult and narrow ascents, because they have not yet received power from on high. But whoever is immature in understanding and wants to grow up quickly should seek a nurse for himself. And whoever is sick should ask our Lord to enable him to receive the true word. He should also make room for someone who can remove the sickness, so that he may heal him quickly and he may have strength. And he should ask and pray that God, or a man of our Lord who is in the Spirit, may show him how to serve our Lord in the Spirit through these great commandments of love, and that he may see this road in the Spirit with the eyes of his understanding, and travel along it blamelessly in the Spirit to that city which is in the Spirit. For it is in the Spirit that he can be with the Lord of the commandments, and he gives him strength to love him, keep his commandments, and become perfect. That is, the Lord himself accomplishes his perfect will in him. Otherwise, he cannot become what his perfect will requires. But, my children, let us come to this narrow road. Let us endure a little suffering so that we may reach that place of rest. And look, everything has been explained to us above in this very discourse, which is called “The Distinction between the Commandments.” Read, learn, and understand everything with humility. And pray for me and remember me before our Lord when you have traveled on and reached that great place of peace, holiness, and love.

Look, then, my beloved, and see how people flee from the perfect way, which consists of the great commandments through which a person serves our Lord in the spirit, because of the hardship of the ascents along it. Instead, they stroll along the paths that are the lesser commandments, because these do not involve as much hardship as this way does. For along these paths they avoid the very high ascents, and travel entirely along their lower slopes toward the meeting point with the great way. For when someone separates himself from a person who has wronged him, or imprisons him, or becomes his enemy, or regards him as a pagan, he finds relief, because he has done what he wanted to him, whether a little or a great deal, but he falls short of perfection. It is better for me not to punish wrongdoers, so that I do not fall short of perfection and am not excluded from the city of the holy ones and from the presence of our Lord Jesus. Those who flee from hardships do not know that these are the difficult, narrow ascents that lead straight up to the city of our King. But to avoid suffering hardship, they seek lesser commandments in which to shelter themselves. For when someone says to them, “Come, endure a little hardship, and then you will emerge into a spacious place,” as it is written, “You brought me into fire and water, and brought me out into a spacious place; now I will come to your house with honor.” You see how people travel between fire and water and endure many hardships, and only then come to the house of our Lord and enter his rest.

But people find it more restful to stroll along paths that are not as difficult as the way, and they want to become perfect and inherit a great portion, without knowing that unless they submit themselves to the hardship of these great commandments while they still have time in this world, they will not become perfect. For the day of their departure comes suddenly, arriving like a thief, and then they can no longer reach that great city in which our King is plainly seen, face to face. Although they inherit their life in other places according to their deeds, yet from that city of the holy ones—those who kept the great commandments and love, and became perfect before departing from this world— they are excluded and cannot enter it, because they did not know its King's law or conduct themselves according to his pleasing and perfect will. Do you not know that someone who does not know the law, the commandments, and all the practices of this earthly king, and does not do everything he wills, cannot enter his palace? So too with that heavenly King, who is hidden and revealed: the one who knows his entire pleasing and perfect will and does it is the one who enters his city and lives with him forever and ever, without end; the days of that new world cannot be reckoned, nor can its years be counted. But a thousand years of this world do not equal one of the years of that new world prepared for the righteous who have kept his commandments. For the days of that world do not pass away, and its years cannot be counted. It is built and established in light that has no limit and does not pass away. Here ends the nineteenth discourse, on the commandments of the way of perfection and on the distinctions among the commandments. By the same author.
Discourse Twenty: The Difficult Ascents on the Road to the City of Our Lord

There are three very difficult ascents on this road that leads to the city of our Lord Jesus. The first is this: if someone has enemies, although he has wronged no one and troubled no one, he must go to meet these enemies who hate him without cause and reconcile them to himself. The second is this: a person must not work to feed himself or clothe his body, and must part with everything he has. The third is this: men ought to lift their hands in purity before the Lord, without anger and without evil thoughts. That is, their hearts must be pure from sin, just as the heart of our father Adam was pure before he broke the commandment.

As for the ascent of reconciling to oneself those who are enemies without cause, a person climbs it through humility, together with much fasting and fervent, prolonged prayer. As for the ascent of neither worrying nor working, a person climbs it by placing his hope in our Lord, saying, “If I make the ascent, I make it; and if I remain behind, I remain behind.” That is to say, food and clothing come from our Lord and from begging, in poverty. “If I die, I die; and if I live, I live. Only let me not stop traveling along that great road.” Thus, as regards food and clothing, a person climbs this ascent with this hope. He resolves in his mind to endure great suffering, because he gives himself over to death, as our Lord said: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.”

But this last ascent, by which a person finally reaches the city of our Lord Jesus Christ, is harder than all the other ascents. For on this very ascent a person [?] to death, and on it a person stands firm to the point of bloodshed in the struggle against sin. Although there are many ascents on the road of our Lord—those described for us above— and all of them are difficult, so that a person climbs them all through endurance, these three are exceedingly difficult. And this is the last ascent: when a person has kept all the commandments, he uproots sin entirely from his heart, together with its thoughts and its fruits— that sin which was planted in our father Adam and our mother Eve on the day they sinned, and which spread and came into all their children. This ascent is exceedingly difficult. The closer it is to the city of our Lord, the harder and steeper it is, so that no one climbs it except through suffering. But if a person climbs it, he overcomes and escapes captivity and death. Thus there are people who travel up these ascents: When they reach this ascent, they are astonished and dismayed by its difficulty. They settle down and rest opposite the city of our Lord, without entering it. Because they tremble at the difficulty of this ascent, they either turn back or withdraw a great distance from the city of our Lord, where he dwells openly with his holy ones.

This ascent is difficult because a person struggles against sin on it, and because, if he climbs this ascent, he enters the house of our Lord. Sin stands fiercely and violently against him, either to kill or to be killed. For this reason, the athlete himself, seeing it standing fiercely before him, to prevent him from passing into the place our Lord promised him, fights fiercely against it and struggles with it. It was about this ascent that Paul said, “You have not reached the point of being killed, nor have you stood in the struggle against sin to the point of shedding blood.” “You are still,” he says, “breaking off the leaves, shoots, and branches of the dry tree, and you have not yet approached its root, nor have you learned how hard it is to uproot it.” That is, he says, “You have not yet overcome even the visible sins, which are the leaves, shoots, and branches of sin. When you reach its root,” he says, “then you will see the deadly battle and struggle that sin and Satan’s forces wage against you,” as it is written: “Battles outside and fear within.” Outside, Satan’s forces wage war, and within, sin takes its stand in the struggle. The whole reason this ascent is difficult, then, is that there a person uproots the hidden death that Adam tasted by transgressing the commandment, and all the thoughts of sin, which devises everything hateful within a person, as our Lord said: “It is in the heart that all thoughts of murder, adultery, false testimony, and all the evil things a person does arise.” From within and from outside, this sin targets him. It is the death that our ancestors Adam and Eve tasted by transgressing the first commandment. For as long as a person outwardly performs the hateful deeds that sin devises within him, the sin within does not trouble him very much. But when he stops his hateful deeds, fights and overcomes the evil spirits that battle against him outside, and puts an end to these visible sins, then he reaches the inner root, which sends up growth from within and harms many outside, as Paul said: “See that no root of bitterness sends up growth and harms many.”

A person therefore travels all the ascents of the way of our Lord Jesus and comes to wage a struggle and a deadly battle on this last ascent. That is, a person puts an end to all visible sins when he becomes humble and loving, and comes to wage a struggle, a deadly battle, and a great fight against the very root of sin and its thoughts. But if a person uproots sin and climbs these ascents that I have described, he then enters and is with our Lord in spirit, and [?] in our Lord. As the prophet said, “The name of the Lord our God is a strong tower, and to it both rich and poor may run.” For a person who climbs this ascent reaches the city of our Lord: that is, when he has uprooted the whole root of sin and its fruits—the sin that stands against him. For this sin stands before him at the entrance to this ascent: unless our Lord comes and delivers him, he cannot pass through; and a person is not delivered except through a great struggle. This ascent is difficult, but through it all a person's shortcomings, both bodily and spiritual, come to an end.

Understand this too, my brothers: unless a person carries out all the commandments, as our Lord and his apostles did, and as our Lord commanded us to do, he does not strip away all his outward and inward shortcomings. And unless a person is filled with our Lord, his heart is not emptied of sin and its fruits. Thus, by putting sin to death, and through that humility, self-emptying, love, holiness, and ascetic discipline, and through these ways of life that our Lord showed us to practice as he did, a person acquires the living soul that Adam had before he sinned, and at the end of this ascent he enters Eden, the home of his life. And just as he left the paradise of the kingdom when this thought of sin and its fruits arose within him—the very thing he now struggles to uproot and kill— so, when that sin and its fruits, which are everything evil and hateful, have ceased within him, he enters the bridal chamber of the kingdom. For toil and harmful anxiety are also its fruits. Through transgressing the commandment, Adam and his descendants descended into these things: and unless they abandon the earth's wealth and possessions and all its beauty, they will not become as they were in the beginning. For through these things the evil one tempted humanity long ago and cast it down from perfection, as our Lord said: “Unless you turn back and become as you were before you sinned, you will not be made perfect in the glory of the kingdom.” For if someone compares the deeds of the righteous with those of the perfect, they are as nothing in his eyes. For although the righteous overcome evil, condemn sin, and cleanse their hearts of evil thoughts, some of the fruits of sin still remain in them, since their hearts have not been cleansed of anxiety, toil, and marriage: these things befell Adam through sin's counsel. That is why they are its fruits. For when Adam listened to sin and despised his Creator's word, his Creator gave him toil, anxiety, and marriage. Although he had not needed these things, after he sinned he came to need them. And because the righteous have not emptied themselves of everything on earth and sanctified themselves apart from it, they have not risen above that with which the evil one tempted Adam in the beginning, so that he desired the earth and everything in it and fell from heaven. Therefore, because the righteous have not been freed from everything on earth, or from marriage, anxiety, and toil: They still eat from that tree from which Adam ate, and they fall far short of perfection. But our Lord, in his mercy, wished to grant them the ability to keep the righteousness that comes after perfection, so that, while living in marriage and among these visible things, they might fare well on the day of our Lord.

When, therefore, we have climbed these ascents and uprooted sin and its fruits from the heart, then we are filled with the Spirit, the Advocate, and our Lord dwells in us completely. And we eat freely from that tree of life, which is our Lord, from which we were deprived through transgressing the commandment. Then we are able to have compassion for and love all people, even those who kill us. Then we are able to pray with love for all people and for those who kill us. When we thus have compassion for and love everyone, including those who kill us, with our heart pure, then we grow in perfection and become in accordance with our Lord’s will, which is great, acceptable, and perfect.

In this way, too, a person climbs this difficult ascent through that prayer and that example which our Lord became for us, when he cried out in prayer with a mighty cry and shed many tears. He was distressed, it says, in his prayer, until his sweat became like drops of blood. Then a helper came: an angel appeared to him, it says, strengthening and delivering him as a human being. And the one who perfects all those who have been perfected in that same likeness is himself made perfect. For it was not that he was imperfect— he who can perfect everyone if he wishes. Nor was he subject to sin, so that he needed to pray to be delivered and perfected. Nor was his strength deficient, so that his angel, who is his creature, came and strengthened him as he prayed and brought him through the place of affliction. Rather, in these things our Lord took on the likeness of us who are under the bondage of sin and death. And through the many afflictions of sin, he showed us how to climb this ascent. For there is no other way up this ascent for the athletes to pass through in battle, except by this way of ascent that our Lord showed us: through keeping vigil at length, together with much fasting, great humility, mighty crying with many tears, much supplication, and the sweat of afflictions. Then our Lord comes to us and delivers us, according to that example which is written: that an angel came to the aid of our Lord himself and appeared beside him, strengthening him as a human being. Because of these things and others like them in our Lord’s conduct, Paul wrote: that the Lord of creation took the likeness of a servant, becoming like a human being, his own creature, for the sake of creation, so that all flesh might contemplate his death and his submission. For thus it is written: that our Lord, though he had no need, pleaded with much supplication and vehement crying; and then his angel appeared beside him. Our Lord rested from the fierce battle, won victory over death, and took the crown of his victory. He showed human beings how to conquer and win victory over death.

Look, my son: our Lord became an example for us. For he went back and forth, praying and waking his disciples, so that they might see how he conquered and conquer as he did. For if he himself had needed prayer, he would have prayed alone and would have been heard, just as he was heard. But to make everyone know that he himself did not need prayer, he went back and forth to his disciples and woke them, to teach them how they should pray as he did, just as he taught them fasting and combat through his forty-day fast and his battle with Satan, who tempted him as a human being. Our Lord persevered patiently so that he might be an example for us to imitate. And see also how long our Lord persisted in his prayer: from evening until the time the rooster crowed, when those who crucified him seized him, he kept praying. And, it says, he went back and forth to his disciples three times and said to them: “Wake up and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation. See how I pray and conquer. Pray in this way, and in this way you will conquer death and sin.” Sin fought against the disciples that night and put them to sleep under the weight of sleep and anxiety, because he had told them, “Today I am being handed over.” In this way sin weighed them down and did not let them see how our Lord struggled in his prayer. Our Lord wrote down the struggle he undertook against death and placed it in the New Testament, so that we might act as he did and conquer as he conquered. Indeed, every day our Lord struggled in this way, with loud cries, tears, much supplication, and many prostrations.

Supplication, as we showed above, is patient perseverance, when we kneel for a long time before our Lord, pray to him, and make requests of him. Prostration is when someone perseveres patiently, kneels and stands before our Lord, and bows down to him in spirit many times. This, then, is what our Lord used to do when he took his disciples and went out to the mountain, away from the great crowd. He would show them how to fast, how to pray, how to conquer death, and how to kill sin, and how they themselves should teach others, just as our Lord had taught them. For a long time, then, our Lord acted in this way before his disciples, praying and crying out in his prayer, although he had no need, but only to give us an example to imitate. On that one night he went back and forth to his disciples because he was going to be arrested that night. He woke them so that they would get up and keep watch with him, and see how a deliverer came to him and strengthened him and gave him victory, so that, when they themselves made an effort as our Lord himself had done, the deliverer, who is our Lord, would come to them and deliver them and all who imitate this earnest effort of our Lord, his humility, and his poverty. For he had nowhere on earth to lay his head. Rather, he walked the earth like a stranger and a wanderer, for as long as God walked on it among human beings as a human being.
