If, then, the Savior had not appeared openly to our Lord, what would have become of us? We would have said: “Is a person left like this until he departs from this world, and only then freed from sin? Does the Savior not come into this world, but instead we depart just as we are from the world?” But now the Savior has appeared openly to our Lord and to his apostles, and everyone has been comforted, as it is written: When the apostles prayed and pleaded, as our Lord had shown them, the place where they were shone with light, and the sweet fragrance of the Spirit, the Paraclete, came over them as though from incense. Therefore, anyone among us to whom the Paraclete does not come as he came to our Lord and to the apostles, and whom his sweet fragrance does not touch— it is because he has not been freed from evil thoughts, and his heart has not been cleansed of sin. Let him know that the Savior has not yet come to him. Instead, let him walk in the footsteps of our Lord Jesus, imitate him, become poor, humble himself, and pray as he did. Let him fast continually, and then the one who grants victory and saves will come to him, as he came to our Lord. And then he will become great and be glorified in that likeness of our Lord, who in his great love exalts all who obey him and love him. For our Lord answers those who keep his words, as David said: “Answer your servant, so that I may live and keep your words. Uncover my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in your law. I am a sojourner with you; do not hide your commandments from me, for my soul has desired and longed for your judgments at all times.” Do you see how our Lord answers those who promise him in prayer: “We will do your entire, perfect will, and we will dwell with him”? He uncovers their eyes, and they see his glory and grasp his whole truth. They explain the wonders in his law, and he does not hide the truth of his commandments from them. For this reason they have made themselves poor, and they long at all times for that day of our Lord’s great judgment. They do not fear that coming judgment, because our Lord has saved them and exalted them, so that those who have done our Lord’s perfect will shall judge the wicked on that great day of judgment.

Our Lord, although he had no need of prayer, prayed and was heard and was made perfect; and the Savior came to him, although he was not in subjection. If, then, our Lord had no need of prayer, because there was no sin in him and he had no master to whom he should pray— for he was not in subjection, but he himself is the Savior of everyone who seeks him and waits for him— if, then, our Lord labored, fasted, and prayed although he had no need, how much more ought we ourselves to pray beyond what our Lord prayed, and to fast continually, as he said: For it is by fasting that you overcome this kind of Satan. And how much more ought we to cry out than he cried out with strength and many tears! For we are in need, and sin still remains in us. For our Lord was not in need, nor was there sin in him as there is in us. From this we should know that our Lord had no need of a savior, but he himself was the savior of himself and of everyone who took refuge in him. For this is what is written: “Sing a new song of praise to the Lord, because he has done a wonderful thing. His right hand and his holy arm saved him. The Lord made his salvation known and revealed his righteousness before the eyes of the nations. He remembered his grace and his faithfulness to the house of Israel, and all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of our God. Praise the Lord, all the earth! Rejoice, sing, and give praise! Sing to the Lord with lyres and with the sound of singing.” You see that our Lord had no need of salvation from an angel, for it was his own right hand and his holy arm that saved him. See, my son, what the prophet said: “The Lord made his salvation known and revealed his righteousness before the eyes of the nations.” You see that he was indeed showing us how to fight against Satan and overcome him. And see how he revealed his righteousness to us so that we might imitate him. He pleaded in prayer and made his request with a mighty cry, like a person in whom sin remains, although our Lord was holy, as it is written.

It is to us, then, that our Lord shows how a person is cleansed from sin. You see how he died for sinners. As for Satan, if it had not been for our sake, to teach us how to fight against him, he would have blown on him and destroyed him. You see how he humbled himself for our sake, to fight against Satan, that lowly fox. For just as a righteous person is seized to be killed for God's sake, and his Lord sees him but does not intervene, so that he may endure a little suffering and triumph, and that person sees that there is no one to help him, and is filled with sorrow and weeps over his killers, who are being killed through him, so our Lord chose to be afflicted by evil people and to endure sufferings. His heart was filled with sorrow because of our wickedness—that is, because of his love for his creation, so that it might not perish. For in this way it had an opportunity to accept persuasion and return to the house of life. Our Lord also grieved over those who betrayed him and those who crucified him. He wept over them and prayed for them with tears, so that we might take him as our example, pray with tears for our killers, and plead with them, just as he asked his Father to forgive his killers. For he and his Father are in one another, and they are one, and the Holy Spirit is in them. And his whole purpose in saying, “Forgive them,” was to teach us also to speak to him as he spoke to his Father.

You have seen how our Lord endured and became an example for us in everything: how we should overcome evil and sin, and how we should overcome evil people who attack us unjustly. He says, “Be patient, and pray for them so that they may live. If they repent,” he says, “then they will be ashamed of their offenses, come before you, and live. But if they do not repent and persist in their wickedness, take comfort in this: on that day of judgment, when I am revealed in my glory, you will be glorified with me before all creation, while they will be brought low before me and before all creation, both those above and those below. But you,” he says, “must not rejoice at their downfall. Instead, pray for them to rise again.” Look, my son: although our Lord had no need of any of these things, for our sake he chose to become needy. This was because of his great love for us: he desired us and wished to give us life. For our sake he endured everything, to teach us how to overcome the bitter master whom we acquired by our own free choice long ago through transgressing the commandment, when Adam’s household transgressed against the word of the one who gives life to all and nourishes all in his mercy. Glory to him. Amen.

We also know this: unless a person becomes poor, empties himself, becomes holy, and humbles himself, following the example our Lord showed us—he who kept all the commandments, loved his enemies and his killers, and prayed for them with love—that person does not become perfect and grow. And unless we pray as our Lord prayed, with cries and tears, and plead for a long time, the Savior does not come to us. For our Lord said, “If you love me, keep my commandments, just as I have kept God’s commandments. And you will remain in his love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments. And I will love you, and I and my Father will come to you. I will make you my brothers, my dwelling, and my resting place. I will take you to myself and will not leave you orphans.” Therefore, when we reach perfection, unless we plead and exert ourselves in prayer as our Lord did, we do not become perfect, and the Savior does not come to us. And if the Savior does not come, sin is not removed. And if sin is not removed, evil thoughts are not taken away from the heart. And if those thoughts are not taken away, the heart is not purified. And if the heart is not purified, we do not lift up our hands in purity. And if we do not lift up our hands in purity together with our heart, filled with love for everyone and love for our Lord, we cannot enter our Lord’s bridal chamber to be with him, even if we are standing right beside his bridal chamber, as it is written: The king came in to see the guests reclining at the meal, and there he saw a man who did not have fine clothes suitable for that lavish feast and that glorious bridegroom. The bridegroom gave orders to his servants, and they bound the man’s hands and feet and threw him out into the outer darkness, because he had dared to enter when his heart was not pure. The clothes for our Lord’s feast are complete purity of heart, as it is written: “Blessed are those who are pure in heart.” That they may see God and enter the bridal chamber of our Lord Jesus, our King, our glory, our crown, and our kingdom. And they will see his face inside his bridal chamber, live with him, be glorified with him, and delight with him, because they suffered with him and loved him. With him they rejoice, are comforted, and are glorified in his light, in his inheritance, and in the place he chose and prepared for them, which is higher than all the places in the house of life.

For although there are many places prepared for each person according to their deeds, that place is exalted, and not everyone ascends to it. As our Lord said, “Not everyone can accept this saying.” That is, he means, not everyone does deeds worthy of this saying. “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow in my footsteps and my way of life,” he says, “is not worthy of me.” So let people not regret it when they go to that world and see that they are excluded from the presence of our Lord and from the city of his glory. For he has already told them here. Therefore, whoever wishes to see the face of our Lord and live with him, let him take up his cross and imitate him while still in this world, so that when he departs from this world, he may be with our Lord. As Paul said through the Spirit, “When we depart from the body, we will be with our Lord.” If you do not know how to take up the cross and follow in our Lord's footsteps and his way of life, read the Gospel and come to this discourse, and you will learn. Ask someone who knows, and he will show you. Or humble yourself and plead before our Lord, and he will reveal it to you. Be humble toward everyone, for where you do not expect it, there you will find people of knowledge who will show you the way of our Lord Jesus. For our Lord's disciples are despised and [?], and insignificant in appearance. Just as our Lord made people perfect on earth, so those he has perfected raise up perfect people on earth through our Lord himself. For our Lord makes people perfect through them. For if everyone were able to hear from the Holy Spirit, our Lord would not have appeared in the flesh as a human being, nor would he have sent the prophets and apostles to be his heralds and show people his truth and his glory. And Paul said this: “This is my labor and my struggle, through the activity working powerfully in me: to present every person perfect in Christ.” “Just as Christ raised me up and perfected me by his power, so I will run to present every person perfect in Christ himself.” “And so I run to attain that for which he took hold of me.” Therefore, do not despise one of these little ones, for perhaps it is through him that you are to receive perfection from our Lord Jesus Christ, the King of glory. Glory to the Father, to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

Now concerning the banquet I mentioned: the king who held a banquet for his son—the king is the Lord, and his son is our Lord Jesus, our heavenly King. The banquet is our Lord's kingdom, and those who invite the guests are all the apostles and prophets. Now this is the invitation: the Father wished to be reconciled through his Son to all humanity. Their coming to the banquet means that whoever repents is accepted. The good and the evil alike—this, then, is the invitation with which he invited us, calling them in this world, long beforehand, so that they might put on good clothes, which are good deeds, and go to that banquet, which is the kingdom of our Lord. Those invited guests who excused themselves are those who excused themselves from the coming of our Lord and did not wish to believe in him. And those who entered and were accepted, wearing good clothes: these are those who believed in our Lord, kept his commandments, and did all his acceptable and perfect will. And the one who entered and was thrown out and departed represents those who believed in our Lord but did not keep all his commandments, and received his body and blood to their condemnation, as it is written: Whoever eats the Lord’s body and drinks his blood unworthily receives it for judgment and for the fire that burns on the day of judgment. It is not that they actually enter the kingdom on that day of judgment and then leave it. Rather, those who entered are those who believed in our Lord and were baptized in his name. And those who departed are those whom our Lord rejects on that day of judgment, who stand with their evil deeds, because they did not keep his commandments, just as that man was wearing filthy clothes, which are people’s evil deeds.

But listen to me, and let us prepare good deeds for ourselves. These are the clothes whose wearers are accepted in our Lord’s house. Our Lord calls everyone, the rich and the poor, and despises no one. Rather, he accepts the good and the evil alike—everyone who repents and turns to him. And on that great day of judgment, he has his treasury from which to repay everyone according to their deeds. He quickly answers anyone who keeps his words and seeks him, just as the Holy Spirit explained through David, saying: The Lord appears in his glory and turns toward the prayer of the poor, and does not despise their prayer. Let this be written for the generation to come, and let a people yet to be created praise the Lord, because he looked down from his holy height. The Lord looked down from heaven to earth, to hear the prisoner’s groaning and to free the children from death. You see that the Lord turns toward the prayer of the poor and does not despise their prayer and their plea. And for this reason, he says, let this be written, so that the generation to come may see it and seek his truth from God, and he may reveal to them the depth of the riches of the wisdom of Jesus Christ, and they may believe in him and say this: “Listen, God, to our prayer, and do not neglect our plea. Hear us and answer us; turn toward our cry and hear us, because of our enemy and because of the affliction of sin.” Let them be patient and say: Have mercy on us, God, according to your grace, and according to your abundant compassion blot out our sins. Wash us thoroughly from our wrongdoing, and cleanse us from our sins. For we know our offenses, and our sins are always before us. Against you alone, my Lord, have we sinned, and we have done evil in your sight. My Lord, see that sin has been mingled with us from the womb. But you have desired truth. You have made known to us the hidden things of your wisdom, and we have been justified by your word. Sprinkle upon us the hyssop of your mercy and cleanse us; wash us with it and make us much whiter than snow. Turn your face away from our wrongdoing, and look upon our humility and our repentance. Blot out our offenses and give us your delight and your joy, and let our bones, which have been humbled before your splendor, rejoice. Let that old self, corrupted by deceptive desires, be truly humbled. And let us put on that new self, which is renewed through good works in the likeness of its creator, our Lord Jesus Christ. Let our bones remain humbled until our Lord hears us, answers us, turns us toward himself, and binds us with his love, and frees us from subjection to the slavery of death, creates a pure heart within us, and renews his steadfast Spirit within us. Then we become a new creation and praise our Lord, who has had mercy on us in this last age. For he looked down from his holy height and heard our groaning when we were held captive in slavery to death. He made us his children, freed us from harsh subjection to death, and brought the children back to their own territory. That is, they become human beings who are a new creation in Christ through purity of heart, as Adam was before he sinned and transgressed his Creator’s commandment. These are the ones whose hearts are cleansed from sin and who love everyone: the children who return to their own territory. End of the twentieth discourse, on the difficult ascents along the road to the city of our Lord.
The twenty-first discourse, on Adam’s tree.

I will now begin to explain the good tree: what it is like and how it stands. And the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is evil, toil, anxiety, and preoccupation with passing things, through which Adam’s household tasted death, because through it they came to know the evil they had not known. Once they ate from it, they knew evil, which is death, and which they had not known. And once they obeyed the evil one, looked at the earth, saw what was in it, and loved it, evil gained power over them, and they came to know it, as it is written: On the day that you transgress my word, you will surely die. For God had taught Adam’s household only goodness when he created them. And they did not know evil until they obeyed Satan, and he taught them evil. For this reason Satan is called the tree: through him Adam and his family came to know evil and good. They learned good from God, but evil from Satan. Thus, it says, they became knowers of good and evil. From that point the hatred of unbelief took hold in Adam and his children. For this reason God said to them, “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” That is, do not obey him, for he is the one who teaches you every kind of evil and separates you from heavenly things and from the goodness of your Creator. He binds you to passing things, toil, anxiety, and pride, and makes you deny your Creator and destroy one another. You will become children of the curse and children of darkness. He will become your master and feed you deadly poison. And look: today Adam’s children, in the hardness of their hearts, eat from this tree, which makes evil known and teaches them to bind themselves to the earth through passing things. They are bound and choked by anxiety and concern over these passing things, because they do not humble themselves, sanctify themselves, and free themselves from the things that pass away along with the earth. And all of it [?] they are bound to the earth. For they do not free themselves from it and learn, either from God or from a man of God, how to bind themselves to our Lord in that world where there is no death, and there eat the words of our Lord, which are life that gives life, and eat our Lord himself, and live and grow and become perfect through him.

So if you want to come alive from the death caused by the tree that killed our father Adam and us as well, and never die again, free yourself and keep far away from Satan and his teaching—that is, from Satan, from everything evil, from the world and its anxiety, and from everything that Jesus said to escape from— through humility, prayer, and fasting, while keeping the commandments. I will also explain what the evil one’s teaching is, which harms the righteous because they are caught up in the passing things of this world and are far from the perfect, for the perfect are bound in spirit to that world of light. And I will explain how God commanded Adam from the beginning to be holy and perfect like the watchers and angels in heaven, so that, while standing bodily on earth, stripped of everything in it, he might dwell in spirit in heaven with the angels, his mind clothed in the glory of his Creator, with the earth no longer visible to him. Our Lord Jesus is the good tree in that world of light which cannot be seen by bodily eyes. He is the tree of life, giving life to everyone through his fruits, where God’s perfect will is done, as our Lord said: “Pray that God’s will may be done on earth as it is done in heaven.” That is, just as there are peace, harmony, and concord among the great and the small, and they rejoice together equally, with no one there exalting himself over someone smaller than himself or despising someone greater than himself: Pray that all human beings may be like this.

The fruits of that good tree are these fruits of the Spirit of which the apostle spoke: Let us follow the Spirit and yield to the Spirit, and let us not be conceited, provoking one another and maliciously envying one another. Everyone who imitates him bears these fruits and becomes perfect. For it says, “It is good to be zealous for good things at all times.” But these, it says, are the fruits of the Spirit: that we clothe ourselves in mercy, tenderness, concord, peace, and praise of our Lord. That is, we should yield to one another in these fruits of the Spirit: in love, patience, kindness, humility, endurance, gentleness, and holiness free from lust. These are the fruits of the Spirit on which the saints feed in Eden, as they distinguish them from these harsh things for the children, so that they may see these, abandon the harsh things, and follow those who are humble, as the apostle said: “Choose humble things and pursue them.” “Conduct yourself by these things,” his Creator commanded Adam, “with your mind in heaven as a resident, and your body on earth as a stranger and a temporary settler. And through this conduct, serve and offer praise above, like a watcher among the watchers.” Our Lord and his apostles bear witness that you were like this from the beginning, for they came and showed Adam’s descendants what they should do after the exaltation of the one who, through this very conduct, broke down the barrier of hostility that had stood between him and Adam’s descendants. The apostle made this clear when he said that everything was renewed afresh in Christ, in accordance with how he had wanted Adam to be, and how he had created him before he transgressed the commandment. Our Lord’s later will agreed with that original will which I have described as being like this. See how the later resembles the earlier. At first, our Lord made Adam free from anxiety and troubling thoughts. Later, our Lord and his apostles likewise commanded: “Be free from anxiety and troubling thoughts.” At first, God created Adam pure. Later, he likewise commanded: “Be pure in your hearts, and blessed are you.” Before Adam transgressed the commandment, he said this to him: “Do not obey the evil one, and do not desire the earth or anything in it.” The later will from above bears witness that anyone who does not distance himself from the evil one, abandon everything on earth, and look toward heaven while crucified does not attain what Adam lost.

And when the apostle said that Christ came and renewed everything afresh, in accordance with how he had wanted Adam’s descendants to remain, understand that it was according to these commandments of perfection that I explained to you above, and according to these fruits of the Spirit, which the apostle distinguished from those of the flesh, that God wanted human beings to conduct themselves, just as he wants them to do today. The whole purpose of Christ’s coming and humbling himself was to teach us how to humble ourselves in his likeness and to reveal that truth which existed from the beginning. And what is written about his coming forward and being tempted was to show us how Adam was tempted in the beginning. And what is written about his defeating Satan was to show us how Adam, if he had wished, could have overthrown him with a word, just as God overthrew him by that word of refusal to obey him, when he was enticing him to look at the earth as Adam did, to desire the earth’s wealth and its fleeting beauty, just as Adam and his household desired them. They exchanged heaven for earth, abandoned heaven, and loved the earth. They gave up what neither passes away nor is dissolved, and acquired what passes away and is dissolved. They exchanged that perfect delight for a shadow, as the apostle said: everything visible is a shadow of what is invisible, and passes away. Likewise, neither the worship that Moses showed the Israelites nor the Tent of Meeting was the perfect delight. Rather, they are a shadow, as it is written of that true tabernacle into which Jesus Christ entered ahead of us, so that we too might enter it in his footsteps. It is in the highest heavens, as Paul said: “I know a man who was caught up above the three heavens into the spiritual paradise.” His whole purpose in saying “a man” was to avoid boasting that it was he himself. For it is not fitting for anyone to boast, “I am perfect,” even when he is perfect. Instead, he should condemn himself along with sinners before everyone, and regard himself as less than everyone on earth, so that he does not become exalted and fall like Adam. But even now, the one who opened the road to the heights for us does not want us to remain among shadows, but to pursue that perfect delight. For he says, “Seek the things above and set your minds on the things above, where Christ sits in the highest heavens.”

See, then, that what the Lord wanted at the beginning is also what he wanted at the end. For this reason he said, “I am the first, and I am the last. And this is my great and perfect will, first and last: that a person should not be earthly or turn toward the earth, but should be heavenly, and that his mind should die to the earth.” Just so, Paul was dead to everything on earth and said, “If you have died to the practices of the world, why do you conduct yourselves as though alive, taking and relinquishing, receiving and giving—things through which no one is made perfect unless he dies to the world?” And if they say to him, “You eat and drink and speak,” he tells them, “Those who speak this way are dead to the world. Food and clothing,” he says, “will be given in addition. And as for these words that I speak,” he says, “it is not I who live, but Christ lives in me, the one who speaks in me. It is by Christ’s word,” he says, “that I stand and sit, eat and drink, sleep and wake.” And not with foreign speech, or [?] tales, or matters that are not suited to perfection, or matters of receiving and giving, or of passing gains. Rather, he says, “Christ lives in me,” setting his mind on things in heaven and not on things on earth.

You see how Paul was dead to everything visible that is contrary to perfection, which pursues what cannot be seen by bodily eyes. For he did not even live for his clothing and food, since he was not concerned about anything visible. Instead, while setting his mind on things above, he was sometimes hungry and sometimes naked for lack of clothing, as he said: “I am trained in everything: in hunger and fullness, in nakedness and being stripped bare, in honor and dishonor, in many beatings, while half the world curses us and half blesses us, amid blessings and curses, while we love everyone and are rejected in everyone's eyes—as deceivers,” he says, “and yet we are truthful.”

Adam, then, was originally perfect according to God's will. This is what Jesus came and demonstrated in himself to anyone who wishes to imitate him and become perfect. And Adam looked toward heaven and not toward earth. He rejoiced with the heavenly watchers, without worry and without pain. He was concerned neither about clothing nor about food; instead, God fed him, as befitted the riches of his kindness, with heavenly bread, as it is written: “A human being ate the bread of angels.” This toil, the pains of childbirth, and bodily pains did not exist, as David also explained: “Because human beings rebelled against God's word”—the word in which he told them, “Do not transgress my commandments”— “and rejected the counsel of the Most High”—his desire that they should be like angels—“for this reason,” he says, “he broke their hearts with toil, and they became weak, with no one to help them,” unless they kept our Lord's commandments and pleaded with him. And the Father was reconciled to them through his Son and saved them for his name's sake and through the love of our Lord Jesus Christ. And in this way our Lord would have made children for them, just as he made Eve from Adam, without desire and without sexual union, either from the hairs of their heads or from their nails. If he wished, he would have made children for them, and human beings would have been like angels. And the one who created them would have provided them, without toil, with whatever food he wished. He himself would have carried their burden, as our Lord said: “Do not worry about your body or about your life. For the one who created you cares greatly for you.” So then, it says, cast your cares on the Lord, and he will sustain you, give you rest, and protect you. Thus human beings lived on earth in body and in heaven in spirit, until their Creator was pleased to raise them to the heights. Nothing on earth harmed them, neither a creeping creature nor a fanged beast, nor Satan, if their own will had not chosen to obey the creeping creature and Satan. For on the day he created them, he said to them, “I will put fear and dread of you upon everything on earth.” The Lord’s hand was over Adam, and Adam’s hand held dominion over everything on earth beneath him, through the power of our Lord, who holds all things. As for their having been created without earthly desires, this means that we must not attribute weakness to God, as though he wanted it this way but his will did not come about as he wished.

It was certainly not that Adam and his children overpowered God. Rather, in his grace and kindness he gave them freedom and a will of their own, so that he would not subject them like the rest of the other creatures that are subject to him. These do not have the freedom Adam has, nor do they come to judgment, since they have neither a soul like Adam’s nor his freedom. For if he had wanted to restrict their freedom, he could have brought them into conformity with his will with a mere signal, in the blink of an eye. Instead, he gave Adam freedom and established a law for him to help his soul, so that he would not abandon heaven and inherit the earth. For it was from toil, care, and evil that he restrained him, not from perfection and heaven. And to confirm for you that the earth was not visible to him: they did not even know that their bodies were naked. Rather, as it is written, Adam and Eve were naked, and their nakedness was not visible to them. But once they ate from the tree—that is, once they abandoned heaven and loved the earth— and their minds came down from heaven to their bodies, then they saw that they were naked. For they were in heaven while walking on earth. They spoke from their bodies, as our Lord showed them to be in this latter will, when he said, “I have come to do your will, O God”—the will that Adam lost at the beginning. For he said concerning this latter will, which resembles the former one, “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound.” So it is with those who are born of the Spirit. And just as you hear only the sound of the wind, but do not know where it comes from or where it goes, so the voices of Adam and Eve could be heard from their bodies, while their minds stood in heaven before God. It is like today: there are people who, in spirit, speak with people on earth while contemplating the greatness of our Lord and how deeply it humbled itself. Their minds are with our Lord in heaven, even while they pray on earth and their voices go out from their bodies. They gaze into heaven in spirit, with what is born of the Spirit, and they resemble our Lord in humility. They are thus in heaven because they have humbled themselves and abandoned everything visible, so that they may turn their gaze and their minds upward. But if they wish to exalt themselves and turn back to the earth to acquire possessions and make use of it, they are left behind, the door is shut in their faces, and they leave the heavenly Jerusalem, like Adam leaving the spiritual Eden. For this is the spiritual Jerusalem, the city of God. So then, in the same way as this illustration we have given, Adam’s mind was in heaven in purity and delight, amid those fruits of the Spirit that the apostle described.

But when the deceiver approached Eve and Adam with his deceit, he tempted them just as he tempted Jesus. He said to the Creator of all, “Look! See how beautiful the earth is, with its possessions and its kingdoms. Listen to me: acquire possessions and reign. Do not become poor and empty-handed, a stranger on the earth.” Our Lord said to him, “Get behind me, Satan!” Immediately he was worn out and overthrown, and he ended his assault and his temptation. In the same way, he also tempted Adam deceitfully. He approached him as someone concerned for him and bearing his burden, and he advised Eve to advise Adam. He instructed her to tell Adam to acquire property and become a king: “Look, there is gold and silver in the earth, and every kind of luxury. Acquire possessions, enjoy yourselves, reign, grow great, and multiply,” the evil one advised. “Cast off self-denial, dispossession, holiness, and humility. Know evil things and know good things; become great and be like God who created you.” Eve advised Adam, “That rebel has advised us well. Indeed, since he came before us and is older than we are, he knows.” Adam said to Eve, “Go back and tell him, ‘Our Creator commanded us not to listen to you or eat of it, and not to become entangled in earthly things—that is, not to toil or acquire anything on earth.’” He changed his words and persuaded her: “It is because he does not want or consent to your becoming like him.” Adam said, “If he does not want us to become like that, will he not hold us accountable for our insolence?” The evil one said, “Once you have become like him, what will he matter to you?”

Look, man, at the kind of thought Adam entertained about the one who created him from dust and brought him into the company of the heavenly Watchers. Adam and Eve obeyed in the hope of becoming like their Creator. For Paul said, “Created things were subjected to futility, not willingly,” he says, “but because of the one who subjected them in hope.” That is, they did not conceive this of their own accord, but through the advice of others. Still, Adam had a will of his own. If he had not consented, the evil one could not have led him by force during those thousand years that he lived on earth. So Adam and Eve were persuaded, turned their minds toward the earth, and came down from heaven. Their minds became earthly, like their bodies, and they broke away and descended from the heavenly paradise, which is perfect delight. They came to be on the earth, which is a shadow of what cannot be seen by fleshly eyes—that is, a shadow of that heavenly paradise. Adam descended and stood in the earthly paradise, which is the shadow of heaven. They became poor, deprived of the wealth above, and began running after the wealth below, which is something that passes away and dissolves in a single hour. Yet they did not toil on the earth before God cursed them. Rather, the moment they accepted the evil one's promise and despised God's word, he cursed them, and they went out from the spiritual paradise. Then they cultivated the earth from which they had been created, for the sake of wealth that passes away. When they saw that they were naked, after their minds had stripped off that glory above, they began to concern themselves with clothing, because they became aware of shame, which had not been apparent to them while they were gazing toward heaven. They saw that the heavenly bread had been withheld, and they began to toil on the earth for food. They were left alone, deprived of the Watchers and the great heavenly hosts, which surround those who keep the commandments, not those who despise God's word. They began to desire sexual union and to reproduce like animals. They gazed at the earth and became like it, because they did not understand their heavenly honor, or their fellowship and love with the Watchers above.

Adam and Eve willingly chose all these things and were brought low through an evil mediator. They abandoned heaven and heavenly wealth, and loved the earth and everything in it. Now Adam and his household were naked, without this clothing that is seen in this world. This was how Adam and his household were before they sinned; and it was not unknowingly that they sinned in their rebellion. But in this they were childish: they supposed that they would become like God. They forgot that nothing can become like the Creator of all the worlds, the one who is himself the Creator, and who is our Lord Jesus Christ. But God watched and refrained from intervening; he was patient and forbearing, while Adam despised his words, broke his commandments, and sought to seize equality with God through pride rather than humility. For this reason the apostle said that Christ did not wish to become equal to God by grasping at it, as Adam did. Instead, he emptied himself even of this very thing that Adam loved, when Adam sought to become God through earthly wealth. He took the form of a servant, becoming like the first human as he had been created, in his obedience, love, and humility, to show us how a person becomes a brother, a son, an heir, and a close relative. who freely wished earthly beings to dwell with him. He took, as it is said, the form of a servant, so that he might obey his Father like a servant. He did not act as Adam did, who took on a form of exaltation so that he might become an opponent and adversary of his Lord and Creator, sit opposite him, and defy him. For nothing brought Adam down on the day he fell except the pride by which he wished to become God's equal in his exaltation. It made him presumptuous, drove him out of the paradise of the kingdom, and brought him down to the earth. My brothers, let us flee from pride, so that we do not become salt that has lost its taste and is not even fit for the manure heap, because it has no flavor with which to salt sacrifices, nor can a field be fertilized with it and wheat made to flourish through it, as our Lord said: “Whoever exalts himself like Adam will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself like Jesus will be exalted, just as he was exalted.”

It was because of Adam's pride that God shut the gates of paradise before him—that is, the gates of heaven. Therefore, just as God drove Adam out of paradise because of his pride, so through his humility he brings him in, that is, he raises him to the highest heavens, to the place where God dwells and appears to him. For he said, “With what will you appease me after you have angered me? With possessions, or with sacrifices of speechless animals? From now on, my sacrifice, and what reconciles me, my desire and my rest, is the person who is gentle and humble in spirit, whom I regard and in whom I dwell. And he ascends in me when I ascend to the place of my rest.” And again it says that God chose Moses because he was humbler than all other people. Humility was weighed against everything, and it outweighed it. For God weighed Moses against six hundred thousand men bearing swords, together with their wives and children. He placed that humble man on one side of the scales, and stubbornness and pride proved lighter, while humility and gentleness proved heavier. The Lord said to him, “Come out from among this people, and I will destroy them in a single hour.” Moses said, “If you wipe them out, wipe me out with them.” And he said, “No, Moses. Whoever has sinned against me, I will wipe him out.” Moses said, “No, my Lord. If you will forgive them, as you have forgiven them from Egypt until now—otherwise, wipe me out with them.” Through this Moses became great: he placed himself alongside sinners who sinned every day. “Forgive them,” he said, “as you have forgiven them from their time in Egypt until today.” He loved those sinners as himself and did not separate himself from them.

Likewise, he was pleased with Noah alone. For he said, “You alone, out of the whole earth, I have seen to be blameless and humble.” The Lord said to him, “Come out from among them, for I am wiping out all flesh that I have created, because all flesh has corrupted its way.” And Noah said, “Far be it from you to destroy the whole earth!” And the Lord said to him, “Look, I am putting the whole earth on the scales with you. If they outweigh you, I will spare them.” And the Lord weighed them against him, and Noah, through his humility, far outweighed them all. And the Lord swept away all flesh, both the exalted and the lowly, at that time.

Likewise, in the days of Job, he weighed everyone against him. And Job outweighed them through his humility, and no one like him was found in his days. Our Lord bears witness, saying, “[?] my servant Job, who is blameless and upright and turns away from evil, and there is no one like him on earth.” As for what I said about the scales, this is what is written: “All human beings are deceitful, like a breath; weighed on the scales, they are altogether empty.” What are we saying? Because they alone were humble, were they perhaps drawn into the pride and frenzy that filled the whole earth? And today, when we tell someone, “Humble yourself, turn away from evil, and do good like the people of old,” he says, “There is no one who acts like that today.” But why do you and I not become like Noah, Job, and Daniel, who was also humble like them, so that the Lord assigned his portion with theirs? Yet because there is no one like these, he says, “I will not humble myself.” But there are people today who are humble and more virtuous than these—one among many. But unless a person has humility and gentleness within himself, he is not acquainted with the humble, God does not dwell in him, and he does not grasp the truth.

Paul too is very great, for he loved the wicked more than himself and said: “The Lord is my witness that I wished to die so that the wicked might praise the Lord of glory, if God were willing to accept me and exchange my death for their lives.” For he imitated our Lord, who died for sinners. And all the apostles died for sinners, suffering many kinds of death through scourging, the sword, and the cross. How, then, can we measure up to them, when we do not even forgive sinners? And how far we fall short of perfection, when we do not even care for our own souls! How guilty we are of this: we persecute them and kill our own souls, having become persecutors rather than the persecuted.

Again, the angel said to Mary, “Peace to you, blessed among women”—that is, humble among women. “My Lord is with you because of your humility.” And Mary said, “I give thanks to God, who looked upon the humility of his servant, not upon beauty or wealth.” For if there had been another woman humbler than Mary, Christ would have been born from her—he who is the humblest of all human beings and a lover of humility.

From then on, Adam was on earth; the heavenly one became earthly, the spiritual one became bodily; the living soul [?] tasted death. And Majesty stooped down and spoke with Adam. And Adam and Eve fled and hid among the trees standing on the earth. And the Lord said to Adam, “Where are you, Adam, since you are not among the heavenly Watchers?” And he said: “I heard your voice and hid from your presence, for I am ashamed to see you even on earth.” I am the one who used to stand continually before you in heaven, and now you see my nakedness. But I am ashamed of what I thought and of having despised your word. I did not know that dust cannot be like the one who formed it, and that a creature cannot dwell with its Creator except through mercy, when it humbles itself. The Lord said to Adam, “Look, you have made use of the very thing I warned you against. That is, you rejected heaven and chose earth. That is, you abandoned the good tree, the one in which you had known no evil, and descended to the one in which you came to know evil and good. That is, you fell from heaven to earth. Why, Adam?” He says to him, “Eve advised me.” Eve says, “The serpent advised me.” The serpent says, “The rebel deceived me and sent me.” For God had commanded Adam not to obey him, neither he nor Eve—the one who rebelled against his Lord’s word, as we explained above how he rebelled. For this reason he sent the serpent, because he had deceived it and it had become subject to him.

For when he rebelled and God cast him down, he became Satan, a son of darkness, by his own choice. God left him alone and did not kill him because of his patience, but he would not repent because of his stubbornness and rebelliousness. And rather than serve the Lord—as our Lord said, “It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve and implore”— he instead deceived other creatures and made them rebel, just as he taught the serpent, Adam, and Eve to rebel. Adam fell from heaven through the same stumbling by which the rebel stumbled and fell. For the thought had arisen in the rebel that he would become God. When he was overthrown, he came and deceived Adam so that Adam would stumble and fall, becoming his son and disciple. But God did not gratify him as he had intended. Instead, he showed mercy to Adam and Eve in their repentance, and established a law for them on earth, so that anyone who observes it will live by it. And because he himself became corrupt and corrupted others, the right hand of Jesus does not spare him from his destruction and torment: just as he destroyed, so he is destroyed. For every soul he has led into rebellion and destroyed, he demands from him a soul for a soul; and everything he snatches from his creatures, he demands back from him. For the torment of all the wicked will pass away, but his own torment will endure forever and ever, and it will be more severe than every other torment and [?] than all of them.

Far be it from our Lord to make hell burn for human beings as it does for him, because no one has caused destruction as he has, except the unclean spirits, who became his daughters and are subject to him. For they too had been created for service—the service for which God wished to create them. Obey Satan like the serpent; become defiled and become Satan, and never again be sanctified. For all those who acted wickedly in generation after generation provoked him. But this one provokes him in every generation; as long as this world exists, he provokes him. For Adam and his sons were pleased to grieve the Spirit of our Lord through the evil one's own teaching. Likewise, as long as that world to come exists, he will be embittered and tormented in a flood of fire, just as the flood of water came upon Adam's descendants through his word and his deception.

Then God began to have mercy on Adam and Eve. God made tunics of skin and clothed them in his mercy. Adam's Maker did not treat him according to his foolishness and according to what Adam had intended. For if he had treated him according to his foolishness, he would have utterly destroyed him and made him as though he did not exist. But Adam himself, in his freedom, chose toil for himself, something opposed to perfection. By his own will he took on anxiety, something that chokes those who seek to rise to the highest height, because he listened to the advice of one who presented himself to him as a bearer of good things, but deprived him of heavenly beauties and bound him to the beauty of the earth. Adam desired the beauty below and was deprived of heavenly beauty. Because this passing beauty is visible to bodily eyes, it is greatly loved by anyone who lacks spiritual eyes with which to gaze upon heavenly beauty. Adam had eyes and could see it, but the evil one blinded them, by telling him, “You will grow still greater and be with your Creator.” End of Discourse 21, on Adam's tree.
Discourse 22: On the laws by which those who practice them do not live.

Let us now explain the laws by which no one lives when he observes them: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a cheek for a cheek, a burn for a burn, a wound for a wound, a life for a life. That is to say, everything amounts to this: evil for evil. It says, “Love the one who loves you, and hate your enemy.” “If you strike your father, present an offering in the temple.” And it says, “Whoever wishes to divorce his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce,” even though she has not committed adultery—something pleasing neither to our Lord nor to human beings. These are the commandments that are not good, and the laws by which they will not live. Why did our Lord give them? Only because they themselves wanted them. And why did they appoint evil judges over themselves? And why did he allow them to repay evil for evil, even to one another? But because there are people even today who want to rebel against the commandment, They follow their own will and say, “Justice does not consist in harming no one. Rather, this, they say, is justice: to do good to the good and harm to the wicked, just as God also acts on the day of judgment and the day of rebuke.”

If we do not understand from the Scriptures, then from the world itself, when people accuse one another, do we not learn what justice is? They cry out and say, “So-and-so wants to inflict terrible damage on me, in my property and my pursuits.” And everyone says, “So-and-so is acting not justly but unjustly.” See how everyone cries out that justice does no harm. And anyone who has harmed someone, wronged him, or taken his property pleads with everyone and says, “I have done wrong. Forgive me, and I will repay it. Have mercy on me.” And if the other person will not be persuaded, everyone who hears says, “Alas! So-and-so is not acting in a way worthy of God, for God said, ‘Forgive one another seventy times seven. And if you do not forgive, neither will I forgive you.’” He wronged him and turned back. It was for the sake of wrongdoers that our Lord said, “Blessed are the merciful, for mercy will be shown to them.” If a person does not show mercy to someone who has done wrong, who shows mercy to someone better than himself or equal to himself? For that person says to him, “Why are you showing me mercy? Am I not better than you?” And if someone says, “It is written that one should show mercy to the hungry and the naked,” the saying is not restricted to the hungry and the naked alone, but also applies to anyone who does wrong in any matter. If a person shows mercy and forgives, he is doing an act of charity in this too. Therefore, whoever in this world shows mercy to a wrongdoer, will be shown mercy in that world, and his offenses and sins will be forgiven. Therefore, if a wicked person wrongs someone, let that person make his love shine upon him, just as the Father makes his sun shine upon the wicked.

You see how God and human beings cry out that justice does not repay terrible harm. For justice suffers wrong and does not repay evil for evil. But if it rebukes, it rebukes before one or two or three, or before the whole church. And if someone is unwilling to give you what is yours, accept the loss of what belongs to you and do not fall into evil. The Lord will secure justice for you, rather than your securing justice for yourself. And you will not become poor because of the thing you lose. And if someone says, “I do not attack anyone, but whoever attacks me, I stand against him and harm him,” this too is not justice but evil. For all battles and wars happen because both sides stand against each other, whenever one man rises up against his fellow and neither of them yields before the other. For this reason, righteousness departs from both sides, and evil reigns. For God commanded neither those who are wronged nor those who do wrong to sin against one another. But to the person who is wronged he said this: “If you remain righteous and do not exact justice for yourself, I will see that justice is done for you,” says God. Do you see how he commands you not to harm anyone even when you have been wronged, so that you do not fall away from righteousness? But if someone says, “I am imitating God, who calls wrongdoers to account”: It is very wrong for you to imitate God in this and compare yourself to God, who is subject to no law: Even if he were to sin, there would be no one to blame him—though far be it from him to do wrong. So you want to be a judge on God's behalf? Then become a creator like him, and make yourself a heaven and an earth where the Lord is not present, and create human beings for yourself where the authority of the Lord Almighty does not extend. Then do good to the good and harm to the wicked, once you have become self-existent rather than created, and subject to no law, like him.

You weak creature! Remember your father Adam and Satan: consider the depths to which they sank because they intended to become gods. And you, who have not openly gone astray—look, the Evil One is secretly leading you astray, so that you say: “I do as God does,” so that you suffer a wound that cannot be healed. For Adam's wound was healed. Take care, I tell you, lest your own wound prove incurable. And if you say, “He commanded the righteous people of old to take vengeance on wrongdoers, and I am imitating them”—you are not permitted to imitate them, nor has God spoken to you as he did to them. It was not because they were sinning against one another that God destroyed them through the prophets, but because they were saying, “What good is the Lord?” For this he disciplined them, until they acknowledged that the Lord is God Almighty. And so that you may know that this is so, observe that from the day they acknowledged him, he no longer sends prophets against them. Instead, if they are unwilling to repent, he keeps them for the day of judgment. But today God does not commission anyone as he commissioned the prophets. But if you wish, of your own will, to become a murderer, that is your own decision. For the Lord said, “Not even an offensive word is to come out of your mouth.” And if you say, “I am imitating the judges, for there is no authority that does not come from God”: Observe that they exercise authority over evil and pronounce judgments by which no one can live. And observe that evil judges judge the evil world. God established evil judges and gave evil judgments so that neither the judges would be justified nor those being judged would find relief. But because human beings rebelled even against righteousness, which consists of the commandments given after our first rebellion, that of our father Adam: Just as our father rebelled against goodness of heart and purity of mind, and by his own choice acquired a heart that knew evil, so we too rebelled against the righteousness our Creator commanded us: although it knows evil, it does not practice it unless it chooses to.

So when God saw that we had rebelled against this too, and that we were not merely repaying evil for evil, but many evils for one evil—something the Lord did not command, nor is he pleased even with evil repaid for evil— they accept bribes and show favoritism, something the Lord did not command. For a person cannot live by these judgments either, because they were given in anger. For the Lord said to appoint evil judges who show no mercy, because the people themselves were crying out and saying: "Give us a king and judges who will subject us to harsh rule."

And the Lord said to Samuel, "Tell them how the king will subject them to his rule: he will take their sons and daughters and take a tenth of their possessions and their crops." And they cried out, "These are precisely the judges we need, who will kill everyone who does wrong with the sword; otherwise we will devour one another." And God said, "Just as they have rejected my commandments, so they have rejected me too. Appoint evil judges over them, so that wrong may be avenged upon wrongdoers, and I will take vengeance on both of them. For neither the judges nor those who do evil can live by these judgments of evil for evil; both die by their own choice. For unless people choose to, they do not become judges or evildoers. But because they love money, honor, and fleeting glory, they pay bribes and become governors, acquiring the authority of the sword so that they can kill whomever they wish. Through bribery they become executioners so that they can be killers. And they obtain every rank through bribery so that they can do harm and plunder. For if someone wishes to flee from evil, he does not become a king, a governor, or an executioner. But those who have not attained this sit waiting for the time when they will become evil rulers, so that they can carry out their evil desires. For if people wanted each person to go his way in righteousness, they would neither wage wars nor kill; they would not plunder one another, and judges would not be needed. But now neither do the judges flee from evil, nor do the evildoers stop. They all destroy one another—everyone who does not repent during his lifetime and flee from evil. Where have you seen a righteous person who wants to become a king or a governor, or one of the rulers of this evil world? Since our Lord stopped anointing kings and appointing prophets and leaders for the former people?

If you say that the Lord incites them against one another—whether kings or other people—as he did formerly, far be it from you to say this or anything like it. He is the one who desires peace from human beings, the one who said, “Accept blows, and do not strike; be wronged, and do not wrong others.” And if formerly there was hostility between God and human beings, today God has reconciled what is on earth and what is in heaven through the blood of his cross, and he said, “Let wars cease from the ends of the earth.” If, then, our Lord said that there should be peace throughout all the ends of the earth, it is human beings themselves who now do not want peace, and they die at one another’s hands. Did God perhaps say to one person, “Love your fellow human being as yourself, and pray for the one who strikes you,” while saying to another, “Harm the one who harms you; wage war and kill him”? Far be it from the Lord! He is not to blame for these things. For evil people do evil of their own free will, and those who seek revenge demand, of their own free will, many evils in return for one evil. But judges like these are suited to this world, whose people do not refrain from evil and devour one another. And against the one who likes to avenge evil, a people worse than this one goes out, pursuing him in turn. For he finds satisfaction in evil. Therefore, when God saw that human beings were like this, that neither the people nor their judges merely repaid one another one evil for another, he wrote and instructed them in that former law to repay evil for evil, as he said: “I established ordinances for them by which no one could live.” They were evil people. “I gave them,” he says, “commandments that were not good, and ordinances by which they would not live”—in keeping, he says, with what they themselves wanted. That is, he says, because they abandoned the good commandments of love, those in which the entire force of the Law and the Prophets was fulfilled, namely, “Love God and your fellow human being.” For if we or they had kept them, Satan would already have been defeated. For it is through another human being that a person sins, and through another human being that a person is made righteous. “They loved,” he says, “murder, hostility, and hidden hatred. Therefore I gave them commandments that would bring them death when they kept them. If you behave perversely toward me, I will behave perversely toward you.”

And again he said, “They loved a curse and did not desire blessings,” because they rejected the blessings promised to those who walk in righteousness, which harms no one, but keeps itself from evil, flees from judgment, and is afraid to speak harshly to anyone, lest that person strike it. And if someone happens to strike it, it endures, and our Lord judges its case. Anyone who walks in righteousness, love, and perfection has no right to avenge himself on someone who treats him violently, unless our Lord calls that person to account and brings severe suffering upon him until he is humbled. Therefore, because we loved curses, we put them on like armor; and because we behaved defiantly, evil judges rose up against us, who have no mercy and pour out blood like water. They repay one evil deed with a hundred evil deeds, love bribes, and judge unjustly. We made the punishment harsher by refusing to restrain ourselves, while those who became the agents of wrath brought condemnation upon themselves. Neither we nor they remembered the true Judge, who repays everyone according to their deeds. But evil judges who judge the wicked, kill them, and die because of them are like Satan, who kills the people who obey him, yet does not himself escape the fire.

Even the apostles taught the murderers until they killed them, and they did not turn back. Those who became evil judges were not afraid, nor were they righteous people who harmed no one, like Adam, of whom it is not written that he struck Cain, who killed his brother, even with a slap. Instead, he let him go on his way, and the Lord exacted justice for Abel from Cain. For if each of us had gone on our own way, even in this world, which we have loved as Adam did because of its visible, fleeting beauty, and if we had each been righteous in our own affairs, working and living, and had not done to our fellow human beings what we ourselves hate, but, just as we want everyone to treat us, had treated everyone else, there would have been no murders, no wars, and no wounds. There would have been no need for evil judges or kings, and no one would have hated a fellow human being. God saw what human beings were doing to one another: they were plundering one another, and no one was holding back from evil. All flesh had corrupted its way, as it is written about the beginning, and as is also true today. Everyone sharpened his sickle, as it is written, and they made swords for themselves and appointed kings and judges over themselves—that is, masters and murderers. They attacked one another, bound themselves in enmity, and waged wars, until finally God gave himself to them for their sake, so that through his blood everything on earth and everything in heaven might be reconciled. Yet they had no pity on his life, felt no shame before his blood, and did not obey the Son by making peace on earth as he did.

Woe to us! Unless we repent, he will not listen to us on the day of judgment, just as we have not listened to him. “Whoever does not obey the Son,” it says, “God’s wrath will remain upon him.” For he said in the Law: “Cursed is everyone who harms his neighbor, secretly or openly.” And let all the people say, “Amen.” You see how everyone who harms his neighbor becomes accursed, like Satan. For it is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and for someone who has become a slave of sin and obeys it to be like his master. And when he submits to the humility of Christ, he becomes like his master and teacher. But the law is not laid down for the righteous, because they are a law to themselves. For a person can be a law of love to himself, as the ancient fathers were. And they imitated God, who makes his love shine upon the good and the evil, and sends down his rain upon the righteous and the wicked. They were not blamed by God, but were indeed praised.

And here, in this very discourse of ours, we explain the love of the fathers in the appropriate place: it is in these beautiful and good deeds that God wants all people to imitate him, and in this way to look to him and imitate him, as he humbles himself and asks everyone, through the prophets and through the apostles, to be reconciled to him and live; as he washes the feet of those who mock him, greets those who betray him, kisses Iscariot, and calls him “my friend.” He did not say to him, “Where are you going, murderer?” Instead, he humbles himself and kisses him, so that he might be an example for us, that we might act this way toward anyone who harms us and overcome evil, as our Lord showed us. And he became the founder and perfecter of our faith, so that we might be perfected in his likeness and imitate him in this way: as he prays for those who crucify him, and as he covers with his love the sins of those who were calling him foul names, which the apostles could not spell out because they were so vile. Instead, they wrote this: that they called him a son of adulterers and a deceiver, and, it says, other insults about which the apostles kept silent because they were so vile. At that time he was looking at the adulterers who were there, and at the murderers, thieves, and oppressors. He knew where they had murdered, where they had stolen, and where they had committed every kind of evil, yet he covered their sins and did not expose them. Meanwhile, they were spitting in his face and striking him on the head, piercing his hands and feet, and giving him vinegar and bitter gall to drink—something they did not do even to murderers—and they pierced his side. And although they did all these evil things to him, besides the evil things they had done to others, he did not hate them or expose them; instead, he truly loved them and prayed for them: “Father, forgive them,” so that he might be an example of perfection for us, that all of us, the children of Adam, might imitate him.

And let us also imitate him in this: he calls tax collectors and prostitutes and shows them mercy, and he bows his head before someone less than himself. And he is baptized, though he has no need of it, to give us an example of receiving a blessing from someone less than ourselves who depends on us. And let us imitate him in asking after the well-being of his male and female servants and being the first to greet them. And in becoming poor, with nowhere on earth to rest his head, so that through his poverty we might become rich. And in making himself a sinner, pleading and begging like an offender, and making himself sin because of our wrongdoing, so that in him we might become righteousness. This is how human beings ought to look to God and imitate him in all the good things he has done and does for all creatures. And they should act in this way toward all Adam’s children, good and evil. Then the righteous and the perfect are permitted to be a law to themselves and to imitate all the good deeds of our God. But no human being is permitted to imitate God when he judges, kills, curses, hates, or becomes angry; or when he condemns and calls people offspring of vipers, or calls them children of the Evil One, who was a murderer from the beginning. No human being may imitate God in any of these acts without incurring condemnation. Rather, let us imitate him in these things: he calls his servants “my brothers and sisters, my mother, my sons and daughters,” and he calls a woman of the world “my daughter.”

For God is not subject to law, and he has authority over what he has formed. It is fitting for what he has formed to be under God and subject to him. “And if I,” he says, “who am not subject to law and am your Lord and teacher, have humbled myself in this way, how much more ought you, who are under God and have a lord and teacher, to humble yourselves more than I have!” Yet even when we imitate our Lord’s humility, our humility does not compare with his. When we offer our cheek to blows, since our nature can be seized, this humility is small compared with that humbling: that nature which could not be seized or struck was seized and struck. And when we become poor as our Lord became poor, since we are poor already, this humbling is small compared with that of the one who enriches everyone and became poor so that through his poverty we might become rich. And when we experience need, as our Lord experienced need and asked Zacchaeus for bread and the Samaritan woman for water, our own need is small compared with that of the one who feeds everyone and experienced need. And when we die for evil people, as our Lord died for evil people, our humbling is small compared with our Lord’s. For we are mortal by nature, unlike that nature which gives life to everyone and tasted death. In short, if all our humility is compared with our Lord’s, it is small beside his. And by his grace he makes us equal to the measure of his full stature when we humble ourselves as he humbled himself. And for this reason he said, “When you have done everything I commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants.’” And insignificant, having done what you commanded us by your strength, which rescued us from the snares of death, because we were calling on you at all times to rescue us. And now that you have rescued us from the evil one’s burning arrows, receive us into your presence in your grace, and make us forget everything we saw in this world, through which we have now passed.

But let us not act presumptuously as Adam did, and fall as he fell. Rather, God gave human beings authority to do good and beautiful things as much as they wish and however they see fit, because no limit has been set to love and good deeds, as Paul said. And if all human beings acted this way, he says, no law would have been laid down. But the law was established for all evildoers: for murderers, adulterers, thieves, liars, the sexually immoral, oppressors, deceivers, and idol worshipers; for sorcerers, omen readers, diviners, those who curse, quarrelsome people, hot-tempered people, and oath breakers; for the greedy, drunkards, singers, and those who speak obscene words, who are themselves obscene and filthy; and for those who commit adultery through laughter and amusement, through tales and unnecessary stories. “Let no hateful or idle word come out of your mouths,” he says, “but only speech that gives grace for your own building up.” The law, then, was not established for the righteous and holy, for those who bless and those who show mercy, for loving people and those who do good, for the compassionate, the kind, and the blessed. No law was established for these people, because they become a law of love to themselves by loving their God and all human beings, good and evil alike. They imitate our Lord, have compassion on them, and make peace with them, even when they are not worthy of peace, just as Iscariot was not worthy, yet our Lord made peace with him. For all his beloved learn this from our Lord himself and imitate him. And everything that our Lord and all his heralds, the first and the last, wrote at length was so that human beings might be good among the wicked, as our Lord Jesus, our teacher, was. But if someone says, “I imitate God, and I do good and inflict harm as he does,” that person is utterly mistaken. The law will condemn him on the day of judgment, because the law does not permit him to imitate the harmful things God does, but only the good things. It also permits him this: to teach humility to all human beings, following the example of our Lord. Only he must not entertain the thought of cursing as God cursed, or of becoming angry or hating as God does. Therefore, whoever imitates God in these harsh deeds falls away from the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But when our Lord saw that we do not merely repay evil for evil and pass judgment accordingly, but repay many evils for one evil, and are unwilling to turn away from evil, do good, and live, for these reasons he prescribed for us in the law that we should repay only evil for evil, so that on that day our punishment might be a little lighter than that of someone who repays many evils for one evil. “I gave them commandments that were not good, and laws by which they would not live.” But why do they not even abide by these laws of evil for evil, so that their punishment might be lighter, but instead do many evils in return for one evil, so that their hell will be severe? For our Lord explains and says, “It was said to the people of old, ‘An eye for an eye.’ But I say: if someone strikes you on your cheek, offer him the other, and you will be perfect. And it was said to the people of old, ‘Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: love your enemies and bless those who curse you. And whoever divorces his wife when she has not committed adultery and takes another wife,” he says, “commits adultery.” The scribes said to him, “You are abolishing the law of the Lord God. How, then, are you his Son?” Jesus said to them, “I am not abolishing the law.” They said to him, “Then why did Moses tell us, ‘This is what the Lord says,’ while you say, ‘This is what the Father desires’?” Jesus said to them, “It was because of your hardness of heart that this was said to you.

Otherwise, the Father did not desire you to act this way. But because your ancestors’ hearts were hard, and they would not be content with evil in return for evil, God therefore permitted them this: ‘Let evil in return for evil be enough.’ For the person who was told, ‘An eye for an eye,’ wanted to kill the person who had done wrong and blinded an eye. For this reason God said to him, ‘Let an eye for an eye be enough for you,’ so that his death might be a little easier for him than that of a murderer. What do you say? Was he right to give these laws by which no one lives, or not?” Then they began to understand that they ought to move beyond them, as Jesus said. And in the case of ‘a blow on the cheek for a blow on the cheek,’ he wanted to cut off the hand of the person who had done wrong and struck a cheek, or was ready to deliver a hundred blows on the cheek in return for one. For this reason it was said, ‘Only a blow on the cheek for a blow on the cheek,’ so that it would be easier for him on the day of judgment than for someone who cuts off his fellow’s hand or strikes him a hundred times on the cheek. With skill and ingenuity the Lord restrained them from great wickedness, so that it might be a little easier for them on the day of judgment.

See what is written: “I meditated on the work of your hands, and I reflected on your deeds.” “God,” it says, “your way is holy, free from every evil, and repays good for evil.” Because of the hardness of people's hearts, he prescribed evil in return for evil, as though this were his way, so that he would not make their judgment too severe. As for “wound for wound” and “burn for burn,” a person wanted to inflict many injuries on someone who had done such a thing to him. For this reason he told him: “A burn for a burn and a wound for a wound are enough,” so that his punishment on the day of judgment would be a little lighter than that of someone who inflicts many burns and many wounds. And the person who was told “a life for a life” wanted to kill many people in return for one life. This was so that his punishment and death would be lighter than those of someone who kills many people. And the person who was told, “Hate your enemy,” wanted to kill him. For this reason he told him: “Hate your enemy, then, and do him harm, but do not kill him,” so that his punishment on the day of judgment would be a little lighter than that of murderers.

Again, he said that they should be angry with one another—something that is not good—but, he says, “Do not harm one another and sin.” For it is better for them to be angry without doing harm than to be angry and do harm in their anger, so that they may be better than evildoers. For just as someone who does many good deeds is raised higher, so someone who commits many evil deeds is brought lower. Our Lord Jesus is just in his judgment: he will inflict many punishments on the person who commits much wickedness. But someone whose offense is slight receives few blows. And our Lord is good in his kingdom: he will exalt everyone according to their labor and according to the measure they have attained.

And the person who was told, “Divorce your wife,” was coveting the wives of his neighbors. Because the law did not allow him to divorce his wife and marry another woman—the one he desired— he would kill his wife with poison or by some other means, and go and marry the woman he desired. And in the hardness of his heart, if she had a husband, he would kill him, just as David stumbled and killed Uriah because of his wife. To this person he said: “Put it in writing and dismiss her without guilt, but do not kill her,” so that the death of the person who divorces her would be lighter than that of the person who kills her. And to confirm for you that this is so, this is what is written in Malachi: “I will reject your offerings.” Because I bore witness between you and the wives of your youth, whom you have betrayed, though they are the wives of your covenant. And he confirmed it with you. For people who carry out such judgments are not acquitted; rather, like a deadly poison, these judgments burn those who carry them out, unless they repent and turn away from them, as our Lord said in the Gospel. When he commanded them, this was not what he wanted. Rather, he only reluctantly allowed those stiff-necked people to repay evil with evil. For example, today, if a man becomes angry and strikes someone stronger than himself with a single punch, the other man punches him a hundred times and is not satisfied, or strikes him with a stone and smashes his brains—all because of one punch. Look, a cheek for a cheek, as it is written, would have been better for someone who cannot control himself, rather than striking the other person many blows. And his torment will be severe on the day of judgment unless he repents and turns away from evil. But if someone repented or repents, whether among those of earlier times or those of later times, our Lord has forgiven and does forgive him.

As for the person who was told, “Whenever you insult your father or your mother, bring an offering to the temple,” he commanded him this for a reason. Otherwise, he is certainly not forgiven while he insults his parents, unless he repents and turns away from evil. For he said in the Law itself: “Whoever insults his parents must surely die.” But they gave him this command for the following reason: either because of the loss he would incur, or so that he would feel ashamed before the priest and the congregation, since every day the priest says to him, “Are you not ashamed to strike your parents, who gave you birth and raised you?” And if he insults them again another day and comes to present an offering, the priest and the congregation actually spit in his face. For the reason each person presented his offering was known. The reason for a whole burnt offering and for votive offerings was known, and the reason for a sin offering was known. The priest would ask what the sin was, and only then would he present the offering. This is why he had been told this: so that, either because of his loss or because of the priest and the congregation, he would feel ashamed and would not insult his parents, so that his death might be delayed a little compared with that of someone who actually strikes his parents. For if someone insults and hates his parents and dishonors them, he will surely die.
