But if he becomes angry and does wrong, then repents of his sins and does good things, the Lord has compassion on him because of his mercy.

For when he said that he made both into one covenant and abolished the law of commandments through his commandments, it was so that he might renew everything in one covenant. “From now on,” he says, “not a single letter, a yod, will pass away from the Law and the Prophets.” “As for the rest,” he says, “the entire Law and the Prophets had been appointed until John, to serve and then pass away.” For, it says, whatever has grown old has worn out and is close to destruction. And it says that we are no longer obliged to speak about these things. From now on, that one letter yod remains for him: it consists of ten commandments, which are called yod. This amounts to ten commandments according to the numerical value of the sign. These are the ten commandments that I list here: This is the yod that does not pass away from the Law and the Prophets: Hear, Israel: our Lord and our God is one. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your strength, and with all your soul. And you shall love your neighbor as yourself. You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not give false testimony. This is the letter yod, and look, it is written in the Gospel. From now on, let no one observe those other commandments that have been abolished, or those through which no one lives, which were given because of the people's stubbornness and were given because of their rebelliousness.

As for the rest, these ten commandments are sufficient for human life, for whoever practices them lives through them. For the entire effort of the Law and the Prophets is to bring people to these commandments of this yod, as our Lord said: The whole force of the Law and the Prophets depends on these two commandments, and whoever practices these two commandments fulfills the whole Law, as Paul said: It is all fulfilled in a few words—in this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

But know this, my dear friends: all the beauty of the good commandments that you find in the Law or the Prophets— their force is this: these commandments that are called yod, as our Lord said, that you should love the Lord God, and human beings, who are all children of Adam, who are your neighbors and share your flesh and ancestry. Let us therefore follow the Gospel and the yod, which are one covenant by which people conduct their lives in a new way. But whatever is in the Law and the Prophets apart from this yod is called a covenant of sins, because the covenant of sins was drawn up because of the people's sins.

Therefore, for all those among the people of old who observed this yod in the Spirit, it became a source of praise, as Paul said: In the righteousness of the Law I was blameless—which is the yod. For the Spirit saw their humility and taught them to abandon commandments that were not good, and ordinances through which no one lives, and showed them these commandments on which the force of the Law and the Prophets depends, through which people live. And the Spirit taught them how to observe them in the Spirit. Thus the covenant became a source of praise for them. And all those outside the yod who served in the flesh because of their calling—the Spirit did not teach them to carry out in the spirit the commandments of righteousness and life. Because of sins, they had commandments that were not good, and ordinances by which no one lives: a covenant inscribed because of the sins of the stubborn people.

Listen with an open mind, O hearer of the truth, and see that all the harshness found in the Law and the Prophets is contained in that great commandment: “Love your fellow human being as yourself.” Where have you seen an offender who kills himself when he has done wrong, while he kills his fellow without pity, whether that person has done wrong or not? Whom have you seen, among offenders or among those who have done no wrong, who blinded his own eye, as he blinded his fellow human being’s eye, whether that person had done wrong or not? Whom have you seen who struck himself and publicly shamed himself for having done wrong, as he strikes and publicly shames his fellow human being? Who shows himself no pity, as human beings act toward one another and torment one another? But if we loved our fellow human beings as ourselves, just as we do not do evil to ourselves, neither would we harm our fellow human beings. And if we loved our fellow human beings as ourselves, the good things we would do for ourselves we would likewise do for our fellow human beings. Instead, we want everyone to forgive us, while we exact payment from our fellow human beings without mercy. We have never sharpened a sword and prepared it to strike ourselves. Instead, we prepare armor for ourselves to protect our lives; we prepare a sword for ourselves to strike at the lives of our brothers, our fellow human beings. End of the twenty-second discourse, on ordinances by which those who carry them out do not live.
The twenty-third discourse: On Satan, Pharaoh, and the Israelites.

On Pharaoh and the Israelites: they themselves did wrong of their own accord, and it was not the Lord who constrained them. For the Lord does not prevent anyone from believing in him and doing good, except for the prophets alone, whom he held back from perfection at that time, so that they would be zealous for him. Apart from that, he did not prevent anyone else from doing good, either in the beginning or at the end. For our Lord revealed this so that everyone might know how Adam had been created. Our Lord himself demonstrated in his own person the creation of Adam, and showed how Adam had been like the angels in heaven, without anger, without desire, without thoughts, and without deficiencies, like the likeness in which our Lord himself was born. For our Lord came in Adam’s likeness to show human beings their original nature, how they had been created, as the apostle said: “Everything was renewed afresh in Jesus”—that is to say, as it was before. And our Lord himself made known that Adam had been created pure, in that parable in which his servants came forward and said to him, “Our lord,” “You sowed good seed in your field. Where, then, did the weeds in it come from?” And our Lord said that the field is the world. That is: “You created Adam good. Where did these evil deeds he committed come from within him?” And he said to them: “An enemy did this”—that is, Satan led him astray. For it is written: “Everything that God created was, indeed, very good.”

So God did not make anything hostile. Rather, God created the one who is now an adversary as one of the powers above, and made him one who stood at his right hand. In the same way, he placed Iscariot at his right hand, but he crossed over to the left side of his own will. So too this wicked ruler, because God had given him authority like the Watchers, and had exalted him and made him one who stood at his right hand, acted wickedly in exercising his authority and wanted to become God. The Lord cast him down from heaven to earth. The light departed from him, and he became a child of darkness. His authority over the light was revoked, and his dwelling was in darkness. And as for its being written that God made him to wage war, it is like the statement: “I raised up Pharaoh in opposition,” although it was Satan who raised him up against the Lord, so that he might become his son, like himself. For God did not act unjustly by raising him up in opposition so that he would not obey, and then turning around and killing him. Rather, these words have an interpretation, as when the apostle said that God confined the children of Israel so that they would not obey, although to this day God asks them to obey, and they are unwilling.

He sent his messengers to Pharaoh until the messengers grew weary, but Pharaoh did not obey. Nor did he make Satan so that he would fail to serve his righteousness alongside the angels. Of his own will, Satan wanted to become God, and he fell. Pharaoh died through his own choice. And the children of Israel, of their own will, refused to obey and killed the Son, the Messiah. For this reason Satan is judged justly, not unjustly, and the children of Israel are judged justly, not unjustly. If they did not act wickedly of their own will, they are being judged unjustly, and our God turns out not to be acting justly. Far be it from the Just One to be unjust—he who showed goodness to the wicked and died for them. There could be no injustice in the Just One. Then this would mean that Pharaoh was righteous and the Lord made him crooked, and that the children of Israel were righteous and the Lord made them crooked. Satan did what the Lord commanded him, and remains as he created him, yet the Lord judges him and destroys him in the end. He always calls him an enemy and a rebel, hates him, and condemns him to unquenchable fire and burns him.

If God tells someone to do evil, he does not judge him, because he himself commanded him. But if someone harms another person without our Lord’s command, he is judged according to his deeds. If God had told him to become Satan, he would not have judged him. This is not acceptable to those who have understanding and comprehend with the saints what height, depth, length, and breadth are. As for what Scripture says, “Fear the evil one, because he created him for evil,” this refers to a human being whom our Lord created with his heart full of good things. But he obeyed Satan, who changed his created nature through his evil teaching, filled his heart with every kind of evil, and made him into something different. For this reason he said, “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil person.” He obeyed Satan and became Satan. But the Lord made Satan wage war in this way: he was patient with him and utterly overthrew him when he wanted to be God in heaven, an evil eye in good places, and division amid harmony. And in this way he made him wage war: he knew that he was doing these evil things on earth, yet he did not kill him, but gave that evil one room for repentance. When he stood before our Lord on the mountain, he said to him in the Spirit, “You are to serve the Lord your God with good deeds, but you have not served him.” Nor, even in a book written in ink, did Satan turn back to serve the Lord with good deeds in place of what he himself had failed to do. And if you say that he spoke to him as to a human being in the Law, saying that he should serve the Lord his God, then, as you have said, Satan himself rebelled of his own free will. He did evil things like an evil person, and did not serve the Lord in righteousness like a good person. That is, in the authority above, he had a service to perform and also a law among the angels on high. But he was found to be wicked and unfaithful in his authority, unlike the angels who are faithful.

And finally, worst of all, he wanted to become God, and he was overthrown and fell. In the same way, Iscariot was not faithful in the ministry our Lord gave him, but was a thief, and in the end he rebelled outright. How like his master Satan he was, and not like Jesus! For he accepted Satan’s teaching, not our Lord’s. Our Lord also said, “I chose you, and one of you is Satan.” Satan and Iscariot were therefore fittingly compared with one another. And just as Satan was found among those on the right at the beginning, so at the beginning of the second creation, which is in Jesus, Satan was found among those on the right. For our Lord knew that Iscariot was Satan, and chose him so that through him he might show us how Satan rebelled from the right-hand side in the beginning. For Jesus renewed everything and showed it to us anew.

Thus the Lord’s kindness made Satan an adversary, by giving him room and not killing him. And his kindness made Iscariot betray him, by not breathing on him and destroying him. And if you find it difficult to understand how God watched Satan, yet left him alone, was patient, and tolerated him, while he was plotting these things and carrying them out by his own will, be convinced by this: he knew what Iscariot was plotting and what he was doing, yet did not kill him. Instead, he called him, brought him close, bestowed honor on him, washed his feet, and greeted him with love.

Be convinced also by this: Adam, at Satan’s advice, wanted to become God, yet our Lord did not kill him, because of his loving kindness. Instead, our Lord increased his love still further, had mercy on him, showed him favor, and gave him life. And see also how human beings have rebelled and still rebel against God’s kindness, yet he is patient and does not destroy them. Instead, he takes them by the hand and grants them repentance. And see that human beings not only denied him but even rose up against the Lord, yet because of his mercy he did not erase or destroy their memory.

And if you say, concerning what is said about him, that Satan wanted to become God on earth: he wanted to be God in the days of paganism over the earthly creation of flesh, not over those spiritual beings in heaven. Consider what he said: everything visible is a shadow of what is invisible. But if Satan wanted to make his shadow on earth, it was the shadow of what he wanted to do in heaven. For this is what he did on earth, in that we human beings obeyed him, and he ruled over all who did his will, and he was called God, as it is written: “The god of this world blinded the minds of the wicked, so that they would not believe in the Lord of glory.” As he says: “You are slaves of the one to whom you give an obedient hearing, whether to sin or to righteousness.” And if you say that wickedness was present in Satan by his created nature, because he called him a wicked ruler, do not say such a thing. For if God had created wickedness in him, he would not have hated him in anger, nor would he have reproached him in wrath, nor would the prophet have written by the Spirit in this way: “Everything God created— look, it is very good, and everything, according to its kind, is excellent in its created nature—everything that was created.” Instead, he would have said: “Everything he created is good, except Satan,” if God had created in him wickedness, something that is not good.

It was also in this sense that he said of Pharaoh, “I raised him up in opposition”: for whenever he sent punishment upon him, Pharaoh said to Moses: “Pray that it may pass, and I will comply. I will let you and your people go in peace.” And in this way the Lord hardened him: by listening to him whenever he called upon him through Moses, and by healing the land of its plagues. Thus it was the Lord’s willingness to listen and his patience that hardened Pharaoh. For whenever distress reached him, he humbled himself, but whenever relief came, he became hardened. In sickness he is humbled, but in health he grows stubborn. As someone might say, “I myself made him hold his head high— this man who was sick and whom I healed, who was naked and whom I clothed, who was poor and whom I made rich. And now, look, he stands against me.” This is how the Lord hardened Pharaoh: through the good things he did for him, the mercy he showed him, and the opportunity he gave him to repent. That is why it was written that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he would not obey. That is, Pharaoh grew hard through mercy and through health.

In this same way God shut the Israelites in: through his humility and his lowliness. For Isaiah said, “He was despised and lowly among men. He had no beauty or splendor. We saw that he was despised and lowly, and we considered him a liar.” It was therefore Jesus’ lowliness and humility that shut them in. That is, they despised him and would not obey him. Yet he said that God had shut them in so that they would not obey. But let the reader consider whether he shut them in through his humility or through his harshness. The matter appears as though it involved injustice on God’s part, although God is beyond reproach in all his deeds. His humility, then, shuts no one in; rather, it appeals to them. His harshness, however, drives by force. Our Lord performed all the earlier signs for their sake and said to them, “If I do not do the works of the Lord, do not believe me.” They said, “This is Joseph’s son, and he is a human being like us. We will not believe him.” Our Lord said to them, “At least believe the works themselves, that the Lord has sent me.” Do you see? Was it God who shut them in? Rather, they shut themselves in by despising him because he made himself small and humbled himself. For our Lord came to show humanity humility, and the way and the gate to the spiritual paradise from which Adam departed— the paradise to which Paul was caught up, above the three heavens. His whole purpose in coming, then, was to show humility. He saw that they had shut themselves in because of his humility and were unwilling to obey. When they had wearied him with their wickedness, and he had performed signs but they had not believed, they said to him, “Give us a sign from heaven.” He called them an evil and adulterous generation. He used this expression and others like it to show that he is a judge, not to set an example by it for his chosen ones, but to show that he repays everyone according to their deeds, so that people would not say that he does not call evil deeds to account on the day of judgment, and so treat him with contempt and have no fear of his judgment, and fail to keep his commandments and live.

It is written, “Humiliate them there and kill them before me.” And he said, “You are children of the evil one.” And he said, “Go away into the fire, you accursed,” while commanding us not to use harshness or hateful speech. And he said to them, “I have performed all these signs, and you still ask for a sign for yourselves? So, just as you were not persuaded by the earlier ones, you are not persuaded by the later ones either. But I will give you an insignificant little sign over which you will stumble, because you were not persuaded by the great ones. You have stumbled over the fact that I am humble, because you hate to be humble, to imitate me, and to become my disciples. Furthermore, I will die at your hands, humbling myself, and I will be in the heart of the earth for three days, so that those who believe in me may humble themselves to the point of death, while those who stumble over me may be trapped by my humility, and say with a hard heart, ‘God would not humble himself like this, nor would he die at the hands of the weak creatures he made.’ For they know that no one can overcome the one who overcomes all, but they do not understand that he humbled himself because of the wrongdoing and pride of Adam and his children, to teach them, so that they might return to that original likeness of theirs from which they fell.” End of Discourse Twenty-three, on Satan, Pharaoh, and the Israelites.
Discourse Twenty-four: On Repentance

Now there are people who say that if someone sins after being baptized, there is no room for repentance for that person, citing what the apostle said: “If someone turns aside and sins after receiving the knowledge of the truth, and tasting the sweetness of the world to come, there is no other sacrifice to be offered for that person's sins. Instead,” he says, “the fury of fire awaits, consuming people who have become their own adversaries and have not repented.” And we know that not everyone who is baptized has already received the knowledge of the truth. Rather, those who receive the knowledge of the truth are one in many. The apostle therefore did not say that there is no repentance for them, but that there is no other sacrifice for them. It is as if someone were to say that there is no other God besides the one against whom they sinned, and no other knowledge besides that truth which they knew but in which they did not remain. And they have no place or region apart from this God where they can go to offer another sacrifice to him, unless they return to this God in whom they first believed and offer him that very knowledge and thanksgiving which they used to offer before. He did not say that they would not live, but that they have no other worship except that truth which they knew and from which they turned aside. And if they do not return and offer sacrifices as they did at first, he says, the fire is ready to consume them, since they have become its adversaries to their own harm, and have said, “Now that we have sinned, God will not accept us. One or a hundred—it is all the same.” And evil teaches them to speak this way, so that they will not repent and live, just as it taught Iscariot, and he hanged himself. For if Iscariot had repented, our Lord would have accepted him, because he does not desire anyone’s death, but rather that they should repent and live. And there are people who say, “If a garment is torn and the place is patched, it is noticeable.” “And if a wall is breached and rebuilt, the place is noticeable.” And they break the hearts of those who repent, although we are all repentant, and we all have sins. But let us speak to everyone with discernment: let whoever stands take care not to fall; and whoever has fallen— let us show him repentance and raise him up. “If you keep account of sins, Lord,” it says, “who can stand?”

Have you seen how the Holy Spirit said that if the Lord keeps account of former sins, human beings cannot stand before him? For they all sin, and it is through repentance that they are accepted. For who has overcome sin from his mother’s womb? Rather, people sin and repent, and then overcome sin: those who persist in fighting against it every day, diligently and vigorously. But a repentant person should not be compared to a garment or a wall. Instead, let us compare them to something that goes into fire. For people are baptized in the Spirit, who is love and truth. So if they go astray and sin after being baptized, whenever they repent, love is available to them, so that they may be baptized in it and be cleansed. And just as vessels of gold or silver, or bronze or glass or iron, whenever they are broken, a mortal craftsman puts them into a passing fire and renews them, and their forms are stamped, and they are called new after they have worn out, how much more can God, who is the craftsman’s own craftsman, renew them in fire, which is love, while his Spirit is truth and his water is faith? But if we receive baptism, and these things are not in us, we are baptized for judgment and condemnation. Rather, we ought to be baptized and acquire love and truth and faith. But if we stumble after being baptized and repent, there is the love of Jesus, which is a living fire that cleanses our filth and grime, conceives us and gives us birth anew, and stamps us as before. Nor does the seal that the priests gave us depart from us until our departure. But on the day of departure, a person is led away in whatever condition he is found. And if he has continued in sin until his departure, the owner of the flock removes from him even the mark that the priests gave him, and he is left naked. “Whoever has,” it says, “will be given more, and it will be increased for him.” And whoever does not have righteous deeds, it says, but only that seal. “Even what he has,” he says, “will be taken from him,” like the man who received money to trade with, but went away, wrapped it up, and put it aside without increasing it. Our Lord called him a wicked servant: “Since you knew that I would hold you accountable for the commandments I entrusted to you, you took my covenant on your lips but threw my law behind your back. You were sealed with my name, yet you transgressed all my commandments. I and my apostles pleaded with you every day, but you did not repent. ‘On God’s behalf,’ it says, ‘we beg you: be reconciled to God.’” “Take that money from him,” he says—that is, that seal—“and give it to the one who keeps my words. And throw the wicked servant into darkness and the gnashing of teeth.” You see that the seal of baptism remains even upon the wicked until their departure. For Jesus was waiting for sinners to repent so that he might receive them, as he said: “There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance.”
Let us therefore admonish with discernment those who are healthy, so that they do not grow lax, and those who are sick, so that they make an effort, are healed, and stand without falling.

Again, this is written for married people: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him, and if he is thirsty, give him something to drink.” When you do this, you yourself become greater before our Lord, while it will be hard for the other person unless he repents. But the perfect have no enemy except Satan alone, nor do they possess anything. Is it not clear, then, that this was said to married people? For they are the ones who become angry over their possessions, and they are the ones who have plentiful food with which to feed their enemies.

Again, it says, “If your enemy’s donkey is lying under its load, help him lift it up.” “If his ox goes astray, or if you see anything lost from his possessions, gather it up.” “When you do these things, you will be righteous and holy people to me.” For this is how righteousness does good to everyone who harms it, just as it wishes to receive good even from those with whom it became angry and whom it harmed. It too turns away from evil and does good to the one who does harm. In these matters, too, one person is greater than another: the one who has mercy on his enemy, gathers up his property when it strays, and is reconciled to him; and the one who neither gathers up his property nor does him any harm—that is, who neither does him good nor does him evil. He is better than the one who inflicts severe injuries on him. And the one who inflicts severe injuries on him receives a lighter punishment than the one who actually kills him. But of them all, the one who does him good and is reconciled to him is righteous. For all these, too, everyone is repaid according to their deeds, whether good or evil.

Again, someone who becomes angry commits a lesser offense than someone who strikes another person. And someone who strikes another person receives a lighter punishment than someone who kills him. And someone who becomes angry with a person who has wronged him but is reconciled with him at sunset does not sin like someone who becomes angry with a person who wrongs him and is not reconciled with him at sunset. “If you become angry,” it says, “do not sin.” This means that a righteous person is not permitted to become angry, but must restrain his anger, bear with the person who harms him, allow himself to suffer a little wrong from him, and depart from him in love. Someone who is not reconciled by evening but does not harm his enemy is better than someone who is not reconciled with him and harms him. And someone who harms him and is not reconciled with him suffers a lighter death than someone who is not reconciled with him and kills him. All of them, however, fall away from righteousness. These two, however, deserve death: the person who harms, strikes, or curses another, and the person who kills him. The murderer’s punishment, however, is worse. But if they repent, they will all live. And if they pursue the greater commandments, they will also grow and become perfect.

Someone who gives freely to everyone in need, without asking who is worthy and who is unworthy, has greater love than someone who picks and chooses and gives only to certain people. For someone who gives to the needy, both good and evil, resembles our Lord. Just as he makes his sun rise and sends down his rain upon the righteous and the wicked, upon the good and the evil, so this person makes his love shine upon the good and the evil, upon the righteous and the wicked. Again, our Lord sent his servants and commanded them: “Invite everyone, both good and evil, and let them put on wedding garments, so that my house may be filled with them.” Someone who makes his love shine only upon certain people, however, is better than someone who loves no one at all. And someone who has compassion on no one but harms no one is better than someone who harms, plunders, and defrauds. And someone who harms, plunders, and defrauds suffers a lighter death than someone who kills. But someone who harms no one and does good to everyone is the righteous person who ranks next after the perfect. And if he gives up his possessions and sanctifies himself, he will soon become perfect. But someone who has compassion on everyone, both good and evil, is the blessed person who is much greater than the blessed person who has compassion only on the good. And someone who humbles himself before the good and the evil, and considers them better than himself, is the person who has grown great in the Spirit, the Paraclete, far more than someone who humbles himself before the good and the evil but does not consider them better than himself.

Blessed are the merciful, who show compassion and forgive everyone who wrongs them, for mercy from God will rest upon them. For we are sinners, and if we forgive those who have wronged us, our Lord forgives us for having wronged him. Even though we sinners taste death because of our offenses and shortcomings, we will nevertheless be raised on the day of our Lord. For death consists of sins, offenses, and shortcomings. For a person’s shedding the body is one thing, and tasting death is another. “On the day you transgress my word, you will taste death,” Adam’s Creator told him. That is: “On the day you sin, an evil thought arises in you; and the more you transgress my word, the more it grows, and you die.” For Adam shed his body through the word spoken after he had tasted death. For God said to him, because he had rebelled against the word of his mouth: “I will surely return you to the earth from which you were taken,” when he told him, “You are from dust, and to dust you will return.” “But if you repent, you will live and be raised by my word, like a master.” His mercy is not in proportion to our offenses. For if it were in proportion to our offenses, he would have made us vanish like smoke. Instead, he had mercy on us, and established for us these lesser commandments, which fall short of perfection, on the day Adam transgressed his word and fell from perfection, so that through them we might be righteous until the day when he would come who showed us perfection in his own person. For he said to those who cannot find the strength: “If you do not compel yourselves to attain this perfection, keep these commandments of the righteous people of old, and you will live forever. Let whoever has the strength persevere, enter through the narrow gate, and attain this good and excellent portion. But if someone does not renounce everything he has, let him, while retaining his possessions, act as has been written above for the righteous. Everyone is repaid according to his deeds. But if someone is righteous while remaining with his children and on his inherited property, he is blameless on the day of our Lord. As for the rest, everyone is repaid according to his deeds. End of Discourse Twenty-Four: On Repentance and Forgiveness; on Not Cutting Off Anyone’s Hope; on Mercy; and on How One Person Surpasses Another in Mercy and Love.
Discourse Twenty-Five: On the Voice of God and That of Satan.

Even today the Evil One acts in this way: when someone is inexperienced and wishes to empty himself and become holy, apart from earthly things, he cunningly offers him advice, either secretly or openly. And because that person is inexperienced in discernment and in knowledge of that world above, he does not know how to distinguish the voice of God from that of Satan. The Evil One leads him astray with the many counsels he cunningly offers him, and every single day he changes the snares he sets for him. Even if he recognizes that one, he falls into others. And because he has not grasped the truth, in one of the forms: The evil one leads him astray and binds him to the earth, while that person thinks that he is bound to heaven. For evil has been accustomed, both long ago and today, to bring Adam and his children down from the heights under the appearance of things that seem beautiful.

For long ago it brought Adam down, and only a few individuals ascended to the place from which he had descended, until our Lord called them in his mercy and, with much persuasion, brought back those who listened to him. For God used every means for human beings to live, and God spoke the truth through every kind of mystery. He depicted it in every kind of image through his prophets long ago, until the time when God wished to be reconciled with human beings. He sent his Son, who came and brought about reconciliation between those in heaven and those on earth. In his own person he openly displayed the perfection and holiness of Adam’s original creation, as he said: “Everything was renewed once again in Jesus.” You see that no one openly showed how Adam had been created except Jesus, through his way of life. Therefore, whoever wishes to ascend to Paradise should walk as our Lord walked: humbly, in self-emptying, gently, and in lowliness. For he was good to everyone, and he humbly instructed everyone and helped them. For if someone has no work in heaven, he cannot cease from earthly work. Therefore, when he saw that this was what Adam loved, he allowed him to marry and to be righteous in this world that he loved, so that he might live and not perish altogether. In his mercy our Lord made this possible for us: even though we desired this thing sinfully, we may live in it without sin, if we are righteous.

If, then, the matter is not as I said earlier, why did our Lord, when teaching us holiness and perfection, say that unless someone frees himself from everything on earth, “he cannot become my disciple in holiness,” whereas someone who works the earth righteously is righteous and inherits eternal life, but does not become perfect? And why did the apostles and all who became perfect not desire the earth, or pursue worldly things, or marry? Instead, our Lord instructed them: “Your Father knows that you need food and clothing. But do not worry, because I tell the righteous who work the earth to feed you and clothe you. They live the life of the new world because of you, and they themselves provide for you from their labor, without harming anyone. If it were not for your sake, so that they might live through you, I would rain food and clothing down for you from heaven. And if the whole earth were to pursue perfection and holiness, neither working nor acquiring possessions, I would nourish the whole earth without labor, as in the beginning.” This is how I wanted all human beings to be, but Adam your father brought you into this toil. But if all human beings wanted to be holy, I would have made children for them, just as I made a daughter for Adam from his own body, without sexual union and without desire. Only let no one have any objection or complaint against me. But if they are righteous and work the land, let them harm no one, and let them provide for the needy as I commanded them. They will inherit the kingdom, even if they do not attain perfection.

Even today, under the pretext of something good, evil misleads those who seek holiness and perfection. It holds them back in pride, and they do not rise to the perfection that our Lord showed them. For when our Lord said, “Humble yourselves, free yourselves, and set yourselves apart from the world and from sexual relations; love everyone and come after me. Do not belong to the world, just as I did not belong to it or labor in it. Instead, come after me and be perfect,” the Evil One comes and directs their gaze toward earthly things, so that they will not look toward heavenly things, set their minds on things above, and overcome him. For unless he directs their gaze toward earthly things, he cannot bring them down from perfection. Instead, he holds them back under the pretext of righteous labor, so that, while they are engaged in righteous labor, he may carry out his will in them—even if he cannot do so entirely, at least in some respects. For when they have emptied themselves and become holy, and have turned their gaze toward heavenly things, he cannot fight against them, because they pass above him, while he remains below them. For he is not permitted to pass beyond the firmament, nor to enter that world which is with God, as their own minds pass beyond it and ascend as far as Jerusalem above, as it is written: “He will lead us above death.” And it says, “You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of God in heaven, to the hosts of angels, and to the spirits of those righteous people of old who fell asleep in righteousness, were made perfect in Jesus, and entered the spiritual paradise.”

For the wounds of Adam and his children are healed in this way: when they enter in spirit into that paradise from which their father departed. So even now, since the way to heaven has been opened by Christ, who said, “Leave everything that is visible, and set your minds on things above, not on earthly things. Do not acquire an inheritance on earth, but in heaven, and then you have conquered,” the Evil One comes and offers advice in the guise of good things—things that our Lord commanded only for the righteous. He lies in wait for the perfect person and says, “It is good for you to acquire a little honestly, enough to provide comfort for yourself and for anyone who comes to you. Build yourself a dwelling that is somewhat spacious, so that strangers can come and find rest in it. Plant a small orchard for yourself and make yourself a vegetable garden, so that it may provide for both the healthy and the sick.” Under the pretext of giving relief to the distressed, he uses trickery and brings a person down from that lofty commandment which says to the perfect, “Do not even be concerned about your own life.” And from that commandment, “Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.” And because he has not distinguished one voice from another, and does not understand that these things are commanded for the righteous who belong to the earth, not for someone who seeks heavenly things and perfection, the evil one has turned him, without his realizing it, toward the righteousness that is below perfection. He thinks he is running after perfection, but he is found below it. This is why the apostle said, “Unless I know and distinguish the force of the voice that calls me and raises me to heaven from the voice that brings me down to earth, I am beating the air, like a man who does not realize what he is running for.” “I run,” he says, “in this way: like a man who knows how to distinguish one voice from another.” In this way, then, the evil one deceives him and turns him back toward the earth, as he did to Adam. For although these things are good, it is the righteous peoples of the earth who seek them. For those who belong to heaven, however, they are an obstacle. For all these acts of charity and relief for the distressed— our Lord commanded the righteous who labor on earth to do them, to relieve the distressed and find rest in them. For those who long to belong to heaven should look to those who belong to heaven—that is, to our Lord, his apostles, and the perfect righteous— and they should look to heaven, not to earth, and should not be bound by even a single earthly matter.

“There is no way,” he says, “for a person to serve God in spirit while he is distracted by the affairs of the world. Instead, he must devote himself to pleasing the one who chose him.” Through their prayer and their good teaching, they should go to everyone, good and evil alike, and do good to everyone who is distressed. For see, he commanded those who belong to heaven to do good to everyone through heavenly things. For how do you know, if you say that no one should speak with an empty-headed and misguided person, whether that person will become perfect or righteous? It is as our Lord said to Ananias, “Go and speak with Paul.” Ananias said to our Lord, “My Lord, he is an evil man, and I have heard that he has inflicted suffering on the saints in Jerusalem.” Our Lord said to him, “Go and speak with him, because he is a chosen instrument for me, and you do not know it.” So you too, when you have something to say to anyone, speak, and you are not sinning. “I have made you a watchman,” he says, “to see the coming judgment and warn sinners first, and then the righteous.” When, therefore, the evil one has turned a person away from heavenly things and set him to the labor of righteousness, and he has acquired earthly gardens and orchards, possessions and buildings, the evil one then begins to bring him down even from righteousness. For when he has gone and urged others to harm him, he comes upon that righteous man who has fallen short of perfection without knowing it, to unsettle him and make him evil. And he begins telling him, “They have plundered your house, the one you built with so much hard work.” He goes off to quarrel and argue. There is one benefit he has gained! Again he tells him, “Insatiable oppressors have stripped your plantings and vegetable garden.” And he goes off to fight. There is another benefit that the Evil One advised him to pursue! Again he tells him, “They have attacked your livestock, killed them, and driven them away while they were grazing on your mountain.” Now he wrings his hands and becomes distraught. There is another benefit that the Evil One advised those who belong to heaven to acquire and build!

You have seen how the good things that the Evil One recommends turn into evil things. And unless he perseveres and endures his trial like Job, the Evil One brings him down even from uprightness. For upright people do no harm to anyone. Yet even if an upright person harms no one, the Evil One chokes him with toil and anxiety, and does not allow him to grasp the truth. Unless he finds rest, establishes regular observances for himself, and prays during them, gives alms during them, and fasts during them, as upright people ought to do, he cannot properly follow the path of uprightness. But he cannot reach perfection unless he renounces the world, as our Lord commanded him, takes up the cross, empties himself, humbles himself, becomes holy, and becomes like a servant in his obedience, not like a master giving orders, and loves sinners and the righteous, and desires to give his life for the wicked, like our Lord and his apostles. Then he grasps the height and depth and length and breadth together with the holy ones, who have grasped the Holy One in everything he showed them, through affection, love, and peace toward all human beings, good and evil.

These, then, are the tricks that the Evil One devises against those who become solitaries and want to leave everything behind and ascend to the heights in the footsteps of the one who ascended before them. For those who have chosen a life of uprightness and marriage should use these earthly things to give alms and do good with what they possess, and should be upright in their conduct. And if they wish to renounce the world, as our Lord commanded, and follow in the footsteps of his humility, they will quickly ascend to perfection, because they are not very far from it. For the perfect are like angels, as our Lord said: “Those who are worthy of that resurrection cannot die, but become like angels.” Since, then, they become like angels, anyone who wishes to become perfect ought to imitate the angels themselves. Let us see what the work of angels is. Angels do not work the land. They do not clothe the naked. They do not feed the hungry, and their thoughts do not dwell on earth. Rather, they instruct everyone with the word of our Lord, as each is able to receive it. As they remain constantly before him and serve his majesty, they do not worry about their food, for our Lord cares for them and for everyone. Those who become like angels ought to imitate the angels themselves, and proclaim the word of our Lord, as he commanded them: “Do not worry about food or clothing,” either for themselves or for their brothers, for our Lord cares for them and for everyone. He is concerned to govern his creation. Through the righteous he feeds the needy, while they remain constantly before his majesty like angels. And if everyone wished to leave the earth and come to perfection, our Lord would not hold them back because of food and clothing. Rather, he himself would send down manna, as he sent it down for the Israelites in the desolate wilderness, where there was neither sowing nor harvesting. He himself would make tunics, as he made them for Adam and Eve on the day when they sinned. How much more would he do for us on the day when we resolved to pursue perfection, to follow him and carry out his great will—he who wishes his whole creation to become like the angels in heaven?

For perfection is above heaven, while righteousness is below, on the earth, standing on the border of evil. The righteous constantly suffer at its hands, because they are its neighbors, and their neighbor is cursed. For it says, “The earth is cursed because of you.” For God said to Adam, “Now that you have loved what is on earth and hated what is in heaven, look, it is given to you. Only do not stumble and go down below the earth, descending to Sheol as you descended from heaven to earth. For when you fell from heaven, the earth received you, and you can live on it, even if you do not reach perfection, as long as you toil in this first fall. You have indeed tasted death. Now, if you fall from the earth, you will be cast down into Sheol. You will fall from righteousness and inherit torment, just as you were deprived of the good tree of life, because you tasted an evil thought, came to know evil, and fell from heaven to earth. But if you actually do evil, you will fall from the earth to Sheol.” End of the twenty-fifth discourse.
The Twenty-Sixth Discourse: On the Second Law That the Lord Established for Adam

On the law that the Lord established for Adam after he ate from the tree. “Now, look, I am establishing a law for you concerning this thing that you have loved. This law that I am establishing for you, if you do not transgress it, will keep you from Sheol and give you everlasting life, an inheritance, and resurrection.” And if you defy it as you did the first, you will see Sheol and be tormented. If, then, you keep this law of righteousness and pursue love and perfection, at the end of the years of this world I will reveal myself and bring you to perfection, along with all who pursue love and perfection. And you will enter the spiritual paradise from which you departed. And I will show all who are alive at my coming and after my coming how you were created like the Watchers, and how they may attain that holy state in which you were created. And I will clothe myself in your likeness and show them everything. For after you depart from this world, your children will forget what your creation was like and which tree you ate from. They will imagine your creation, what it was like, and the tree you ate from in all sorts of ways. Only a few individuals will know, until I come and show them plainly what my will was from the beginning. For your children will go astray and fall even from the righteousness that I command you today.

And God said to Adam, when he laid down the latter law for him, on the day when he transgressed the first: “Here are the possessions you loved, while you failed to understand your honor. Acquire as much as you wish, provided that you live righteously. And here is the land you loved, given to you, provided that you do not take what belongs to your neighbor. Here is the labor you sought, given to you, provided that you do not covet the fruit of your neighbor’s labor. Here is the marriage you sought at the evil one’s advice, given to you, provided that you do not desire your neighbor’s wife or take two wives. Your sons must not commit sexual immorality, nor must your daughters become prostitutes. Instruct your children who come after you, and let your children instruct their children, until I come and become for you a model of perfection.

And tell them: When you acquire possessions, do not acquire them as though they were yours forever and forget me. And when you build, do so as people who know that you are not here forever. Rather, know that I will make the earth and everything in it pass away, and there will be judgment and there will be rest. And everyone will be repaid according to their deeds. It is enough, Adam and Eve, that you have fallen from virginity and perfection. Do not fall again, away from uprightness and righteousness. For just as everything beautiful on earth that is visible to bodily eyes stands opposed to perfection, so everything evil that harms a human being or distresses any living creature stands opposed to righteousness.”

After the first commandment, then, Adam and all the righteous people of old stood firm in that righteousness which God commanded Adam. After he transgressed the first command and became earthly. As for the rest of humanity, if they had continued in this righteousness that is recorded, in which Adam and the righteous walked, no other law would have been given until the Lord came and gave this good news that he has now given. For the apostle said that the law was added because of transgression—the law that was given through Moses. Adam and all the upright, the prophets, and the righteous therefore waited for this peace that comes through our Lord. They fell asleep in this hope: that our Lord would come and make peace on earth. When the time approached at which God wished to reveal himself and bring reconciliation and peace on earth, the Spirit pleaded on behalf of all human beings, good and evil, and said: “Remember your word to your servant, through which you gave hope to Adam and all the righteous. Through it they were comforted in their humiliation, because your word gave them life.” And he came whose assurance is true and whose promise is trustworthy, and he brought to perfection those who had left everything, done his will, and pursued love and perfection. They had fallen asleep before his coming, and he brought them into the spiritual paradise, as he had promised. He showed those who came afterward clearly how Adam had been in the beginning. He promised them paradise and ascended from their presence, so that they would leave the earth and follow him.

This good news that Jesus gave is the very command that Adam transgressed and so fell. And the righteousness that Moses and the prophets taught is the very righteousness laid upon Adam after he transgressed the first commandment. The first law became last, and the last became first, just as the last became first and the first last. But for anyone who seeks perfection and loves holiness, holiness of heart comes through these things: he gives everything he has to the needy and rises above what is visible. When a dispute arises against him, he neither takes anyone to court nor makes a claim against anyone. Instead, he loves everyone as a holy person belonging to our Lord, because he makes his love shine upon everyone, like the Father’s sun upon everyone on earth: upon the good and the evil, the righteous and the unjust. End of Discourse 26.
Discourse 27: On the Matter of Raiders

To all whose toil our Lord sees as they imitate his sufferings, he sends someone to show them the way of truth. And if they look to our Lord’s sufferings, receive blows as he received them, and pray for those who strike them, as our Lord prayed for those who struck him and for those who called him a sorcerer, a son of adulterers, and one who leads the people astray; if they offer a greeting of peace to anyone who hands them over to death and wash his feet, as our Lord did for Iscariot; if they act this way and imitate his sufferings, our Lord himself becomes their teacher. And he shows them his way and his gate. Then they become mature and go out, becoming preachers and teachers of Jesus to everyone.

So when we have learned truth, love, and humility, then it is right for us to leave our city for another place. But if they leave their city before they have been weaned from milk, they go away needing a foreign nurse. Perhaps she does not bring them up properly. Perhaps she is not in agreement with the church and makes them followers of other religions or unbelievers. They are led about like little children, and they go astray and die without knowing it. Instead, while they are young, let them remain in their own city, whether male or female, until they can trust themselves to go and come back, so that they do not go away and perish. For there is a good nurse who brings a child up better than its mother. And there is a bad nurse who makes someone either a slave to sin or a slave to her children. Do we not even learn from the world that, while their children are young, they do not let them travel, unless they have entrusted them to someone who will take them along and bring them back? Once they have become adults, then they trust them and send them out alone, and they go and come back without getting lost.

And you, my son, say to yourself: Until you become mature and have established yourself, and know how to go and come back, without becoming a burden on anyone—only then should you go in and out on the way of our Lord Jesus. Otherwise, when you leave the world, someone may abduct you and make you a slave to sin or to other people. But if your parents are wicked and harsh, like Thecla’s parents, do as Thecla did: they beat her, tortured her, and threw her into the fire, yet she did not insult them at all, nor did she carry out the evil wishes they were teaching her. But today the world sits reproaching us, saying, “Now our son or daughter has left for the sake of Christianity, yet even when we said to them, ‘Come and eat,’ they insulted us. And for one harsh word that we say to them as parents, to test whether they have any patience, they answer us with ten evil words. Just because we are people of the world, do we not know how Jesus taught his disciples humility and gentleness?” And they say, “We would gladly work to feed them as we did in their childhood, if only the fruits of perfection could be seen in them.” You see that our parents complain about our harshness, not about our humility. Even when your parents are very harsh and wicked, show them your humility for a year or a month, or even ten days, and then leave. Do you think that when you leave without being humble, you have overcome evil? That is precisely when your [?] increase. When you leave your own people, if you have no humility, sin will corrupt you. But if you resolve in your mind to endure everything that comes upon you—falsehood, oppression, and injustice— when people tell you that you have committed adultery and fathered a child, and you remain silent like a good stone, which receives a hundred axe blows without speaking. Otherwise, do not leave, because you are still a child.

For a grown man endures things greater and more dreadful than these, even if they saw him apart, flog him, and crucify him as they did the apostles. He endures in silence, and his boasting remains between himself and his Lord. But [?] go out. If your parents beat you because of the instruction and the word of God that you went to hear before returning, and curse you, endure them and bow down before them until you become a grown man. By this you test yourself: whether you can endure strangers and go without anxiety, boasting between yourself and our Lord, and saying, “Perhaps, if they beat me where I am going, it is better than my parents and my fellow townspeople beating me: they beat me for instruction and for humility.” In this way you become a grown man, as you carry your own burden and exert your mind through instruction and questions about the word. The humbler you are, the greater you become. And so that you do not say, “He is holding me back,” as our Lord said, “Come after me, emptied of everything visible,” I am certainly not holding you back. I am afraid that you might leave and perish. Rather, I rejoice that today you will learn, and tomorrow you will teach your parents. On the next day your humility will extend to the priests, on the fourth day to the members of the covenant, and on the fifth day to the young men. On the sixth day you will become a new creation, like Adam. You will trade, and your humility will become known to all people. On the seventh day you will rest with the one who called you, in the heavenly Jerusalem. The obstacle to your humbling yourself, knowing the truth, and becoming a father to others comes from you. I advise you out of love, so that you may know what you are heading into; I am not judging you. Be a child of wisdom, understand everything, and pray for me in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For there are teachers today who, when they go to make someone a disciple while he still knows nothing, tell him, “Come, leave.” Once he has left, they tell him, “Go, ask our Lord.” Yet he does not know who our Lord is, nor do they let him learn what the teaching is. Unless our Lord sends him a teacher from somewhere, they leave him idle: he does not know how to pray, and they do not let him learn. He becomes like an inexperienced merchant who does not know how to conduct his business: whatever he gathers, he loses through his inexperience. Perhaps you will say, “God chose the uneducated to put the wise to shame through them.” These uneducated men whom God chose were uneducated in earthly matters but wise in heavenly matters. As it is written: “Because I have not learned book learning, I will enter into the might of the Lord.” That is to say: “Because I rejected earthly wisdom, I will acquire heavenly wisdom.” But I say: Learn our Lord’s sufferings and his humility, and so bind yourselves to his sufferings, whether you are standing or sitting. Bind yourselves to our Lord in heaven. Do not go and be bound with a tether like an animal, knowing nothing, and bind yourselves to the earth. Instead, always be bound to our Lord in heaven, offering sacrifices of knowledge, sometimes as you stand, sometimes as you kneel, sometimes as you walk, and sometimes as you sing in the Holy Spirit. Let no one ever be divided from the church and its priests. It is from the catholic church that the whole truth is known. Let us love even those of other religions and unbelievers, while holding the catholic church in high regard.

When you know how to forgive, then pray and say: “Our Father in heaven, forgive us, as we too have forgiven those who owe us.” Just as Jesus our Lord taught us to love one another and all the children of Adam. And when we know how to act this way and forgive this way, let us go and pray, so that we do not call upon our Lord to our own condemnation. For this is what our Lord’s disciples did, and then they went and prayed, as he told them: “Pray for all people, that they may not enter into temptation.” And as it is written: “Let no foul word come out of your mouths.” [?] Let no one hear a foul word from our mouths, either in our city or in our parents’ home. Let us bow our heads and bow down before everyone. We are obliged to love everyone, as the apostle said: “Owe nothing except to love one another.” And let us know what we owe each person: honor to whom honor is due, reverence to whom reverence is due, a greeting to whom a greeting is due, love to whom love is due, a visit to whom a visit is due, and knowledge to whom knowledge is due. But let us not offer instruction to someone to whom we owe honor and who is greater than we are, lest he become indignant and say: “Are you teaching me?” And let us not offer familiar affection to someone to whom we owe reverence, lest he insult us. And let us not show gloom toward someone to whom we owe familiar affection and distress him. And let us not give a greeting from a distance to someone to whom we owe a visit, lest he complain about us. And let us not linger with someone to whom we owe a greeting, lest he burden us with his accounts and stories. And let us not withdraw from someone to whom we owe knowledge until he is firmly established, so that he does not stumble and perish.

Let us be innocent of evil in this world, and wise in doing every good thing. Let us make peace with everyone and benefit from everyone, and let us benefit everyone. Let us distinguish all the voices of perfection from those of righteousness, and those of righteousness from those of Satan. For this is why our Lord said, “Be wise”: so that we may distinguish one teaching from another and one statement from another, not so that we may drive evil people out from among good people. For it is evil teaching that harms us, not evil people. Even if they kill us, it is to our advantage. End of the twenty-seventh discourse, on the raiding band.
The twenty-eighth discourse, on the human soul: that it is not blood.

Let us now speak about the subject people debate: that a human being contains a created spirit and a created soul. They make the human soul out to be blood, like that of animals, and they say that the soul dies within the body while the spirit leaves it alive. But we show that the soul does not die with the body, but leaves it alive, so that it may be known that this soul is sometimes called “spirit” and sometimes “soul.” By the nature of his creation, a human being consists only of body and soul; and the Holy Spirit of God comes and dwells in him when he keeps his Creator’s commandments, just as from the first day, when God created Adam’s body and soul. Then he breathed into him from his Holy Spirit, and only then did Adam become a living soul. For Isaiah said that he created the human spirit within him. He did not say that he breathed it in, so as to make known that the breath is from the Spirit of the Lord and is not created, just as we also know today that when the Spirit of the Lord is not in a person, that person is rejected, as Paul said. But when that breath dwells in him, then he becomes a living soul, just as on that day when the Lord breathed into him when he created him, just as our Lord breathed his Spirit into the faces of his disciples, so that they might be as Adam was before he sinned. For whenever Adam and his descendants sin, that breath, which is the Spirit of God, departs from them. And when they repent, it comes and dwells in them, in each person according to his capacity, according to the measure of Christ’s gifts, gift by gift.

One person’s gift is great, and another’s is small, according to his measure. Our Lord gives to him according to what his mind is capable of receiving. Therefore, people who have a little of the Holy Spirit in them are neither rejected nor perfect and complete. For unless the vessel of a person’s soul is filled with the Spirit of God, he does not receive the whole of that breath which was from the beginning and become a living soul. And this is the gift with which a person is filled, with nothing lacking in it, which is called the Spirit, the Paraclete. And how do we know that a person has received it? From this: that he has no shortcomings, is full of every good thing, and knows the whole truth. According to the words of our Lord: “I am sending you the Spirit, the Advocate, who will make the whole truth known to you.” So, as soon as a person receives the great gift, which is the Advocate, he knows the whole truth and begins to grow and to root out all his shortcomings. Through the Advocate he is perfected and filled with every good thing, serves in the Spirit, and becomes perfect and acceptable according to our Lord’s will.

The Holy Spirit has many gifts, and one gift is greater than another. “And if you are zealous for the greater gifts,” he says, “I will show you a gift greater than them all.” You see that one thing is superior to another. Yet the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit and the Advocate, is one. And to distinguish the greater gifts from the lesser ones, he calls the Spirit the Advocate and the Holy Spirit, through whose great gift the person who receives it is perfected. But those who receive these lesser gifts are not perfected, because they are lacking. Unless that great gift comes, they are not complete. Rather, each person will be exalted on our Lord’s day according to his deeds and his gift. “You ascended on high,” he says, “and took captives and gave gifts to human beings.” You see that there are many gifts.

The soul, then, is not blood. Rather, it leaves the body, and then the body dies. If the Holy Spirit is in it, it goes with the Spirit to the dwelling of life, to the storehouses of light. But if the Holy Spirit is not in it, it leaves the body alone. When Adam sinned, that breath was taken away from him, and then he tasted death.

Our Lord therefore said: “If two of you agree on earth and keep my words, whatever they ask for in prayer and believe, while keeping my words, they will receive.” These two are the inner person and the outer person, who agree in keeping the commandments. They ask for and receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit from God, and the Spirit mingles with them, and the person is established as a threefold being and lives. And if someone says, “If the Spirit of God was in Adam, why was he foolish, and why did the Spirit not teach him not to listen to the evil one? And why did the evil one deceive him, so that he did not become great as he had told him?” For the Holy Spirit, who is the Lord, said to him on the day he was created: “If you eat from this tree, you will taste death.” That is to say, “If you transgress the commandment and listen to Satan, you will taste death.” You see how the Spirit taught him, but he was unwilling to obey it, just as it teaches us, but we are unwilling to listen to it and follow Satan instead. He deceives us with false promises, in the same way as he deceived Adam.

There are also people who have this outward mind, outward knowledge, outward perception, outward discernment, and outward order, and the outward understanding of their outer person. There are those who perceive and know only this world, and whose discernment, order, and understanding are confined to the visible things here. In short, these people do not see, hear, or understand what the body and flesh cannot hear or see. It is not that they lack inward eyes and ears and inward understanding; rather, they have been blinded by sin and are closed off within. For this reason, such a person neither sees nor hears hidden things. Just as someone whose visible organs are damaged cannot see, hear, or understand the visible things that exist in this world, so also someone whose inward organs are damaged by sin cannot see, hear, or understand the invisible things that belong to that world of truth.

These visible organs are damaged in the following ways: either by God, by wicked people, or by Satan; either through violence or through schemes, or because it is beneficial for that person to be so. Through violence, when someone strikes another person and injures him; through schemes, when someone practices sorcery against him and harms him. A person is injured by the Evil One because he obeys him. By God, he is injured when he is disciplined, because this is beneficial for him. These inward organs can likewise be damaged by the Evil One when a person gives him his obedience and follows his teaching. A human being can also damage the soul’s organs in this way: if the soul is willing to be persuaded, he damages it with his evil teaching. For through evil teaching a person can damage the inward organs; or, if our Lord turns his eyes away on some occasion, a person may harm one of the soul’s senses through sorcery. But God, because he is going to judge human beings, does not damage the inward organs. Even if the outward organs are damaged, the inward ones continue to keep his commandments. But if there is someone whose inward organs God damages, he will not judge him on the day of judgment, because his judgment is just: he will not judge a person without having given him eyes, ears, understanding, and knowledge with which to know and understand him.

For this reason, a person receives the Holy Spirit through baptism, so that he may hear his commandments and keep them in faith. God made two worlds and two forms of service, so that through the visible service the invisible one might be seen. For this reason, the visible covenant resembles the hidden one, and the visible church resembles the hidden one; the visible baptism resembles the hidden one, and the visible food resembles the hidden one. Visible prayer resembles hidden prayer; the visible altar resembles the hidden altar; and visible gifts resemble hidden gifts. In short, the whole ministry on earth resembles the ministry in heaven. And because human beings had not grasped that heavenly ministry, he gave them its likeness on earth, so that, as they stand in the visible church and eat from the visible altar, they may live forever in the hidden church in heaven, and eat from the hidden altar—a ministry that cannot be expressed, one beyond what human mouths can say. That visible ministry resembles the hidden one, and everything that is seen is a pattern of something unseen. This visible thing was formed in the likeness of what is unseen. From the likeness of this visible thing, spiritual people reveal it to anyone who believes and longs to see. “The things that are seen,” the apostle said, “came into being from things that are not seen.” For this reason, God first depicted images of life bodily for the prophets and apostles, and then showed them in spirit the delight that brings perfection.

But because Adam’s household had forgotten the heavenly ministry after they transgressed the commandment—the ministry in which they had served like angels, together with angels— God gave them a visible ministry on earth in the likeness of that heavenly one, so that they would not perish completely. But now, since our Lord has been reconciled, our Lord again reveals it to anyone among Adam’s descendants who longs to minister in heaven in spirit: that is, to anyone who hears his words, leaves the earth and everything visible behind him, and advances in knowledge day by day. Once that person knows this visible ministry, he reveals to him that hidden, heavenly ministry.

Again, he appeared to Moses on the mountain as a human being, and then showed him the ministry of the spirit. Then Moses knew how to minister in spirit and see the glory of the Lord Almighty, as it is written: “The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man speaks with his friend.” He also said to him, “Go down and show the Israelites on the physical earth everything I have shown you. Show them in bodily form the whole ministry of the spirit, just as I showed it to you spiritually on the mountain. You too must show it to them in this way: first bodily, and then in spirit. Teach those who wish to minister in the heavenly tabernacle to minister in the heavenly one. And show those who wish to minister in the earthly tabernacle how to minister on earth.”

You have seen how our Lord revealed himself to all the prophets as a human being, and then they knew how to see and hear spiritually. So today the perfect are immersed as in a mirror, until they see him face to face. And as for all the clothing and food that the perfect need, God does not send manna down to them, so that righteous people who give alms may provide for them. And the pains they experience as they are being perfected: God strikes them so that they may be humbled and not become proud; they plead with him and are healed. And our Lord made them need medical treatment, which Adam did not need, so that they would plead with him and implore him all the more. These are the things the perfect need today, which Adam did not need. Yet this does not deprive them of the spiritual paradise or of the glory of the first Adam, because our Lord told them, “These things will be added to you as well.” They also surpass that original creation, because they suffer and endure at the hands of evil people. For if Adam had not transgressed the commandment, there would have been no evil people. And if someone should say, “Then were those prophets and righteous people who lived before our Lord’s coming— some of whom married women and some of whom acquired possessions—under a curse?” Let no one say anything against them, for they did as the Lord told them throughout all the days of their lives. For look: after Abraham and Sarah had ceased having sexual relations and their bodies were dead to desire, they heard God’s word and resumed sexual relations. Likewise, if God had told him to abstain from his wife while he was young, he would have abstained; or if he had told him to give up his possessions, he would have given them up. Abraham welcomed needy people who did not even believe that God exists. He imitated God, who makes his love shine upon the good and the evil. For everyone has compassion on the good, but no one has compassion on the evil unless his mercy is abundant, like our Lord’s. End of Discourse Twenty-Eight, on the subject of the soul: that it is not blood.
Discourse Twenty-Nine: On Subduing the Body

“I subdue my body and enslave it,” says Paul, “lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected.” “I make my body a slave,” he says, “and subdue it. I do not allow it to dress, put on footwear, eat, or rest as it wishes. I do not allow it to be honored as it wishes, nor even to sleep in luxury. Instead,” he says, “I enslave it through hunger, thirst, nakedness, sleeplessness, and weariness, through ascetic discipline and sorrow, much fasting, much prayer, supplication, and mighty cries, through many bitter tears, humility, endurance, and patience. And I subject my own self,” he says, “to honor everyone like a slave and to stand in attendance before everyone. And that he used to be the first to greet everyone, and that he used to bow his head before everyone. I make it, he says, run on its feet like a slave and go and appease its enemies, even though it has done them no wrong, and bow its head before someone less than itself, just as our Lord bowed his head before John and was baptized by him, although John was less than he was and he had no need of him. The great one received a blessing from the lesser one, who was his own work, whom he had formed, so that he might be our teacher, showing that we too should act this way toward someone who is less than we are and needs us, just as John needed our Lord. And I make it—my body, he says—wash its enemies’ feet and greet its killers, just as our Lord greeted Iscariot and prayed for his killers. And I make it, he says, call other people my father and my mother, my brothers and my sisters, my sons and my daughters, my masters and my fathers, just as the Lord himself called his servants “my brothers.” For he said, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.” And again he said to Iscariot, “Why have you come, my friend?” If, then, he called his betrayer “my friend,” what must he have called those who loved him, and those who gave their lives for him? I take it, he says, where it does not want to go: to those who hate it and those who strike it, just as our Lord used to go and teach those who would crucify him and those who hated him. I make it, he says, visit even a slave of slaves, as everyone’s slave, just as our Lord visited the wicked and the insolent who insulted him, and just as God visited his people for their good, though they acted insolently in their wickedness, killed him, and hated him without cause, as it is written in the Old Testament, “They hated me without cause,” and as it is written in the Gospel, “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.” But to those who received him, he gave authority to become children of God. For this reason Paul himself writes to us, “Judge your bodies, and then eat the Lord’s body and drink his blood.” For whoever, he says, does not discipline his body, judge it, and enslave it until he subdues it and it obeys him, and then eats our Lord’s body and drinks his blood, eats and drinks to his own condemnation, he says. And because, he says, you do not judge your bodies with regard to food, and you do not plead with our Lord to deliver you, for this reason many among you are sick and weak, and many sleep, and many get drunk, indulge in gluttony, and debase themselves, because they do not judge themselves and subdue their bodies.

For although sin became mingled with human beings through the transgression of the commandment and draws them toward acts of frivolity and debasement, of pride and arrogance, of luxury and desires of every kind, of oppression and recklessness, and of drunkenness, laughter, and idle talk, nevertheless human beings themselves also love these base deeds: How, from the beginning, human beings obeyed sin of their own accord and by their own will. For sin itself, knowing that we delight in these deeds, draws us to pursue them, so that people may be caught, while rejoicing, by the very thing they love. For they follow what they love without a struggle. And if Paul had not known that our body becomes an ally of sin, and fights against that little breath of life within our mind, and seeks, together with sin, to kill us completely, so that we will not turn toward the dwelling of life, he would not have said this: “I subdue my body so that it will not drown me together with sin,” which fights against human beings from outside and from within, both sin itself and its kind, the evil spirits. Thus, as it is written, “He craved food,” that is, extravagance and luxuries. But whoever wishes our Lord to dwell within him disciplines his body and serves our Lord with those fruits of the Spirit that are written about in the Apostle. And he guards his body and his soul against those works of the flesh about which he wrote. For the body, in which sin is mingled, finds its rest in the works of the flesh, while the Spirit of God finds rest in its fruits. You see how Paul commands us to judge ourselves until we have the strength within us to keep his commandments and submit to our Lord.

Look, my son, and understand how much power is hidden in the praises of our Lord. Yet we recite them out of habit, not with feeling. For this reason God's words do not produce good deeds within us: we do not give them room in our soul to take root within us. For even pagans are willing to learn our Lord's words as a matter of habit, while they worship in the house of their idols and do the will of demons. For when one of us teaches his brother a psalm and says to him, “Desist from fury and desist from anger,” and neither the teacher takes it to heart nor the pupil understands what his teacher is teaching him, are we not, then, persisting in habit, rather than in feeling and understanding? And because we do not do what we say, [?] we do not know. For this reason the prophet said, “I will meditate in my heart, speak with my mouth, and make my voice heard.” That is, I will understand what I am saying. “As a deer cries out for a stream of water,” he says, “so my soul cries out to you, Lord. My soul thirsts for you, the living God: when shall I come and see your face?” Yet we are not as we teach, nor do we know how to do these things.
