And even if someone reminds us that this is how we ought to act, we do not say, “Yes.” Do not God's words strike us as though striking a lifeless cymbal with no living soul within it? Have we not learned merely by habit, rather than with feeling and inner understanding? When we say, “An evil heart has departed from us, and we have not known evil,” yet we hate one another, so that we do not even return a spoken word or a greeting with our lips to one another, And sometimes we even inflict grievous injuries on one another and repay one another with evil. Has not the truth been hidden from our understanding, so that we do not even learn these words, although we habitually teach them to others? I humbled myself with fasting and prayer; I made sackcloth my clothing, and I ate ashes like bread. My knees grew weak from fasting, and my flesh wasted away for lack of oil. I became a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to my mother's sons. And the people of the world were not worthy of them. They wore sheepskins and goatskins, and they possessed nothing in this passing world. Yet we, who teach these things to others, do not teach ourselves. Instead, we eat meat and drink wine without restraint, while our companions of former times ate ashes and drank their tears as they wept. We wear ornate clothing and adorn ourselves to satisfy our bodily desires, while our companions wore goatskins and unsightly sackcloth. We have possessions and become owners of family estates. We act arrogantly toward strangers, while our companions became strangers and foreigners to their brothers and their fathers, and possessed nothing in this world except meager food and shabby clothing. These teachers of ours in former times were more despised and lowly than everyone else. But we seek to be raised above everyone else. They walked through afflictions, but we want to walk in ease and luxury. When we speak about these things but do not do them, is it not as though we had not learned, since we do not know what we have learned? That is why he said, “Blessed are the people who know your praises. Lord, they will walk in the light of your face; they will rejoice in your name every day, and they will be exalted in your righteousness. For you are the glory of our strength, and by your favor our horn will be exalted.” You see that if we knew and carried out the praises of the Lord, we would already be walking in the light of his face, and rejoicing in the salvation of his name, and our horn would be exalted through the victory of the righteousness of our Lord Jesus Christ. We worship him.

“I ask you,” he says, “my brothers, by the gentleness and humility of Christ, to present your bodies as a living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice in rational worship.” For something that has been killed is called a sacrifice; something that is alive is not called a sacrifice. But because we are put to death while we are alive, we are called a living sacrifice. For the affliction of hunger and thirst, and of eating bread and salt in measured portions: And let him drink water by measure, and let him crucify himself even in regard to bread and water, without satisfying his hunger. Like the example of Ezekiel, who ate and drank by measure and by weight, and was tormented by hunger and thirst without being satisfied. And for a person to wear himself out in prayer, in humility, and in spiritual understanding—these are the body's scourges and its death.

My brothers, listen and understand: there are many fasts that God has commanded human beings to observe, so that they may be helped, humbled, and made better. Therefore, whoever fasts from all foods, turns away from every evil, and does every good deed—his fast is recognized as complete. And if he consumes only bread and water, he advances further. And if he eats bread by weight and drinks water by measure, so that he does not satisfy himself even with dry bread and cold water, he advances further and is purified. And if he also scatters ashes over his bread and eats it, as it is written, “I have eaten ashes like my bread,” while humbling himself before everyone, and making peace with everyone, by these things he greatly breaks down his body, while his spirit is strengthened in our Lord, who has mercy on him and saves him. And if he fasts from fine clothes and from everything he possesses, empties himself of possessions, sanctifies himself, and becomes free from worry, and his mind is on our Lord at all times, by night and by day, our Lord will soon save him and make him perfect. For it is because of lavish foods and fine clothes that people are burdened with worry, are choked, fall away from God, and become unfruitful.

Therefore, just as there are many fasts concerning food, so also those people who fall below these fasts that I have described and are married, whenever they loosen the bonds of injustice, cut through the fetters of deceit, and set the oppressed free, are indeed fasting, as it is written. For this is the fast preferred by God: that a person turn away from evil and eat food, rather than fast from food and do evil. And if a person turns away from evil, gives alms, rescues those in distress, and brings relief to the needy, he advances further and thrives in his fasting, even while eating and drinking well, dressing well, owning property, and living in a lawful marriage. For fasting and prayer restrain a person from evil and urge him to do good. Therefore, whoever turns away from every evil, empties himself of possessions, sanctifies himself, and observes these fasts that I have described above— the person who does this is fasting from the world, and he is able to pray and keep our Lord's commandments. And our Lord gives him strength to live according to his great, acceptable, and perfect will.

Therefore, just as there are many fasts, so there are many indulgences that break these many fasts. For example, someone who craves many foods and many wines, eats greedily, and drinks recklessly: He indulges himself, becomes unruly, and incurs guilt. So too, whoever does as he pleases in his anger indulges himself and incurs guilt. And whoever does as he pleases in adultery, and whoever does as he pleases with fine clothes, and adorns himself to satisfy his bodily desire, indulges himself and incurs guilt. Those who indulge themselves cannot know the truth, nor do they become free people. Rather, even if they do what is good while living in self-indulgence, they are very lowly, and perhaps only with difficulty do they have a place as servants in our Lord’s realm, and not as freed people or as children and heirs. And whoever steals, abuses others, plunders, or oppresses indulges himself and incurs guilt. And through pride, debauchery, and hostility, and through singing, amusement, and chatter, and through laughter and bad habits, a person indulges himself and is judged. And through sorcery, murder, and deceit, a person indulges himself and dies. And through divination, soothsaying, incantations, and everything evil, and through every idle and hateful word, a person indulges himself, incurs guilt, and is blamed. Unless he repents and turns away from these things, he is condemned and judged. But if he refrains from all these things, fasts, and humbles himself, he overcomes and escapes.

For God has no need of our fasts, nor is he harmed by our self-indulgence. Rather, because God knows that through these fasts we return to the abode of our life, and through them we also overcome evil, he therefore commands us to fast diligently. And because our Lord knows that through self-indulgence and excess sin continually gains strength against us, and Satan destroys us, our Lord therefore warns us against self-indulgence and excess, because through them—through self-indulgence and excess—all evil deeds are committed, while through fasting, prayers, and acts of humility all good deeds come about. And when our Lord commands us, “Be constant in prayer,” it is not because our Lord becomes greater through our prayer, but so that we may pray, plead, and ask our Lord to have mercy on us, protect us, and grant us the good things we ask for, and deliver us from all afflictions and rescue us from temptations, as he said, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” But in your grace and mercy, save us and rescue us from the evil one. Glory to him, our Savior and the one who gives us victory, forever and ever. Amen.

Foods themselves are not unclean by nature, nor is a person defiled because they enter his mouth. Rather, the body indulges itself, becomes unruly, and puts into the mouth something that defiles it. A person becomes weighed down by food, and room is made within him for sin. It makes him fall asleep to the truth, eat greedily and drink recklessly, grow fat from luxuries, and kick in rebellion, and forget our Lord and his commandments, as it is written: “Israel grew fat and kicked, and they forgot the Mighty One who redeemed them.” For this reason our Lord commands: “Be careful that your hearts are not weighed down by overeating, drunkenness, and concern for wealth, and you forget the truth, fall asleep to righteousness, neglect my commandments, and become guilty. Wake up and be watchful, for you do not know when the thief is coming. Your enemy Satan is awake and roars like a lion, seeking to swallow you alive.” It is not fine clothes that are unclean, but those who wear them: their eyes become haughty, their hearts swell with pride, they transgress the law and disregard the commandments, and they are condemned on the day of our Lord, who gives life to all. For this reason our Lord said: “This kind of Satan and sin does not come out except through fasting, acts of humility, love, and good works.” For the days when a person fasts are of one kind, and the days when he eats are of another. A person does not turn to prayer and humility except through fasting. A person becomes proud and arrogant only through indulgence in food and fine clothes. For when the body is made strong by food, sin likewise grows strong over the body and the soul through every kind of evil, and the whole person becomes guilty. For when the body is weakened by fasting and acts of humility, the soul is correspondingly strong in spirit and prayer.

So, just as there are many kinds of fasting and also of luxury, there are likewise many acts of humility that overcome sin: you should ask after this person's well-being, bow to this person, honor another, rise before this person, and call this one “my brother” and “my sister,” and these “my father” and “my mother,” and these “my son” and “my daughter”; teach this person, love this one, have compassion on this one, and attach yourself to this one; admonish this person, visit this one, sit with this one, converse with this one, ask this one questions, and answer this one's questions; give relief to another, and be wary of another because he is evil. If you can, honor him so that he may repent and not do evil. Let your humility be known to everyone in its proper measure and order, so that you know to whom you owe each one of these acts of humility, to whom you owe two of them, to whom three or four, and to whom you owe them all: to the one who brings you to perfection and to complete nourishment, as it is written: “Let your humility be known to all people.” And, it says, you should know what you owe each person: to whom a greeting, to whom love and affection, and to whom fear and honor. Owe no one anything except to love one another. And may the Lord of peace be with you, from God our Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ.

So again, my brothers, let us understand that hard-hearted people are many. Just as someone who quarrels or strikes or persecutes certainly hardens himself and incurs guilt, so too whenever someone hates another person, and whenever he becomes angry or envious, boasts or exalts himself, or recoils from a sinful person, and does not rebuke himself in his mind and feel remorse in his soul, remembering that we too are sinners; and whenever he falls into gossip— unless a person guards himself against these things and others like them, he certainly hardens himself and sins. And whenever he begrudges his companion's honor, and whenever he holds a grudge in his heart, and whenever he rebels against instruction, and whenever he despises the word of truth and denies the truth, and whenever he quarrels over things that perish and pass away, and whenever he confirms a rumor from far away without having witnessed or investigated it, and whenever he says something to someone unjustly and without due measure, and whenever he rebukes unjustly or disciplines without mercy, and whenever he strikes in secret and speaks unjustly, and whenever he is unjust and arrogant, and whenever his eye is envious, and whenever he lies and does not keep his word, and whenever he has possessions but gives no relief to someone who needs his help, and whenever he is abusive and fills his mouth with filthy speech, and whenever he does not give honor to someone to whom it is due, and whenever he says ugly things about good people, or mocks the righteous, or slanders the good, and whenever he deceives and maliciously carries tales back and forth, and no one believes him, and whenever he hates strangers and cheats hired workers, and whenever he reveals his companion's secret, and whenever he hates someone or reveals his secret, everyone fears him and flees from him as from a vicious lion. Through all these things and the rest that are like them, a person certainly incurs guilt, is hated and shunned, sins, and is rejected by God and by other people. But whoever has overcome evil and risen above all these things, and is with our Lord in spirit, does every kind of good and has mercy on everyone, good and evil alike, and in his great love has neglected no one, seeking to call him and bring him back to the house of life— blessed is the one who acts this way, for he is with our Lord.

And concerning what the Spirit said through Isaiah: “This is not the fast: for someone to bend his neck like a reed and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath himself. Rather, this is the fast I have chosen: that you untie the bonds of injustice and cut the fetters of deceit.” Scripture did not say that this fasting is not good. For the Lord certainly did not reject sackcloth and ashes, or the person who bends his neck like a reed in hunger and thirst, in poverty, in renunciation of possessions, and in solitude. Rather, through Isaiah the Lord was rebuking hypocrites: For their hearts were full of plots, and plunder and robbery were between their teeth, and they were reducing free people to slavery. They devoured the houses of orphans and widows and did every kind of evil, while ashes and sackcloth lay beneath their feet in a hypocritical display of humility. They hypocritically abstained from bread to make a show before other people. They stooped down, disfigured their faces, and prayed in the streets before people's eyes so that they would appear righteous, while secretly practicing wickedness. The Lord therefore rebuked these hypocrites, who fasted deceitfully and humbled themselves hypocritically, and said: “I do not accept false humility and hypocritical fasting. It is better for a person to eat and drink and wear white clothes than to do evil while fasting and wearing sackcloth, and make everyone cry out because of the evil he commits.”

Moreover, the Lord desires everyone who turns away from all evil and pursues good to fast and humble himself, wear sackcloth, eat ashes, and plead continually until he is saved through our Lord, overcomes every adversity, and finds joy. From this we know that it was hypocrites whom the Lord rebuked through Isaiah. For consider the prophets and apostles who humbled themselves, wore sheepskins and goatskins, wrapped themselves in sackcloth, ate food by weight, drank water by measure, and ate ashes, as it is written: the Lord delighted in them and did not rebuke them, but spoke well of them and exalted them. Likewise, today the Lord desires this of anyone who chooses the solitary life as his portion and loves holiness, and wishes to purify his heart, see the Lord in his glory, become perfect, and dwell in him: that he discipline his body, as Paul said, humble himself, put his body to death, and fast and pray continually, empty himself, become holy, take up his cross, and walk in the sufferings of our Savior. Otherwise, he cannot become worthy of him, become perfect, or attain the portion allotted to the saints in the light.

Moreover, everyone receives in proportion to his labor. He repays everyone according to his deeds and does not deprive anyone who gives a cup of water or a piece of bread of his reward. Not even a single hour that someone fasts with discernment, postponing the time for breaking his fast and praying before eating, goes unrewarded. However very poor someone may be, he is not too poor to give a cup of water or a piece of bread. Nor is anyone who has a home too poor to wash feet, tend the sick, and give strangers lodging. Nor is anyone too poor to offer kind words and a loving greeting, unless he wishes to be wicked. But God sees the eagerness of people who wish to sustain the afflicted out of their own poverty and who endure hardship to keep his commandments. He does them good with visible things and gives them the things that are promised and unseen.

Something shameful is said about a person, either falsely or truthfully. Those who speak these idle words will have to give an account on the day of judgment. They will give up their spirit because of them—both they and those who approve of them and repeat them after their speakers— although they have not seen these things openly or truly examined them. For this reason the righteous guard themselves, so that they do not even speak of what they have seen, lest they cause anyone to stumble because of someone else, and lest they be held accountable for these things on the day of judgment and rebuke. “By your words,” it is said, “you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” And you will give an account of them on the day of judgment. For this reason everyone who fears the coming judgment guards himself against these things, so that he will not be condemned, and flees from many sins. For if nothing concerning the affairs of the kingdom escapes this earthly king and his scribes, how much more will nothing concerning human conduct be forgotten by that heavenly King and that spiritual Scribe, who will rebuke them for everything in order and say: “So-and-so, what did you say about so-and-so? Come, give an account.” And if he says, “I heard it from so-and-so,” no one will accept this from him. Instead he will be told, “Give an account of the statement: why did you confirm it and proclaim it when you had not seen it?”

Again he said through Isaiah: “This is my rest: give rest to the weary.” You see how those who give alms give rest to the weary and give rest to the Lord, and he gives them rest on his great day. Nor does he abandon them in this world, for David said: “I have not seen a righteous person abandoned, nor his descendants lacking bread.” For solitaries, then, abstaining from meat and wine is nothing; rather, they struggle in this way: they do not fill themselves even with dry bread and water, because in this way a person becomes clear, light, and radiant through fasting and prayer, and through the body's afflictions and chastisements. For unless a person, while still alive, dies to the harmful things of this world and its degrading comforts, and to its deadly desires and the condemnable practice of reclining in the places of honor, he cannot be with our Lord when he departs from his body, as Paul said, and as our Lord said: “My way is narrow and difficult.” “Whoever loves me,” he says, “must lose his life for my sake”—that is, he must deny himself all the bodily comforts desired by his lax will. “Whoever loses his life through afflictions will find it, and his heart will rejoice in me,” says the Lord, “and no one will take away his joy.” For this reason the Spirit said through the mouth of David: “Toil forever, and you will live forever and ever and will not see corruption.” Is it, then, in this visible work that he commands us to toil and labor? For we have not been commanded to cut stones, mold bricks, and build buildings that tomorrow will fall or pass away, nor to acquire possessions and lay up treasures on earth that last only a short time. For either we die and our possessions remain on earth, or they pass away and leave us on earth.

My brothers, everyone who does not labor in the service of truth is cast down and debased by ugly desires, even if he wields a hoe every day of his life. But if, while neglecting the service of truth, he does not toil on the land, he falls deeply into deadly desires and is continually condemned. Rather, this is why the Spirit said, “Labor forever.” That is, as long as you are in this world, labor and run and plead with fasting, prayer, keeping vigil, supplication, self-denial, humility, love, holiness, poverty, endurance, sufferings, truth, and understanding, so that you may live forever and ever.

Let us understand, my brothers, and see that we are dead to righteousness and alive in sin, and that we are healthy when it comes to work that passes away, but sick when it comes to work that does not pass away. We labor at it as though being dragged, while we labor at passing things with all our strength. Your bodies are dead to truth, love, and holiness, and we are alive in the falsehood of error [?], although we ought to die to falsehood and desires and live for truth, love, and holiness. Our body is wholly allied with sin and becomes its companion because it tasted death from the beginning through the transgression of the commandment by our father Adam. It strayed from truth, died to good things, and came alive in evil things. Only through great labor does it die to evil things and come alive and become firmly established in good things.

Let us therefore bind ourselves to our Lord and fast and pray until the old person in us is completely gone, outwardly and inwardly. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all people, and may they live. Amen. May his mercy also be upon those who hate us and upon our enemies, and may he forgive us all our sins. May he pour out his grace still more abundantly upon those who love us, and may they reign through his Christ. Amen. And you who read, strive, learn, practice, and teach in our Lord Jesus Christ, remember me in prayer in the name of Jesus Christ. For this is the name through which the Trinity desired that the pains and wounds of Adam and his children should be healed, their stains washed white, and their sins healed. For he is the tree of life in the garden of Eden, through which people come alive from death; this tree is the life-giving Spirit, as Paul said: “At this name of Jesus every knee shall bow, and through it every tongue in heaven and on earth shall give praise.” And this is what we ought to say in our supplication: “Our Lord Jesus, save us from the evil one, and make us according to your will. Our Father in heaven, blessed Jesus Christ, deliver us from temptations and make us according to your acceptable and perfect will.” And because Paul knew that without this name our path does not reach its goal, he therefore commanded us: “Whatever we do in word and deed, do it in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Keep his words, and you will overcome the evil one, and he will deliver you. End of the twenty-ninth discourse, on subduing the body.
The thirtieth discourse: On the commandments of faith and love for solitaries.

On the commandments of faith and love, and on the practices of the solitary life: How a person may know how to pursue love and advance to perfection. Whoever wishes to become a solitary and devote himself entirely to pursuing the commandments of love—the Savior comes to him. For the commandments of love can be distinguished from those of faith, which is less than love. As for the commandments of faith, because faith nurtures all the newborn and the sick, and calls those who do not know God, it therefore commands and warns them to flee from evil people, until they grow, become strong, and distinguish one utterance from another: which is greater and which is lesser, and which is ugly and which is beautiful. In this way faith helps them, even if they keep away from harsh and evil people for a little while. It is beneficial for them to keep away from insolent, disruptive, and dissolute people, and from the sexually immoral, adulterers, and the greedy, so that in their childishness and ignorance they will not be led to follow these people's evil teaching and perish utterly. For this reason faith keeps its disciples away from every brother who behaves very badly, or who has anything unclean in him, until they grow, become strong, and are firmly established. Then they come and become disciples of love, which loves everyone, which is higher than faith and teaches its disciples something that is higher than faith and is not suitable for faith's disciples. For faith commands its disciples, “Keep away from evil people and from every brother who behaves very badly.” For faith knows that its disciples are children and do not yet know how to distinguish which commandments belong to faith and which to love, or how a person rises from love to perfection. And so that they will not become confused and perish, faith lays down a law for them for a little while, until they gain strength and are filled with knowledge. Then faith hands them over to love, so that love may train them in perfection and enable them to acquire that great, acceptable, and perfect mind of Christ.

For the commandments of love are gentler than those of faith, and become all things to all people. But the commandments of faith are stricter than those of love, and flee from evil people. Faith and love, the educators of children, thus appear to be opposed to one another. Faith says to its disciples, “Do not eat with adulterers or with any brother who behaves very badly.” But love teaches its disciples, because it knows that they have strength: I am sending you like lambs among wolves, so that you may be good among the wicked and turn them back. “Be innocent like doves,” he says, “and shrewd like snakes,” so that you may become all things to all people, and know how to speak with everyone: give vegetables to the sick and milk to infants, commandments to the righteous, and solid food to the mature and strong; bear the sickness of the sick, bless those who curse you, love those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you and mistreat you. Resolve in your minds to be like lambs for slaughter, as it is written: “For your sake, our Lord, we die every day, and we have become like sheep for slaughter.” And faith, which knows love, teaches its disciples as though it did not know love. But love knows that wherever its disciples go, they certainly benefit sinners and the wicked, and if they enter the house of dissolute people, they certainly make them chaste, and they certainly make sinners righteous, and they certainly make adulterers holy. And even if they do not benefit them, these disciples of love do not fall away from their steadfastness. Love commands them: “Consider everyone better than yourselves, even though you know in your minds that you are better than that person, so that you may approach everyone and teach everyone. For someone whose understanding is childish, lower yourselves from the commandments of love and teach him the commandments of faith, which is below love. And when you have taught him how to walk rightly in faith, ascend yourselves to perfection, consider him better than yourselves, and give him precedence over you. Greet him and bow down before him as though you were less than he.” Now perfection is bound to love, because it is in love that its structure rises; in love it is completed and perfected, and in love it grows and is glorified. Perfection also teaches the disciples of love something greater and higher, and presents them perfect in Christ, as Paul said. The perfect person, who has loved and become perfect, knows everything, as it is written: “The spiritual person judges everything, but is himself judged by no one,” because he is exalted and rises high. And because this person has loved, he knows everything that he ought to know. Such a person, then, who has loved and become perfect, is able to build up the church, because he knows to whom he should speak the commandments of faith, so that the person may be protected by them and live by them, and to whom he should speak about the commandments of love, so that the person may advance through them, and whom it is right to teach the service of perfection, so that the person may grow in it. For just as solid food is unsuitable for a newborn infant, Thus milk is a burden to someone who has been weaned from the breasts and has tasted solid food. For he said through the prophet, “Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make understand the message? Someone weaned from milk, or someone drawn away from the breasts?” This means, he says, that these are a people who love all the minor commandments, which are milk and limited knowledge. They do not want to come to the greater commandments, which are solid food and knowledge that brings perfection. For this reason, he says, no one can explain to them the whole will of God, which is acceptable and perfect, through which a person knows the whole truth of the new world, and comes to be with the inhabitants of that city of the holy ones, which is Jerusalem above, with our Lord forever and ever.

The disciples of faith, then, stand against the disciples of love, and persecute them without knowledge. The disciples of love endure, as it is written: “Love endures everything and bears everything.” The disciples of faith also suffer at the hands of those who go astray and are persecuted by idol worshippers, because they oppose them; they are killed and become martyrs. For the martyrs of faith are recognizable, and so are those of love. The martyrs of faith are persecuted and killed by idol worshippers and pagans, because they stand firmly against them on account of their evil teaching and tear down their altars. They endure wherever they are persecuted, because, they say, “There must be no worthless idols in the land of the Lord our God. Rather, worship the Lord God, who made heaven and earth and everything in them; worship him alone.” Because of this noble zeal they are killed, yet they do not love their killers and persecutors, but insult them, even though they are dying for our Lord. Some of them have sins, and these are forgiven because they die for our Lord rather than deny him. As for those who have no sins but have not yet been perfected, because they do not love their killers or pray for them, since they do not repay them for the evil they do to them, even when they can, for this reason the martyrs who have no sins are superior to those martyrs who have sins. The martyrs of love, however, are persecuted and killed by members of the household of faith. For because they humbly make disciples of idol worshippers, these do not kill them but rejoice in them. But the members of the household of faith think that through faith they have grasped the whole truth. Whenever a person of love says something hidden from them, they rise up against him and kill him. “Why,” they say, “do you teach something that is not proclaimed throughout the whole congregation?” They do not know that if someone does not love as our Lord and his apostles loved, he does not grasp the whole truth. “He is puffed up without cause by his fleshly mind,” Paul said. But the martyrs of love, who imitate Stephen and the apostles, teach that love is not jealous and does not persecute, does not hate and does not boast, but truly loves everyone and honors everyone. Faith does not command its disciples to kill the wicked, but to flee from them and remove them from their midst. Those who kill, therefore, are not disciples of faith, but disciples of Satan.

My brothers, let each one of us imitate Gamaliel whenever he hears a statement that is hard for him to hear: whether what we hear pleases us or not, let us keep that person away from us, and not kill him and die through killing him. Instead, let us say what Gamaliel said to the people in the Acts of the Twelve Apostles: “Leave these men alone. For if this undertaking is misguided, it will come to nothing, along with those who carry it out. But if it is from God, no one can undo it or put a stop to it.” And let us keep to ourselves. Although the persecution of these martyrs of faith and of these martyrs of love was the same, and the killing of both groups was the same, these martyrs of love are far greater, not only than those martyrs who hate and insult their killers and persecutors, but also than those martyrs who do not hate their killers and persecutors, yet neither love them nor pray for them, nor insult them. For these martyrs of love, while they were being killed, prayed for their killers and persecutors and blessed them in their love, just as our Lord and his apostles did. They are therefore greatly exalted and glorified with our Lord.

These martyrs of faith, however, were killed for our Lord. Some of them hated their killers and persecutors, while others neither hated them nor loved them. All of them died for the name of our Lord rather than deny him. For this reason, their shortcomings are forgiven. Our Lord rewards them for their good deeds. Even if they have no sins, nevertheless, like these martyrs of love and perfection, they cannot become as great, because they have not attained love and perfection as those have. Rather, they remain well below them. But these martyrs of love and perfection, who were killed when they were perfect, Our Lord exalts them above everyone, and they are glorified with him, just as they suffered with him. And if there are people who have loved and become perfect, but have not been killed, they are perfect martyrs like those who were killed, for they too suffer and endure hardships, though no one attacks them and kills them. Likewise, even among the twelve apostles, some died a natural death and escaped without anyone killing them. And perhaps they were greater than those who were killed, just as we know that John, the disciple whom Jesus loved greatly, was great, and it is written that he died a natural death and no one killed him. Was he not, then, as great as those apostles who were killed?

There is peace between the disciples of love and those disciples who serve in perfection. And when they speak with one another, they do not argue about anything. For love does not argue with its teachers; rather, they speak their words persuasively. Whether the disciples of love are able to accept the service of perfection or not, they part from one another in peace, because love reigns over both sides. The understanding of the perfect, however, is rich, and they are greater than the disciples of love, who have not yet attained perfection; they have not yet reached the service of perfection. But when the time comes for them to reach it, through the power of love that brings them to maturity, they accept perfection without argument and are fulfilled in it, grow in it, and are glorified in it through the grace of our Lord, who delivers them from death, which dwells in their bodies and is hidden sin, and from the veil that stands between them and our Lord, which is the hidden darkness, the powers of the enemy. But if the disciples of love do not reach the service of perfection and do not accept it, their love has not yet become rich, and they fall short of the power of the love that loves everyone. But if they wish, they can love more abundantly and acquire the power of love and its understanding; they reach the service of perfection, accept it, and become perfect in it.

The disciple of faith, however, flees from evil people and sinners, because this is what faith teaches him as long as his understanding is immature and deadly sin remains in him, for he does not yet know that he must love evil people and humble himself before them. But the disciple of love, though he knows full well who the evil people are, and the haughty, the arrogant, the boastful, and the sinners, more than anyone else. But love does not allow him to separate them and say to them, “I will not associate with you, and I will not speak.” Rather, he corrects and admonishes. Even if they insult him, beat him, persecute him, and kill him, wherever he sees foolishness and disorder, he cannot refrain from correcting, admonishing, setting things in order, teaching, and stirring things up with patience. But after teaching and correcting, he makes himself small and poor in spirit. He regards those who are less than him as better than himself, bows down to them, and grows in the humility of our Lord. But the disciple of faith, because he cannot yet teach and correct even himself, and has not developed patience, says this: “Why must I teach someone and be insulted?” But the disciples of love despise themselves and say that their soul is wicked, though it is righteous, so that they may love the wicked and honor them, and so that they may love their enemies and pray for them. They are lowly in their thinking, so that they may be fools for Christ and regard evil people as better than themselves, and be good servants to everyone in their love, loving and honoring evil people just as they do good people, just as our Lord, in his love, became a good servant to many, both good and evil, endured their insults, honored them, and prayed for them.

But through discernment the disciples of love distinguish evil people from good people, so that they will not lead them astray, and so that they may repay them with good things in return for evil things. As long as no one leads you astray from our Lord’s way and his love, be innocent as a dove toward everyone, enriching many with knowledge of our Lord’s sufferings and crucifixion. But when someone seeks to lead you astray from our Lord’s love and his sufferings, be shrewd as a snake, so that you do not go astray yourself and lead many astray with you. But the disciples of faith separate evil people from among the good, drive them out, and say to them, “Go away from among the wheat, you weeds, you evildoers! Far be it from us! We will not associate with you or pray with you. You will not stand with us at worship or come among us.”

Listen to me, members of the household of faith, and I will show you how to grow in kindness, as far as greetings, bread, water, clothing, and the washing of feet are concerned. Do not say, “This person is worthy and that person is not worthy.” Instead, whenever you see someone hungry or thirsty, or naked or distressed, whether that person is evil or good, eagerly greet him and give him charity. But when it comes to teaching and the cultivation of understanding, do not say that the teaching of this person and that person is the same, until you have truly examined many things, or that the knowledge of all members of the church is equal. Or do all members of the church teach according to our Lord’s will? Or is everyone’s upbringing the same? But be on your guard until your understanding matures and you know the whole truth as it is, and until you break the power of sin, and until you are trained and know everything. Learn to distinguish one teacher from another and one instructor from another, until you know our Lord’s way and walk in it rightly. But do not give everyone a hearing while you are still immature, so that everyone sows his seed in you and you become mixed with many kinds of seed. For this reason the former law warns: “Be careful: do not wear cloth of mixed materials.” That is, it says, be careful not to accept every teaching, because not everyone’s seed is alike.

For one person sows wheat and is a good teacher. Another sows barley and is deficient in knowledge; another sows the rest of the other kinds of seed that do not enter the storehouses. For it is good wheat that our King gathers into his storehouses of light. And another person sows weeds. And another sows thorns. That is, one teaches falsehood, while another is himself astray and leads those who listen to him astray. So if you give food and clothing to the wicked and the good and greet them, you suffer no harm at all. Instead, you gain great righteousness, for which our Lord will reward you in heaven. But if you give the wicked a hearing and associate with them while your understanding is still immature, you will easily go astray, and your destruction will come quickly. For this reason our Lord said: “Do not throw what is holy to dogs, nor pearls before pigs, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you away from your teaching.” See how our Lord calls the soil that does not know itself a breed of dogs and pigs—that is, the human being who, for the sake of passing gains, makes many masters for himself, namely many teachings or many confidants, and destroys his soul by not entrusting it to the good farmer, who is the true teacher.

A person, then, should not place his trust in everyone; but let his peace extend to everyone, as it is written: “Peace to those far away and to those nearby,” says the Lord, to whom everything belongs. But listen to me, members of the household of faith, and do not conduct yourselves carelessly. When someone teaches you to make peace with the good and the wicked and to give them food and clothing, do not go and associate with the wicked, learn their evil deeds, and die through their way of life. And again, if someone tells you not to associate with evil people or learn their teaching, until you know what the truth is, then, when someone who cares about you tells you to beware of evil people, do not go and become their enemies and persecutors and act wickedly toward them, becoming evil yourselves as well. Instead, if you can, as far as it depends on you, make peace with everyone, especially with members of the household of faith. For no one is allowed to despise any human being, or look down on him, or withhold anything he asks for, if he has what the person asks for and granting that request does not cause distress and hardship. For he said, “Not so that others may have relief while you suffer hardship, but live with equality in this world.”

Conduct yourselves in this way, my children, and see who is upright, honest, sensible, and disciplined, loving and patient, and teaches the truth. Hold fast to him and follow him. Let your feet tread his threshold every day, until you know the truth and properly learn our Lord’s way and manner of life. But as long as you are young, you are not allowed to be all things to everyone and go about with just anyone. That is, while you are growing up, you are not allowed to follow disreputable men or women, but associate with someone who corrects you and disciplines you to keep you from evil, and teaches you to show honor rather than insult, just as our Lord teaches you through his Spirit and his grace to be lambs among wolves and good people among evil people. In your humility, you are allowed to say of yourselves, “We are wicked,” even when you are righteous. But you are not allowed to call anyone else wicked, whether he is wicked or righteous. If, then, our Lord taught with discernment when he taught, and offered each person food that would help his ailment, like a wise physician who knows which food is good and helpful for a sick person, so that he does not eat something unsuitable and his illness grow worse, so too a mature person teaches everyone with discernment: to someone whose understanding is still childish, he gives milk—that is, something small that he can bear. And to someone whose conscience is weak, he gives vegetables, that is, something suited to his conscience. For he says, “With the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. And with those who had no law, I became like a man who has no law, although my heart is within the law of Christ, so that I might also win those who are without law.” And he says, “To those who have reached maturity, I gave solid food.”

For a teacher is allowed to say to one of his disciples, “Go among tax collectors.” and sinners and prostitutes, and among the wicked and the pagans, knowing that he is a good swimmer, and can cross the Euphrates when it is muddy and the sea when it is stormy. But another disciple of his, whom he knows cannot cross even the Little Zab, he commands: “You are not permitted to speak with such-and-such a person, and do not go to such-and-such a place. And beware of tax collectors, sinners, prostitutes, and everyone who is dissolute and reckless and behaves very wickedly. And do not associate with the accursed, the greedy, the debauched, or idol worshipers.” Through one disciple he speaks of love, soundness, and simplicity, and through another disciple he speaks of weakness, doubt, and caution, because he knows that this is beneficial for him. Thus our Lord said to his disciples while they were still immature: “Do not go along the road of the Gentiles.” But after they had [?] the Spirit, the Advocate, he said to them: “Go among the Gentiles and be good among the wicked, and eat whatever they set before you.” He himself used to go among tax collectors, prostitutes, and sinners. But he commands others: “Ask who is worthy, and go to him.” He commanded other disciples of his to love those who hated them and to pray for them. But he commands others: “Consider anyone who does not listen to you as you would tax collectors and pagans.” To others he said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.” But he said to others: “Do not forgive anyone who does not say to you, ‘I repent.’” And Paul commanded his disciples: “Do not eat bread with adulterers, and do not mingle with the wicked.” But he commanded others: “Bear the weakness of the weak, and consider everyone better than yourselves.”

But why is a person unable to make peace with everyone? One reason is that unless his love has grown greater, the law of sin does not allow him to make peace with everyone. Another is that his understanding is deficient: he cannot make peace with everyone, lest, under the pretext of peace, he associate with the wicked and become corrupt, or become closely attached to those who go astray and perish. Again, he commands others: “Work, and then you may eat.” He also commands others: “Be like the dead to the world. Seek the things above and set your minds on the things above, not on earthly things,” along with the many other commandments that our Lord and his apostles gave them, which differ from one another.

Now everything has been explained to us above: likewise, the prophets would sometimes say to their disciples, “Sacrifice bulls, lambs, and young goats to the Lord.” But they would instruct others: “The Lord does not desire sacrifices; he does not eat the flesh of wild oxen or drink the blood of young goats, nor is he pleased with whole burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a humble spirit, and he loves a contrite heart.” And sometimes they would say: “Demand a cheek in exchange for a cheek.” And elsewhere they used to say, “Blessed is the one who took up your yoke in his youth.” He sat alone and was silent because he had accepted your yoke upon himself. He put his mouth in the dust and offered his cheek to the one who struck him. And his life was filled with disgrace. And elsewhere they used to say, “Whoever touches a dead person becomes unclean.” Yet elsewhere they themselves carried Joseph’s bones on their shoulders and did not become unclean. And elsewhere they raised the dead sons of widows to life and did not become unclean. And elsewhere they observed the Sabbath. Yet elsewhere they themselves broke the Sabbath and the observances of the law, and went among the unclean. For the law is not laid down for the righteous and upright, or for the good and virtuous, who establish a good law for themselves and also for those who listen to them. For this reason, the law has no authority over them to judge them, because they do our Lord’s will beyond what is written in the law. But to the others, the sinners over whom the law has authority, they used to say, “If you transgress, you will die.” For they knew that it was beneficial for them to be regarded as subject to the law in this way, because they have no good law in their hearts. And if they were not restrained in this way, the murderous sin hidden in their hearts would kill them.

There are commandments that each individual is permitted to practice, and there are other commandments that most people in the world are not permitted to practice. But those people in whom our Lord dwells, who are filled with his Spirit and have been cleansed of sin, walk as our Lord himself shows them. But those people who have not yet been filled with our Lord, and in whom sin remains, are bound by the law with authority, so that they may not have freedom in everything, because they cannot find the strength for everything unless they have been filled with our Lord and emptied of sin.

But wise and disciplined disciples, who are children of heavenly wisdom, and who want to learn properly, seek out true teachers who resemble our Lord and his apostles, who are his disciples and resemble him in their love, humility, poverty, and self-denial. And when they find teachers like this, they do not disobey the word of their fathers, who are their teachers, just as Timothy obeyed Paul, who wrote to him in a letter even about a cup of wine. For he knew that Timothy would not drink without his command, so he sent him this message: “Drink a little wine because of your frequent illnesses and because of your stomach.” For he knew that Timothy’s body had wasted away and was dead to sin, as it is written: “If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness.” And because he knew that, as long as sin remained in his body, he kept himself from foods and wine, When he had conquered sin, he wrote to him: “Allow yourself a little relief, because your body has died.” We, however, who became disciples only yesterday, while sin still remains in us and our bodies are alive with passing desires, which drown both soul and body, argue: “Look, Paul wrote to Timothy that he should drink wine because of his ailments.” Then we too, when we have developed ailments from much fasting and our knees have grown weak from ascetic discipline, and our bodies have died to sin, just as Timothy’s body had died to evil thoughts, may then drink a little, as it is written, because of our ailments.

We also argue: “Look, our Lord commanded his disciples: ‘When you enter the house of pagans, eat whatever they set before you, and ask no questions.’” To whom did our Lord say this? To those disciples of his who received the Spirit, the Comforter, and were made perfect and filled with the Spirit until it overflowed from them onto others, and whose hearts were pure from sin and full of the grace and righteousness of our Lord Jesus Christ. And when we have been cleansed from sin and filled with grace and righteousness like them, let us eat whatever they set before us—a little, as is proper—and ask no questions. For it is written that the apostles ate vegetables, salt, and olives, and fasted continually. For our Lord wrote this and commanded them: “Take care that your hearts are not weighed down by eating meat, drinking wine, the cares of life, and preoccupation with this passing wealth.” But we sit here, young people whose bodies are alive in sin, and look at old men whose bodies have worn out, who drink a drop of wine because of their ailments, and we say: “We drink just as so-and-so and so-and-so do.” “And what makes so-and-so better than me, when he eats and drinks, goes among wicked people, or so often speaks to women and teaches them?” Because you see him today eating or drinking, or free to speak with everyone, look at him when you were still sucking milk, by night and by day: he was fasting diligently and praying day and night. He struggled and crucified his body to all desires, and reached a good old age, as David said: “There is a good end for upright people.”

Let us rebuke our soul and say to it: “When you have become like so-and-so, have fasted as he fasted, and have died to desires and evil thoughts, and have reached, with a good reputation, the age that so-and-so has reached, then I will allow you to eat and drink with propriety and discipline.” For even those who have advanced in years but are still troubled, and know within themselves that there remains in them sin, and that sin’s power is still strong in them and leads them to improper things— not even they are permitted to indulge in food or to speak with everyone, until they subdue their bodies and their bodies obey them, as Paul said: For he says, “I discipline my body and bring it into submission, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be disqualified.” Rather, let them discipline themselves in their old age, fast, humble themselves, keep vigil, and guard themselves as long as sin remains youthful within them. Even when they have overcome it, let them conduct themselves with a modest appearance and ascetic practices, out of humility, though they have no need to do so, so that they may be an example to their disciples in their deeds as well as in their words, following our Lord’s example, because this is fitting, and so that they may be a good example to those who come after them. For the apostles also did this: although they were dead to sin, they continually fasted, kept vigil, and prayed, and laid up good treasures for their children, as it is written.

But love, because it has conquered death, is not ashamed to rebuke everyone and to speak this way to its disciples: “Jews ask for signs, and Gentiles seek wisdom. But we proclaim Jesus Christ crucified, and we imitate him as he becomes a servant to his disciples and makes himself lower than the creatures he formed.” We are not like these Jews, for whom Christ’s humiliation has become a stumbling block, and who forever ask for signs like people lacking faith; nor are we like these Gentiles who seek wisdom and polished speech, and want to speak of our Lord with grand language and elaborate praises. Because they will not imitate his humility, our Lord’s sufferings and his lowly condition have become contemptible to them. They are ashamed of his humiliation and say, “This is foolishness.” For he said, “Whoever is ashamed of me, of my humility, my conduct, my poverty, and my ascetic way of life, I too will be ashamed of him on that great day when I am revealed in my glory.” Woe to anyone of whom our Lord is ashamed! How ashamed he will be on that great day of our Lord! People like this cannot endure persecution for the cross of Christ. Neither the Jews who ask for signs nor the Gentiles who seek a wisdom empty of suffering and of the love and humility of our Lord can find the heavenly wisdom that is entirely full of the suffering, love, and humility of our Lord. As for the Jews, men of knowledge and love come to them— that love through which perfection and humility grow, and through which the entire structure of the house in heaven is completed— and because they do not perform signs for those who lack faith, they become a stumbling block to them. Let us therefore not be ashamed of our Lord’s sufferings, his humiliation, and his need, as Paul wrote: “Do not be ashamed of Christ’s humiliation, nor of us who are his prisoners.” But look to Jesus, who became the firstborn, the leader, and the perfecter of your faith, and imitate him. And whoever says, “I love Jesus,” should live by his commandments.

There are commandments that our Lord and his apostles laid down for people to keep and live by. Nor is there any instruction to the contrary, that a person should love the wicked or anyone involved in disputes, even a little, because their hearers could not attain the power of that love which loves everyone and makes peace with everyone, which prays for its persecutors and its killers. Instead, they said, “Love the good and those who are more virtuous than you,” for the cultivation of understanding, so that they might learn from the virtuous what is right for them. As long as they do not persecute or kill the wicked, do they not make considerable progress? As long as they do not love everyone or pray for everyone, including their persecutors and their killers, they have nevertheless left behind the former law, which contains commandments that our Lord and the prophets laid down for people. These do not merely restrain them from love, like those of the new covenant, but command them to harm the wicked. In some places they even put them to death, because this was beneficial for their hearers, as was written above concerning these ordinances: no one lives by them, but through them a person's torment is eased a little.

And our Lord was called the firstborn of creation. The apostle did not say this concerning the original creatures, but concerning those creatures that were created anew in him, the Son of God, and were perfected in him. It was of these that the apostle said that the Son of God became their firstborn. For the creatures that existed from the beginning are one kind, and those that have been renewed in our Lord Jesus are another kind. He himself is the creator of the former, and he himself is the renewer of the latter. Everything came into being through him and was created through him, as it is written: “Without him not even one thing came into being.”

For our Lord existed and exists from the time his Father exists—from eternity and forever and ever—and he has no end. But because no human being was perfected until our Lord was perfected before them, although he had no need of it, but did so to teach them how to become perfect, for this reason he calls him the firstborn of the perfect—that is, the first to be perfect. For human beings had fallen short of the perfection in which God created Adam, and of the purity of heart that Adam possessed before he sinned, and of the holiness in which he had been created in the likeness of the angels. The apostle bears witness to this when he says, “In Jesus everything was renewed afresh.” So our Lord came and was perfected, although he had no need of it; he was sanctified, although he had no need of it; and he purified his heart as though it had not been pure. He set an example for human beings, so that they might imitate him and become perfect. He himself became the firstborn of perfection in heaven and on earth. Amen.

Now the great, acceptable, and perfect will of our Lord is this: that all human beings should preserve their bodies in virginity, and that their hearts should be emptied and purified of all the hateful thoughts of sin. And let them imitate our Lord, take up his cross, follow him, and be perfected in his love—he who loves everyone and brings peace to everyone—as he said: “Whoever does not leave everything he has and everything he possesses on earth, his father and mother, his brothers and sisters, his children and his family, and rise above marriage, is not worthy of me.” And truly, my brothers, whoever does not do this is not worthy to be glorified with our Lord. And because our Lord saw that all people fall short of this perfection, since it is acquired through severe hardship, because this gate is very narrow, and a person can enter it only through great hardship, and none attain this share in perfection except a few who exert themselves greatly in humility and patient endurance, and so that the whole world would not be frightened by this hardship, cease to fear him, and perish, our Lord, in his mercy, stooped down and gave other commandments that are lesser and not so demanding. These come after that great commandment, and people can carry them out while remaining in their homes, retaining their possessions, and living with their wives and children.

Now the other commandment, which is below the first, is this: “Live with your father and mother and honor them. Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not give false testimony, and do not covet and take anything that belongs to your neighbor. And whatever you hate others to do to you, do not do to them. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your strength, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and love your neighbor as yourself. Fast on your appointed fasting days and pray at your appointed times, and you will live forever, while retaining your possessions and remaining in your home with your wife and children. But if you wish to attain that great and perfect share, to imitate me and be glorified with me, leave everything, take up your cross, and follow me. Otherwise, you are not worthy of me.”

Understand from this that people will live if they do as they were commanded, fulfilling the will that is below that perfect and exalted will, while retaining their possessions and remaining married. This is shown by the example of our Lord entering the house of Zacchaeus, a sinner, an extortioner, and an evildoer. When our Lord admonished him, he made him a disciple through these very commandments that are below perfection. For he did not say to him, “Unless you leave your wife, your home, and your children, and strip yourself of everything you have, you will not live.” Indeed, Zacchaeus’s words make it clear that our Lord did not admonish him to strip himself of everything, because he knew that Zacchaeus did not have the strength for that great share. For Zacchaeus said, “Whatever I have defrauded anyone of, I repay fourfold, and I give only half my possessions to the poor.” You see, although he did not say to our Lord, “I am leaving everything I have,” our Lord said this to him: “Today life has come to this house, and Zacchaeus shall be called a son of Abraham.” This was when he promised to repay the things he had wrongfully taken to their owners and said, “I am giving only half my possessions.” But someone who gives half his possessions to the poor without wronging anyone— is he not greater than Zacchaeus, who was called righteous? And when he gives two portions of his possessions— does he not become greater still? And someone who gives everything he owns to the poor and to strangers—is he not still more excellent and greater?

Therefore, let no one say that someone cannot live unless he gives up everything he has and follows our Lord. Therefore, if people wish, they can become children of Abraham while retaining their possessions, just as Zacchaeus did. They can also become more excellent and receive something more excellent in the kingdom, as our Lord said to the Jews: If you were Abraham's children, you would do Abraham's deeds, and through Abraham's deeds you would become Abraham's children while remaining with your wives, your children, and your possessions, just as Abraham, while he was with his wife, his children, his servants, and all his property, did no harm to people and delivered them from many evils. He used his possessions to do good to all the people who were in need and encountered him. He lived among them and did good to the good and the wicked, to those who harmed him, and to those who did good to him. Through these things he became an heir in heaven and a fine example for all the generations after him to imitate. For this reason he became great and was glorified. He was called the head of the banquet, so that all the upright and righteous might rest in the embrace of his righteousness.

You see that whoever wishes to imitate [?] and Abraham's hope is called righteous with Abraham's righteousness. For this is what is written in David about people who love material gain, buildings, marriage, and children, and wish to be upright while retaining their inheritance, and to live forever on the day of our Lord. The prophet said this: Lord, who among those who have possessions and a material inheritance will dwell in your tent, and who will reside on your holy mountain? The Lord said to him: Whoever walks blamelessly and acts righteously in his dealings, and does not plan to harm anyone, either in his heart or with his tongue; who accepts no bribe against any human being and harms no one, neither the wicked nor the good, neither the guilty nor the innocent; but speaks honestly, as before God, and settles the lawsuits and disputes that people bring before him. Those who anger God by their evil deeds, it says, are despised in his eyes, so that he will not look to them and imitate their provoking deeds. But those who fear the Lord, it says, he loves and honors. He provides them relief from his possessions and listens to everyone who is distressed and in need. He listens to their words and welcomes them, and [?] in his deeds, and does not lie about anything they ask of him. He does not lend his money at interest, it says, but lends to the poor and takes back from them only the principal of what he lent, without an additional charge. To those who have nothing, he gives for the sake of God, who commanded him: Give, and you will have righteousness in heaven. And our Lord will repay you when this world and everything in it have passed away. And, it says, he does not accept a bribe against the innocent, lest he pervert the judgment of the innocent and die at the judgment on the day of our Lord. Whoever does these things, it says, and is diligent in prayer at its appointed times, and likewise in fasting on its appointed days, will not be shaken on that day of judgment. And whoever is like this, it says, dwells in my tent and resides on my holy mountain, which is the rest prepared for the righteous, says the Lord, the Almighty, who calls to account, judges, and kills the wicked. He gives life, and he forgives everyone who listens to him and does the will of our Lord. For it belongs to him to give life to the repentant or to kill the wicked. The thirtieth discourse is finished. Here end the thirty discourses above in this book, concerning the conduct of perfection and the explanation of our Lord’s commandments, composed by the blessed man who did not disclose his name.
An account concerning this blessed man, who did not wish to write his name and who handed down a wealth of mysteries through his simple teaching.

Since this blessed man did not wish to write his name, and none of the chroniclers has related an account of him, his time has not become known to us precisely, except that we have received by tradition that he was one of the later disciples of the apostles. We have also discerned from his words that he was among the earliest teachers to appear in the Syriac language. And we have understood from his teaching itself that he was no ordinary man.

And so that the greatness and strength of this man of God’s spiritual insights might be clear and readily apparent to the reader, we took care first to bring to light the final section at the end of the volume of his teaching and place it first; we then attach it at the beginning of the volume of his discourses. We did this so that the reader might reflect on this section and learn clearly from it that he was a prophet, that he had received the Spirit, the Advocate, that he had been perfected through keeping the commandments, and that he had been deemed worthy to speak about God, and that through the Holy Spirit he revealed and explained all these mysteries, and that he possessed a great and perfect stature, belonged to the rank of the apostles, and was a companion of the prophets, like those named in Acts: Agabus and his companions.

It was not through human reasoning, nor through instruction received from learned men, that he received this powerful and spiritual teaching that he handed down to us, as the very simplicity of his language, which he did not write in a polished style, makes clear.

And his language is an ancient form of Syriac. Thus, from the simplicity of his language and the power of this section, we have known, discerned, and believed that these things were accomplished through him solely by the power of the Holy Spirit. For he spoke about himself as a prophet in this way: “If anyone says, ‘Where did this man get these things?’ let him know that it is written: ‘The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets.’ And, ‘I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh’—that is, he says, on those who keep our Lord’s commandments and imitate his humility.

For by this he showed that he kept our Lord’s commandments and imitated his humility. And again, he plainly declares about himself: “Do not think that today there are no people who prophesy and speak about God,” along with the other statements of this kind that appear clearly in the first discourse and in this section.

So let this work that we have composed be, for whoever reads it, like an account of his victories, like one of the accounts of these fathers: Gregory the Great, the blessed Basil the Great, and the blessed Evagrius, who is their equal in divine matters.
This, then, is the final section of the final discourse of his teaching:

But if anyone rejects the testimonies of the Scriptures—of the prophets, our Lord, and the apostles—and says, “Who is there who knows that these things are so?” Or if he says, “The prophets and apostles knew, but who today can know that these things are so?” let him remember that it is written: “The spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets.” And let him also remember the prophet through whom the Lord spoke: “In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy.” And let him also remember the other prophet who said: “My heart has poured forth good words; I speak of my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a skilled scribe, who is more beautiful in appearance than other people.”

Do you see how the Lord himself pours out his Spirit in these days, and sons and daughters prophesy— those who keep our Lord’s commandments and imitate his humility? And see how their tongue becomes the pen of a skilled scribe, who is our Lord, beautiful in appearance and glorious beyond all measure. Their tongue becomes his pen, and he writes wonderful ways of life upon it, and they speak to people so that they may know him and keep all his commandments. So do not doubt and say that today there are no people who prophesy and speak about God. And if you say, “I accept the former prophets and the apostles, because the signs that God performed through their hands assure me that he spoke through them,” even if today’s prophets do not perform signs, it is because our Lord does not wish to perform them through their hands, because he is believed in today. For whoever does not believe the former signs will not believe the later ones either. But as for us, through whose hands signs do not take place, let our discourse be accepted on the testimony of the writings of the saints who performed mighty signs. If the prophets, the apostles, and our Lord (whom we worship) are trustworthy to you: They themselves testify through their words that our words are true and agree with theirs.
The final section of this holy man's teaching is finished.
